—that SVez,tern nations have something to learn from China. For example, there is very much to be said for the Chinese rule of filling all public offices by open competition. Again it is part of the ethics of social intercourse in China, that conversation shall be carried on in a subdued tone, that 'the loud laugh which pro- claims the vacant mind" is not to be tolerated, and that neither boasting nor grumbling is to be engaged in. The last prohibition, it is to be feared, would rather handicap conversation among the people who "lick creation" and those ladies who have a tale of woe concerning the shortcomings of the modern domestic servant and their own "often infirmities." This, of course, is only one side of the picture, and, notwithstanding their three thousand precepts of behaviour, it would be easy to find some things in respect of which Chinese manners and, customs leave much to be desired. Politeness to Women.--In London, and the great industrial centres, men and women jostle one with another for seats in trains or tramcars, and the latter are told that as they claim equal opportunities with men, they must expect none of the concessions and courtesy that used to be extended to the weaker sex. But is not this boasted consideration for women like a good many other blessings of the " good old times " something of a myth ? Leigh Hunt whose knowledge of London for the first half of the last century was like Sara Wellers " extensive and peculiar," speaks of the destitution of gallantry among theatre goers of his day. Women he says, would be standing at the side of the pit, but men would not think of offering them a seat' and would often not make room for them when they could. As an epitome to the story, he mentions a man who went out ono night, to stretch his legs, and told a lady that "she might occupy his seat till returned." Politeness to women seems to have been characteristic of the old days,only so long as it cost nothing to offer. A Royal" command."—A "command to play before the King is not often received by music-ball comedians. lhe late Mr. Dan Leno, and also Mr. Albert Chevalier. both had this honour, which was last week extended to Mr. Harry Lauder, who appeared before his majesty at Milford Abbey. A royal "command" is not usually a profitable affair to the recipient, the allpwances being quite out of proportion to the huge salaries of leading artistes of the present day, but the honour is of course, always appreciated by actors and actresses. Mr. Lander, who is now top of the tree on the music-hall stage, is a native of Portobello, and is still on the sunny side of forty. His early life was spent as a working miner, and aftarwards he got a precarious living by appearing at local concerts and sing-songs. His first success was at Belfast and from thence he went to Liverpool, and to London, where he made his first appearance some ten years ago.

div.head: CHESHIRE'S NEW TRAINING COLLEGE.
div.p: CHESHIRE'S NEW TRAINING COLLEGE.
Commencement of Work at Crewe.

At Crewe, on Monday, Colonel Dixon (chairman of the Cheshire County Cheshire) opened a training college for teachers in temporary quarters at the Mechanics' Institute. The County Council's training college and hostel are not likely to be ready for eighteen months or two years. The Rev. J. Grant Bird (chairman of the College Committee) presided. He said that in opening that college, Cheshire was taking a step that would be good, not only for their own county, but for England. (Hear, hen r. ) 6 Colonel Dixon said the Committee thought they saw their way to great success. They were starting work under the rc oat promising auspices. (Applause.) Mr. P. A. I3arnett, H.M. Inspector of Training Colleges, and Dr. Hodgson spoke approvingly of the new departure. Profesor Gonner (Liverpool University) delivered an address to students on the acquisition of the art of teaching, which, he said, was the fundamental ground of all training colleges.

div.head: WOMAN'S REALM.
div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FASHION-HOMg,
THE RETunsrm Fnin.

Slowly but surely frills are returning, says the Queen. In Paris at prbsent one sees them in rather unusual places, high up on short skirts, or forming sleeves, but after so long an abstinence from them, one cannot expect fashionable women to wear them as they used. Otherwise, fashions aro really trying, and the clinging draperies knotted round the figure when not swathed with sashes in all sorts of positions, ex- cept at the waist, are much kss graceful than they mean to be. A SMART AND USEFUL ArTIMIN COAT.

The very smart and useful coat pictured in our sketch is an excellent model for regular autumn wear for walking, travelling, or motor. ing. The original, which was a French model bailing from a very well-known house, was car• ried out in cloth of moderato weight and firm closo weave, and of a very pretty shade of chestnut-brown. Tho coat was cut unusually high at the neck—a sensible style for autumn and winter wear, as it protects the chest from rain and wind. From the neck turned loadik a

simple collar of chestnut velvet, finished with a etrapping of cloth at the edge. A rather deep yoke formed the top of the coat, the yoke sloping down from a little below the throat to a point underneath the arm. The front was single-breasted, and fastened with invisible hoes. and eyes, the outside of the coat being adorned with big brown velvet buttons and heavy velvet loops. Simple sleeves of the regu- lation coat shape finished with neat little velvet cuffs to match the collar. A smart velvet pocket on each side completed this stylish model.

div.head: EXTRAVAGANCE IN DRESS.
div.p: EXTRAVAGANCE IN DRESS.

One of the most characteristic and the most dangerous features of the dress mania is that it sweeps away all distinctions of age and class. Under the present conditions the debutante dresses as extravagantly as the dowager. Save perhaps in the matter of jewels alone, the modern girl's requirements are quite as numer- ous and costly as those of her married friends; while Mrs. Jones, Brown, and Robinson, whose husbands are known to be earning nothing more than a meagre professional pittance, vie in their dress displays with the wife of the multi-million- aire, with whom they find themselves rubbing shoulders as they sup sumptuously and extrava- gantly at the newest restaurant. For since women have become emancipated and have shaken off their burden of domesticity it is an unwritten law of society that the fair sex re- quires to be amused from morning till night. Consequently they go everywhere and see every- thing, an as a matter of course consider them- selves ill-fised if they cannot follow the lead of their fellows and dress so as not only to be in keeping with but to adorn their smart surround- ings. The pity is, remarks Mrs. Hugh Adams in the Daily Graphic, that in spite of the modern extravagance of dress, in spite of the scandalous length of modern dressmakers' bills, English- women never have been, and apparently never will be, able to succeed in achieving a reputation lir being other than badly dressed. They seem to lack the essential daintiness and attention to detail that counts for sartorial perfection. The chief point of failure is that we are ail too fond of imagining that fine feathers make ffae birds.

div.head: SIMPLE AUTUMN SK/11T.
div.p: A SIMPLE AUTUMN SK/11T.

Skirt styles are unusually varied and pretty this autumn. The plain gored or circular de- signs, however, seem to be more popular than the pleated varieties, a convenient thing for the amateur dressmaker, as plain skirts take much lees making than do pleated examples. The neat little model ahewa in our E ketch is smart and up

date, and is quite simple of acbievemeni. This skirt is cut with seven gores, fitting beauti- fully over the hips, and havinF ampls width at the bottom. The front breadtn is finished with tuck seams at either side. producing a becoming panel effect, which is further accentuated by ft TO 17 f buttons down each seam. This design would look well carried out in cloth, tweed, frieze, or cashmere.

div.head: TIIE NEW SLEEVE.
div.p: TIIE NEW SLEEVE.

The new sleeve is a delight to the heart of the thin woman. In general, says "Pepita" in the Mark Lane L's-press, it defines the line of the arm, actually narrowing in at the elbow. Sometimes it is plain, sometinms draped in many "oft folds of a thin material, and the wrist ex- tends in a point over the back of the hand. Sometimes theT whole sleeve is formed of over- lapping folds, like the back of a lobster, each fold falling smoothly over the one beneath. In the coats and tailored costumes the drooping, well-defined shoulder line is emphasised, and even where the sleeves are enormous and partake of the Japanese character the size is in the arm- hole: the fulness is under and across the arm and the shoulder line and outer arm are cling- ing. In many instances this effect is secured by cutting the upper part of the sleeve or the outer part of the sleeve in one with the yoke or body of the coat, but in other models the correct lines are preserved by flat armhole trimming and a sleeve set in without fulness.

div.head: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
div.p: PHOTOGRAPHIC NOTES.
By Veronica.
THE SALON.

This exhibition, which opened on the 11th, will be the main topic of conversation amongst lovers of pictorial photography, and it certainly gives much scope for comment. Politically, it seems likely to be Most important for It seems likely to lead to a drastic re-organisation of its own methods. As it stands, it is almost like .a confession that America leads the world, —the rest nowhere—and 1 can not think that British photographers will settle down to this verdict. Of the 203 pictures, eighty, or more than one third, are con- tributed by four Americans Alvin Langdon Coburn (21), Frank Eugene (10), Edouard Steichen (89) and Clarence H. White (10) ; while four British workers are responsible for a further forty-three, J. Craig Annan (10) Malcolm Arbuthnot (8), Walter Benington (5), and the Baron de Meyer (20). The total number of exhibi- tors is forty-two, E 0 that after deducting these eight men with large numbers, there left thirty-four exhibi- tors with eighty pictures, or an average of little over two each. A. H. Blake, E. G. Boon: Mr. and Mrs. Cadby, Eustace Wand, Reginald Craigie, Charles H. L. Emanuel, Frederick H. Evans, Alexander Keighley, and Mrs. Eva Watson Schutze are amongst those who are represented by only one print each. Of the seventy-five members of the Linked Ring, less that one-third are to be found in the exhibition. THE WORK OF THE YEAR.

As represented by the Salon, the output of the year is very striking, and many of the pictures may fairly be said to be magnificent achievements. But the repre- sentation is of a very partial and contracted field. Malcolm Arbuthnot was undoubtedly the strong man of last year, and again he more than justifies the inclusiotf of eight of his prints. The Baron A. de Meyer, has great variety and marvellous power in his big treatment of subjects which are generally quite commonplace— such as flower and still-life work— and in his subtle treatment of portraits. J. Craig Annan is powerful and reposeful, with good, confident work that satisfies those who wish for definition and detail, as well as those who admire only the subtler qualities.' Walter Benington is in his stronger mood this year, and I think he is at him beet when more tender. Coburn has some very great things—even for him—and his series of autochromes is full of interest.

div.head: GREAT- AMERICANS.
div.p: THE GREAT- AMERICANS.

Edouard F. Steichen, in his best examples, is equal to almost his highest achievement, but I don't think he has anything this year quite equal to his two or three finest works of the past, and a few* are well below his fair level. I refer only to his prints, not to the magnifi- cent antochromes. Clarence White is very welcome back again, and fills his pictures with the old poetry and mystery ; while he co-operates with Alfred Stieglitz in the production of half a dozen studies that are somewhat puzzling and not so satisfying as his own work. Frank Eugene appears strikingly unequal,including two or three commonplace efforts with half a dozen of great interest. The same inequality is noteable in the four prints by Joseph T. Kelley.

div.head: AIITOCHROIVIES.
div.p: THE AIITOCHROIVIES.

In this section, wonderful work is shown. The riotous imagination of Edouard. J. Steichoi revels in weird and startling effects which, however, convince one that he is the master and not the slave of his method. Whether we can, fully appreciate his point of view or not, we can see that a strong individuality has controlled the work. The Baron de Meyer, while less bold, is even MOTO fanciful, delicate and decorative,and some of his studies of flowers and objects-of-art will probably be the most popular and the most lastingly satisfactory of all the autochromes. Alvin Langdon Coburn has a dozen portraits and landscapes, varied and very attractive ; and the smaller exhibits by J. Craig Annan and J.C.Warbnrg show that in autochromy there is ample chance to display personality and individual feeling.

div.head: SOME FOREIGN PHOTOGRAPHERS.
div.p: SOME FOREIGN PHOTOGRAPHERS.

M. Demachy maintains his high level, with notes of uncertainty here and there. Mlle. Laguarde has a small figure study and a landscape quite worthy of her. Mrs. Annie W. Brigman's poetic and dramatic power is qnite individual, free, confident, and unforced, and her nudes in landscape, "The Brook" and "The Thaw" are quite enjoyable. Rudolf Duhrkoop's three portrait studies are at the hest of his style ; Sydney Carter's " Kipling " is good work ; and Mrs. Eva Watson Schutze's "Anna Lisa " makes us regret that there is not more from the same source. Ernest G. Boon's " Diaholo " is one of a most interesting series of essays in treating white translucent draperies in full sunlight.

div.head: MULTI-COLOUR- GUMS.
div.p: MULTI-COLOUR- GUMS.

These great experiments—great in more ways than one—are represented by a couple from the brothers Hofmeister, and a couple from W. H. Miller. They make one feel that although they are intensely interest- ing, and were well worth their places, as experiments, a year or two ago, they must be modified enormously before they will be really satisfactory pictures, and that until they are so modified they scarcely justify their continued inclusion in the shows. THE MINOR BRITISH WORKERS.

It seems curious to class some of the names to be mentioned anon amongst those of "minor" workers, yet the selecting committee has relegated them to that category. Charles H. L.Ernannel's " Curiosity " is an attractive little arrangement of figures against a sunlit wall. J. Dudley Johnston's two city scenes are good, and up-to-date. Mrs. Caleb Keene has two fine virile portrait studies of peasants, and Frederick H. Evans' single piece of architecture tills one with regret that there are not more. A. H. Blake, M.A., has only one print accepted, yet this year he has been prolific and ve-y strong. Mr. and Mrs. Cadby have one print each, and Miss Lilian E. Bland enters the salon for the first time, with three curiouPimpressions of fighting cocks. E. Warner, Harold Jacob, Reginald Craigie, Eustace Calland, and Dr. Evershed, each have their one or two worthy works ; Alexander Keighley, who has hitherto been strongly represented, and who has done much excellent work, this year has only one print. Archibald Cochrane boldly plunging into the broadest " gum" effecta, has four large pictures hunt' wh of ich " Horses Drinking," and "The Lost Piece of Silver" are equal to anything he has dune, and quite amongst the great things of this present exhibition.

Found Dead in Field. Mr. F. A. Jones (deputy coroner) held an inquest at ' the Police Station on Monday afternoon on the body of Walter Smith Cant, aged 32 y eats, of no settled address. Deceased was found lying dead in a field at Howley on Friday afternoon with a''bottle by his side. It was stated that he was subject to fits.— Dr. Smith said be had examined the contents of the bottle and there was no doubt that it contained laudanum. He had made a post-mortem examination of the body and found that there were no marks of violence, but there were a few scratches on the face. If the deceased had taken any laudanum it must have been a small and not a poisonous dose, and absorbed into the system before death took place. If he had taken a poisonous dose, he should have expected to have found some laudanum in his stomach. Internally all the organs of the body were generally healthy. He was of the opinion that death was due to suffocation, this being due to an epileptic fit,—The jury returned a verdict in acc)rn- once with the medical evidence.

div.head: DAY OF RECKONING.
div.p: THE DAY OF RECKONING.
(ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.)
BY ANNIE 0. TIBBITS,
Author of "The Love that Won," •" The Lead- ing Lady," "False Heart and True," "Robes of shame," "Whose Hand?"

Sjj James Fairfax sat in the great hail at ArEley Court, staring dully, almost stupidly, at his son, who .stood before him. Outside the heat was intense. Inside, behind the cool, grey stone walls, it seemed always cold; yet § ir James wiped the perspiration from his forehead as he faced his son.
"You cannot mean it, Jack," he cried.

Jack stood upright. "Father, I do," he said. " I can't help it. I meant to do other things, but I can't help this. I love her so, and nothing else seems to count, and in birthday to-morrow---" Sir James groaned a little. "Your coming of age! '; he cried, "and what a coming of age—to marry a school teacher—is nobody—you--" He broke off. In the dark shadows of the hall his face grew suddenly grey. Hit lips twitched as he looked up at his son. "She is that new girl of course—the girl the Vicar unearthed from some London slum. I re- member I have seen her once or twice. It was she who came and bearded me about old Simp- son's cottage, and thought me a ruffian. Yes, _I remember."

He broke off, with a queer look upon his lace, as though some recollection pained him. His face, always grey and drawn, seemed to look older and more drawn to his son as he faced him. People said that old Sir James Fairfax had aged very much during the past twelve months, and they added that it would not be long before his son succeeded him if he did not improve. To-dty, with the twilight settling upon the great stone hall, it lgoked almost as if the hand of death rested upon him. He sat stiffly in his chair, staring gut across the hall to the window and the garden, whaich stretched out- side, dark and gloomy, and 7 full of shadow. The lamps had not been brought in yet, and Jack Fairfax could not see distinctly the expres- siOn on his father's face.

"Her name?" Sir James said, suddenly. "What did you say her name was'?" "Mildred Davenport," Jack replied. Sir James gave a start, and Jack looked at him in surprise. "What Davenport?", the old man asked, harshly. "Where does she come from? Who was her father?" Jack shook his head. He did not know. When he thought of it he knew very little about Mildred Davenport—so little that now, when he was confronted with the question, a strange sort of cold swept over him. "I don't knoW," he said. "I never asked. She told me that she was brought up with an aunt until she died, and then she went out as a governess. That was three years ago."

Three years ago!" Sir James echoed his son's words in a strange, hollow voice, "and her father?" he added. " Does she know nothing about her father? Nothing, lad? Do you meap to say no one ever spoke about him— never told, her what or who he was?"

Tack shook his head again. "No," he said, "but she did tell me this, that her aunt when she was dying seemed dis- tressed about something, and kept begging her forgiveness. 'I did it for the best, my dear,' she said. 'Oh! child, I did it for the best.' What she meant Mildred did not know, could not find out. There had never been any mystery about her life. Her aunt had told her that her mother had died when she was less than two years old, and her father before that, and that was all. And what she meant by her', dying cry Mildred was worried to know. There was no explanation." " Ah! "

Jack stopped to look at hi l father. He was sitting strangely rigid, with his eyes still fixed ,on the shadowy garden outside. Once or twice his lips moved, but no sound came from them, and Jack bent towards him.

"Father, I know you were ambitious for me," he said, " and , wanted me to marry an aristocrat. I meant to do as you wished, but since Mildred has been in Warley I can't. I can't get her face out of my heart! I love her, father, and, if you are convinced that she is sweet and good and true, you will not mind after all, will you 3" Sir James jerked his eyes from the window and looked round. His face had grown hard suddenly. His grey eyes blazed. "Mind?" he cried, hoarsely. "Mind? I'd disinherit you if I could. I'd turn you out of house and home if I could. Mind? I hate her. I shall always hate her. I know you will marry her. It is Fate. I knew some blow would fall some day. I have waited for .1. expected it, and now—now—" _

He stopped to look round again. The shadows were deepening. In a few minutes the butler would appear with the lamps to draw the cur- tains, and shut out the hot night. In a few moments Jack, his son, would see his face in the light with the terror and fear upon it. He rose hastily to his feet. "Why did you wait until to-night to tell me?" he asked. "Why have I been blind all this time? Somehow the girl, her face, haunted me for a long time, and yet—it was absurd, of course—absurd that it should cling as it did. I—l might have known." He paced 'slowly across the hall, and Jack, watching him, felt curiously uneasy. His father had taken his announcement in a way quite dif- ferent from what he expected. He had expected an outburst of rage and defiant opposition. And, instead of that, Sir James had accepted it calmly—even though he hated it—accepted it as being something he could not help—soma Fate from which he had tried to escape in vain. "Father, you will not speak like that when you know her," Jack cried. "You will like her. Everybody likes her. She has only been here six months, and they all know and worship her." "Only six months." Once more Sir James's voice came like a dull echo of his son's. He had stopped in the middle of the floor, and Jack saw that his hands were twitching. "That is all," Jack said, but I have seen her often and I know she is as good and true as sho looks, even though we don't know anything about her people, and I know you will like her. Father, rnayrshe come and see you—may I bring her here? " He took a step or two towards Sir James, and brought up so that he faced him. "Father, I wish you would see her," he added. "I wish you would see for yourself.---" He broke off quite suddenly. Sir James had given a queer, broken, husky gasp for breath. His face had grown, in a strange, rapid way, grey and ghastly. With a shaking finger he pointed to the window. "Great, heaven! Jack, he is there! Jack wheeled round sharply on his heel. For one brief moment he fancied ho saw a man's face pressed against the window, but at that very instant the door opened arid the butler en- tered with a lamp, and as the light flickered over the room the face vanished. Sir James rocked sharply on his feet and fell. Jack dropped to his knees beside him, and the butler, putting down the lamp, hurried forward. Jack bent over Sir James and caught tho faint whisper that fell from his lips. • " Tho day, of reckoning," ho was saying under his breath, it has come."

IL Why had he come back? Henry Thorpe turned to look once more at the old stone house as he reached the bend in the drive which would take him out of sight of Arkley Court, and then hurried on. Why had he come back? Why, after all the years that had passed, the shame and disgrace and the bitter pain—why had he come back? Why had he gone up to the old house and looked in? It had drawn him like a magnet—dragged him back after all those years—lured him up under the old trees to look into the face of 'his enemy! Why? His face was grey arid set as ho hurried on. He was a strange-looking man. His hair was white and his face was lined, and yet he had the air of a man who was younger. than he looked. He was like a man aged before his time, and more than one person stopped to look at him be- fore he reaChed the house in which he had lodgings. A ,girt stood on the dpor-sten. She looked round as he came up, and smiled at him. "I bum you," she said. "You aro the new lodger." Henry Thorpe stood quite still. Into his face had come a strange look, into his eyes a strange light. He thought he had never seen a more beautiful face; but he was indifferent to beauti- ful faces, and yet—why did his heart stop? Why did a strange feeling—a passionate longing for a dead woman—seize upon him then? Ha stared into Mildred Davenport's face as though he had been suddenly confronted with something he had forgotten. . "And you?" he asked, huskily, after a minute. "Oh! I," she answered, "I am only Mildred Davenport, the governess. I lodge here too." Henry Thorpe gave a sudden queer gasp for breath. " Davenport ! " he cried. "For heaven's anla where -do you come from? Who are you? What brings you here of all places in the world?" Mildred drew back, a little startled, and her mew f§c9 grew white as she looked hit° his. Zip

was trembling all over, shaken as though by palsy. Perspiration stood out upon his forehead in big drops. "What brings you hero," h? repeated, "of all places in the world?" Mildred hesitated for a moment, half fright- ened by his strange manner and the grey look of his face.. Then she smiled. Ho was mad, no doubt, and she had heard that the best way to treat a madman was to humour him. "Well, really I don't know,"- sho said, "ex- cept that there was an opening hero for • governess, and I was lucky enough to get the post. I had not been well in London, and the doctor stiid I ought to have country air. That is why I came." "London!" Henry Thorpe passed his shak- ing hand across his eyes as though they had de- ceived him. "So you—so you had lived in Low don all your life?" "Yes," she nodded her head gaily. my life until I came here.'-' Henry Thorpe stared at her again, with the startled look in his eyes giving way to some- thing different. He ,drew himself up, as the-ugh conscious of a blunder. He steeled him- self to look at her calmly: and his face set a little. Yet her face; bright and sweet in the creeping twilight, was like a dream to him, and in those few moments his lifo seemed to have gone back twenty years. But before she had turned to open the door he had recovered himself. "I Was taken aback," lie said, "for your face reminded me of—of someone who died years ago. It reminded me so much that I—that I almost thought she had come to life again." Mildred looked 'it him quickly, and her face softened. She. put out her hands. "Oh, I see-d understand," she said,. softly: "Likenesses are strange sometimes." Yes," he answered, very strange—yea, very strange, and you are incredibly like. Do you mind telling me something about yourself ? " She turned quicklep and pushed- open the doer. "Came into my sitting-room," she said, "and I'll tell you anything you like." Afteievards she _v:eridered why she did it, but so:nething in his face touched her, and five Minutes later he was sitting watching her while she lighted the lamp. "I suppose," he said after a few minutes, "that your father and mother are dead?" "Yes," she replied, "they died when I was qeito a baby—father first, and mother when 1 v:as about two years old, so that I remember neither of them.' " Ah!" •be stared at her still curiously. "I was brought up by an aunt," she went on, slewly ; "she was both mother and father to me until she died. Poor aunt!" ' " Her name?" said the man, hoarsely. Mildred was fumbling About the mantelpiece, and as be spoke she turned with a couple of photographs in her band. " That is my aunt," she said, holding out one to Henry Thorpe. Her, name was Ellen Davenport. And this is my mother." If his manner 'had astonished her before it. sur- prised her more ms. He almost snatched her mother's photograph from her and sat holditig it. looking down at it so long that she grew more bewildered than ever. ' When he handed it back to her his face looked grey and drawn' and strangely old. " Does she—does her face remind you too?' he asked, softly. • He rose suddenly. • "Yes," he answered, hoarsely. "It reminds me—it reminds me of something I had almost forgotten—of a purpose I have to accomplish. It reminds me—oh, heavens! it reminds me that I have to make someone pay for all I have suffered." Ile passed his hand across his faces and she watched him almost nervously. Who was he? What was he? And what did he mean? She opened her lips to speak, :but stopped abruptly. Another photograph had caught his attention. and before she had time to speak he had turned and looked" at her questioningly. A -flush sprang to her cheeks, and the.word s faltered on . her lins. Decidedly he was curious, this Henry Thorpe. "Forgive me for asking" he said, "but are you engaged? I know it as impertinent, but tell e • me.
"Yes, ati

She did not answer" for a minute, then she lifted her kead and looked him squarely in tho eyos. "Yes," she said. "I am. lam engaged to that young man, and he is the son of Sir James Fairfax of Arkley Court." The photograph dropped sharply from Henry Thorpe's fingers. A sudden Swift grey spread over his face. "You are—engaged to him'?" he Said, un- steadily. • The flush deepened ,on Mildred's face. 'Why not?" she asked. Henry. Thorpe turned awry. Forgive rue," he 'said, and crossing the room let himself out wikhout another word. Hr. "But who is he? Where does he come from? Why does he want to take the Red House?" Sir James Fairfax's voice Caine weak and trembling from the bed. "I don't like the sound of him, Jack." he said. "But that- is merely weakness," cried Jack. "It would be folly to refuse a, tenant for tho Red House. It has been unlet. for so long, and he has the money, and if we don't like him we can turn him out. Ho only wants it for a short term." Sir James stared uneasily across tho great room in which he lay. "I don't like it,. Jack," he said: "I must see him myself. Send him here to me." "Rut you are not fit yet," cried Jack. "Why • not let him take the house, and if you object when you are Well again we can turn him out." Sir 'James did not speak for a moment. When he did he asked a curious question. Has .any stranger been seen in the neigh- bourhood lately?" he -asked. . "Why, no," Jack replied. "Why do you ask?" Once more, as on the night when he had been stricken by illness, a queer haunled look came info Sir James's eyesiz But only for a moment. The next it bad gone. "Never mind," he said. "Never mind. When I am better I will see this man myself. What did you say his name was?" "Thorpe—Henry Thorpe," said Jack. Sir James repeated it with unsteady lips. "I must see him for myself," he muttered. Jack went downstairs slilhtly puzzled, and there was a somewhat anxious look on his face as lie crossed the. park. On the other side stood the Red House—a gaunt, ugly building of rod brick and atone; It was in, the park but not of it, for it had a sepa• rate entranpe, and the wide drive up to the Hall did not come near it. Jack crossed the grass towards it. Two men watched him as he came—the one was Henry -Thorpe and the other was Sir James Fairfas' solibitcr. Henry Thorpe, looking ;lore old, mc, careworn, more strangely drawn and haggard, watched him from under his knit brows. "Sir James's son!" he muttered, "And ycu say .he is honest—his son?" There was a bitterness in his voice that sur- prised the solicitor a little. " Youtig Jack honest?" he cried. "Why. I don't know a better fellow in any way than young Jack. Look at him now as he comes to- wards us. He is as good as he looks, and that is saying a good deal. But it is a pity he is going to marry that little governess. He might have done so flinch better." Henry Thorpe's faze grew hard set. Honest? As honest as he looked? Sir James's son? Ah I but it could not be. The son of his enemy could not be an honest man. It was impossible. Nevertheless, Jack surprised Henry Thorpe. While Sir James lay ill ho transacted all busi- ness for him, and during the next week or two he saw a good deal of the new tenant of the Red House, and the new tenant began to fight a liking that was growing up in his heart for the son of the old man at, the Hall. And yet why should ho fight it? Why had he come back to Warley? What was he waiting for? Mildred was asking herself the same questions. "I don't understand him. Jack," she cried. "I am afraid of him, I think. He is so strange T can't make him out, and yet somehow I am desnerately sorry for him. He seems so lonely. and he looks as if he had gone through so wool" mffering." Jack pulled at, his moustaehe. "Yes, perhaps he does," he said. "Father seems to think there's some mystery about him, hut e.verything WPM/ straight enough. Ho is an Australian went out there years ago. it seems, and has a longing now to settle in Eng- land. There doesn't seem anything funny about that." • Mildred said% nothing. She was rememberiroa the scene in her sitting-room—the strange look en Henry Thorne's face when he had seen Jack's photograph, and somehow she could not speak of it then. "I'll wait and see." she said to herself. is only a little bit strange. I daresay." And as the weeks went by it seemed as if her idea was right. Henry Thorne seemed only a little bit strange. He lived alone by himself in the Red House, receiving no visitors and mak- ing no acquaintances except herself and Jack. nil between them almost a friendship had sprung at last. Yet even they knew no moro about him than they had done at 'first. Sir James recovered rapidly, and was soon up and about again, but the nervous restlessness and uneasiness which had taken possession of him seemed stronger than ever, and, try as ho might, Jack could not get him to see Mildred 'or to make friends with her. But he was strangely anxious to see this new tenant, and his walks always took the same di- rection—towards the Red House. For a time they did not meet, and Sir Japes had mad., 410
~ Ile

special effort to see him, but suddenly they met in the middle of the park; and Jack, who watt with him, never forgot. The two men stopped abruptly, and in that instant he, saw fear and horror and recognition leap to his father's eyes. His thin hand clenched, itself upon his arm. He stood trembling. "So it is you!" he cried. "You come back. What have you come for? How have you dared to come back?" His voice shook. Henry Thorpe stood his ground. Into his face, too, had come a strange. dead grey look. "I came," he said, slowly, to see the old place. It lured me back. I thought no one would recognise me, and no one has except you, and the longing was too strong. Life haw been hard upon me, and I have not long to live, and I could not die without coming back— without seeing once more the place where - she—" He stopped, checked by a cry from Sir James. He went on more slowly. "Where she and I were married," he added- " I could not help coming. At first I did not Intend to stop or to see you, but something ehanged my mind." He stopped again to look into Sir James's face. He had losseried Jack's arm, and was leaning heavily against a tree. Jack turned as if to go, but Sir James beckoned him hastily to stay, and Jack waited, with a sudden cold upon him as he watched the two men's strange grey faces as they spoke " Well—well ? " Sir James said. g need you to change your mind?" Henry Thorpe passed his hand across his face. It was shaking like a leaf, and in ono, minute he seemed to have grown -years older. "Twenty years ago she—Ellen Davenport— wrote and said that my wife and my child were dead," Henry Thorpe went on heavily. " I got the letter twelve months after they sentenced me. Ellen believed me guilty of your uncle's death, and she wrote boldly. They were both dead, she said, her sister and my child." He- took a sudden, sharp step forward, his eyes Mashing like steel. "Why did she lie? "he ' added, fiercely. keaven's sake, Jim, why did she lie?" His voice shook and broke. Sir James had started a little, and his hands trembled on his' stick. "Not dead!" he said, in a husky whisper. "DO you mean that—that—Margaret is not, dead? " Thorpe shook his head. "Not Margaret! No, no, she was faithful and true to me. She believed in me, and she would have come to me if she was alive. Oh, my poor wife died when Ellen said. But mY child—my little girl—Mildred—why did she say that she was dead too? I can guess why Ellen always believed me guilty. And when you— when you bore false evidence against me—to get rid of me—she believed you, and she wanted to keep the child from me. I can see it now. I wrote to her from prison, and said she would never hear from me again. At the end of my term I went abroad without communicating with anyone. I cut myself adrift. I cared for ,nothing—for no one. There was no reason why I should look her up. I went abroad, and by cruel luck made money. What was the use of it to me—an ex-convict---a man convicted of manslaughter? You were the cause of that, James Fairfax—you, my best friend, who de- liberately lied when I stood upon my trial—. lied to get me out of the way—lied to get your uncle's money. You knew of • his will—you. knew that he meant to share his money equally., between us—between you his son and me the son of the woman he had loved—and when he died—you lied to get me out of the way. I was unfortunate. I had quarrelled with him only ten minutes before ho was found dead—he did _ not want me to marry Margaret, and was bc-. side himself when he found I had already done so, and it was that that killed him, perhaps. ? but it was you who nearly got me sentenced for murder--you with your lies I " Sir James shrank back. His face • was livid, ; drawn, ghastly. He put out his hands help- lessly. He rocked on his feet and fell. "It is tho day of reckoning—at last ! " cried. ri • • •
"What in•
"For

"What does it mean For heaven's sake What does it mean?" cried Jack an hour later. when he and Henry Thorpe faced each other over, Sir James's bed. "Is it true—all you said —that my father lied—that ho—that he let yott suffer—' The stricken man stirred on his bed. "Heaven forgive me—it is true !" he whispered, feebly. "I was jealous of him—l hated him-- wanted him out of the way, and the opportunity came. I overheard the quarrel between him and my uncle, and I saw uncle fall, striking his head against the fender ten minutes later; but I swore to a lie—l swore I saw Henry strike him. "And you Piave let him suffer—" Jack be- gan again, but Henry stopped him." "I deserved it," he said. "I had murder in my heart when I faced the old man. It was in my heart—the thought—though I did not• de it, and now—" He looked straight into Jack's eyes. "There is my little girl," he added. Once more Sir James roused himself, and the two men, the wronged and the dying, looked into each other's souls. "Henry," Sir James cried, "car' you forgive —can you let her marry my son? He is good and honest and straight. Ho has been a re- proach to me all these years. Forgive me for his sake, and let him have your girl." Henry did not hesitate. Jack grasped hig band. "One other thing," Sir James added, "and 1 shall be happier than I hylve been for twenty. years. I've had no peace. The thought of you has been a torment, and yet I dared not confess. nut now I can, and it will make me happy. If I had killed uncle myself I couldn't have felt worse. But let me put things straight now. Get me some paper and a pen, Jack, my boy, and send for the lawyer. I will put thingr' straight, and you, Henry, shall take your proper name and place—you shall have the money InY uncle intended you to have—and then I can die in peace." And in years to (*Me the remembrance of Sir James's repentance and his last act of justice did much to wipe out the years of bitterness for Henry Davenport. And when Jack and Mildred came across tha park to him he seemed to live again in them— he seemed to see himself in Jack, as he hail been when Mildred's mother had been young. and before the shadow had fallen upon hiro, Via END.]

ISupertinonsWedding Gifts.—Mr. Winston Churchill's marriage created an amount of interest far beyond that displayed in his father's wedding with Miss Jenny Jerome in IB7L Lord Randolph Churchill was then only on the threshold of his political career,and had not filled the public eye to the same extent as his brilliant son has done. The long list of wedding presents received by Mr. Winston Churchill, and his bride, corresponds to the popular interest in his wedding, but a glance at the list reveals once more the lack of imagination amongst the givers of wedding gifts. There are a dozen or more silver inkstands, quite as many cigarette cases, and clocks, and vast numbers of silver jugs, bowls, sugar castors. trays, and so on. Unless one is rich it is no doubt difficult to depart frqm the commonplace in the selection of a wedding gift, but a new idea, and not a bad one, is to pay the Eubscribtion for five or seven years, of some or other of the high-class illustrated weeklies, which may happen to be the favourite journal of bride or bride- groom. Of course if one can write a cheque for three or four figures, or present a motor car, a balloon, or a flying machine, there is never any difficulty in the selection of a wedding present that will be welcome, and if we are to believe enthusiasts, it will not be long before the airships is included in the category of such gifts, and be used by couples for going away for the honeymoon. Simple but Effective.— Gowns relying entirely upon buttons for trimming—save for a touch of lace about the yoke, collar and sleeves—are likely to find favour with our great modistes. The notion hails from Paris, and several models found their way to London last month. Mrs. Winston-Churchill's going away gown followed these lines and like so many of her beautiful toilettes was very sheath-like. A "Grey" Wedding.—At the reception following the Hozier-Churchill wedding. it was remarked that grey toilettes were far in excess of those of any other hue. The bridegroom's mother was in mushroom grey, the bride herself, when attired for her journey, in biscuit grey, then there were many banana greys, and yet other greys verging towards mauve. But the majority had selected that extremely beautiful pearly shade of grey, which permits of almost any colour being used in relief. Black in some form or other appeared of course upon all these toilettes,huga black velvet or satin buttons being seen in many instances. All black hats too, many of gigantic proportions were much in evidence with coloured toilettes. the ostrich plumes which adorned them being magnificent. The Demand for Black Satin.—Not so very long ago, black satin was regarded as quite impossible for out- door wear' being reserved entirely for smart afternoon gowns or for the evening. But we have changed all that, and at the Hozier-durchill wedding many entirely charming suits consisting of the trailing skirt and long and very fanciful coat were of the softest of soft black satin Then the soft black satin sash and wide belt were seen upon vast numbers of the gowns, moreover this particular fabric had been utilized by the furlong for trimming gowns and suits, especially those in nega- tive tones of cloth. The Coiffeur's Diffculty.—flairdressers, it seems are experiencing some difficulty in obtaining the where- withal to be made up into these additions which the modern coiffure demands. Some of the Central States of Europe from whence most of their supplies used to come, have prohibited merchants from buying the tresses of the peasant girls, and in France neither the fair Normans or the dark Bretons are any longer willing as they used to be for the 40s. or 50s. offered them for it. Village fashions require that the most should be made of the coiffure, and in vain do the merchants offer the girls fancy prices for their locks. Plenty of human hair comes from China, but the coarse black hair of the Orientals is very different from the fine luxuriant tresses of the peasant girls of Europe. JOTTINGS. imam.— Amateur AcLor : "low do make up?" Manager: 'You don't have to, that's why yun were chosen for the part." "I MIGHT have known better than to trust my money to that broker." "Why so? Are appearances against him r "No, confound him; It's his disappearance." "You must know Jenkins, surely." sa;d Mr. Stodge; "he's a sandy-haired man; had smallpox when a lad, and he's deeply pitted." "Anyone who's had smallpox," I said, "deserves to be deeply pitied." Stodge gazed at me in indignant surprise. "De* serves to be deeply pitted," he echoed; "why, hang it all, you seem to blame the man for his misfor- tune." "Oh, but you don't understand me," I re- joined with a smile, "what I meant was---" " Well, it's a funny thing to say," he muttered. "I meant it to be funny," said I. "It seems hardly in good taste to me, rentaiked Stodge, who is a suc- cessful business man and a church member, "to make fun of a man's appearance." "But I made no fun of his appearance; you know I would not do. such a thing.' • "Oh, excuse me, you certainly did," retorted Stodge. " I said Jenkins had had the smallpox, and you said he deserved to have it. The man never did you any harm, and yet you want to see him and his family stricken by a fell disease." "Quite so," I shouted savagely. "I want all his re- lations and friends to be swept off the earth, his house raised to the ground and sown with salt. I wish his business to go to ruin, and his name to be lost for evermore." Then I went away. The next time I make a joke I shall try it on the dog; if he doesn't laugh, I shall know it is too subtle for practical man like Stodge.
SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.
A LONG WAY BEHIND LIGHTNING..

The glass tubes formed by lightning strik- ing in sand—iin. or more in diameter, and sometimes 27ft. long—have been feebly imi- tated by powerful electric eurrenta dis- charged through powdered glass. Compared with Nature's - product, the tiny pipes, of darning-needle size and less than lin. long, suggest the tremendous energy of lightning.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, September 19, 1908.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 19, 1908.
PROTECTING IRON FROM RUST.

A new method of protecting iron from rust has been invented by Mr. T. W. Coslett, of Birmingham. The iron is immersed in a hot phosphorised %solution of some iron com- pound. The surface of the iron is thereby converted into a mixture of ferrous and ferric phosphates. The protected iron has a pleasimr dull black appearance, and is himilv resistant. It is suitable for cycle frames, gun- barrels, &c.

div.head: DEPTH OF SEA STORMS.
div.p: DEPTH OF SEA STORMS.

Experiments by marine engineers all °Ter the world have now demonstrated the fact that the depth to which the wave disturbance of the surface of the sea extends averages 15ft. A homely proof of this is to be found in the way in which a diver can work on the bed of the ocean without feeling the slightest effect -from any motion of the waves over his head. And in many of the long-time submer- sion tests of submarine craft the crews have sunk below the level in a cahn and risen to the surface in a storm without feeling any indications of the above-surface disturbance.
RAILWAY DRIVEN FROM WATERFALL

An interesting electric railway, driven with power generated by a wak•cfall, has ken opened in Norway, from Thamshavn to Svorluno, a distance of 'twenty miles. The power station is about six miles from Thams- havn, while the power is, according to Elec- tricity, generated by a waterfall, fifty-eight metres high, developing 3,000 h.p., and driv- ing five turbines representing the same total of power. The railway is owned by the pro- prietors of the MeMal Copper Mines, and will carry ore from the mines as well as con- ducting a passenger traffic.

div.head: BEETLES AND FUNGUS CULTURE.
div.p: BEETLES AND FUNGUS CULTURE.

In the tunnels formed by certain wood- boring beetles a fungus which has been called ambrosia 16 found. And in a report of the German Botanical Society F. NV. Neger gives an account of his investigation of the 6ame. He tried to grow these fungoid IN-Ace, but failed to get them to develop. The am- brosia was found to be a kiitd of fungus that infests pine nec.,.clles, probably a species of Geratos-tomella.. The beetles do not pur- posely carry the fungus spores as do many species of ants, but these clinging to their bodies are carried to any new wood they may attack.

div.head: VISIBILITY OF THE EARTH.
div.p: VISIBILITY OF THE EARTH.

As we look up through the transparent atmosphere on a clear night and see the moon beaming brilliantly down upon us, we may think: "What a wonderful sight the continents and oceans of the earth would present if we could view them -from the moon!" But, according to the conclusions of Mr. C. G. Abbot, the director of the Astro- physical Observatory of the Smithsonian In- stitution, a man on tie moon would catch but fleeting glimpses of the outlines of our continents. " The true radiating surface of the earth. AR a plane," says Mr. Abbot, "le chiefly the water vapour at an elevation of 4,000 metres (13,000 ft. or more, above filo .ea-level." In consequence, the man in the moot would see the features of the earth ihnly outlined in the glare of light reflected from the atmosphere. MEDICINE BY OSMOSIS.

Osmosis is the passage of a liquid, or a gas, through a membrane. Sometimes medi- cines are administered in this way. But how far we are from understanding the details of this subject as related to the human body is indicated by some experiments of Professor Louis Kahlenberg. All attempts to introduce lithium salts into the system by absorption through the skin have failed, and yet the same salts make their \ray readily through the mucous Inembrane. When the feet are. soaked in a solution of hydrochloric, or sul- phuric acid, an alkaline reaction quickly takes place internally. But citric acid refuses to act the same way, although both of these acids have a similar effect when taken throut.-rph the digestive tract. Sulphuric acid, then, has quite a different physiological effect when it enters through the skin in- stead of through the mouth. Living mem- branes act differently with regard to osmosis from dead ones, and the same membranes which behave alike with regard to some sub- stances behave very differently from one another with regard to other substances.

div.head: WHAT MAKES HAILSTONES.
div.p: WHAT MAKES HAILSTONES.

The formation of heil through electrical action, according to the theory of scientists attached to the Weather Bureau at Washing- ton, is an interesting and even wonderful proe2fts. The wind draws out a cloud into a long, narrow strip. In that form, owing, to the great ainount of surface exposed to the the cloud evaporates rapidly, and the rapid evaporation produces intense cold. Dry particles of snow are then formed, and these, by friction with the water drops, quickly become charged with negative elec- tricity. But the water drops themselves carry positive electricity, and, since negative at- tracts positive, a film of water is formed upon each snow particle, and is instantly

div.head: FROZEN INTO A LAYER OF ICE.
div.p: FROZEN INTO A LAYER OF ICE.

At this thickness its outer surface remains moist, the water not freezing there so rapidly, 114tereupon the electrical charge changes from negative to positive, and the particle is repelled by the water drops and driven to the outer parts of the cloud. Here the increased cold covers it with snow again, and friction charges it anew with negative electricity. Repulsion is now once more changed for attraction, and the 'particles rush back into the cloud, receiving upon their surfaces another film of water, which is turned into second ice layers. Thus the grow- ing hailstone darts zigzag through the clouds, piling up its alternate layers of snow and ice until gravitation gains control, and sends it, with a jingling crowd of its fellows, spin- ning to the ground.

div.head: GALLS AND GALL-FLIES.
div.p: GALLS AND GALL-FLIES.

Certain kinds of -vegetable galls are among the most familiar objects of the Countryside, yet few people realise what they really are or how they origintn.e. That they are a fungoid growth is a commonly-accepted, but erroneous, theory. As a matter of fact, galls are part and parctd of the plant on which they are folmd, albeit a morbid production, and are gonerally the result of insect activity, althougn certain well - known kinds (for example, the witches' besoms of the birch tree) are due to the action of fungi, says air. Harold Bastin in the Country Home. A gall is, in effect, a nursery wherein the immature insect finds food and shelter pending the completion of its metamorphosis. Most people are familiar with certain bean-shaped swellings, perhaps hfl. in length, and bright scarlet as to colour, which occur abundantly on the leaves of the "crack" willow. These swellings are

div.head: KNGWN AS HORSE-BEAN GALLS."
div.p: KNGWN AS HORSE-BEAN GALLS."

Science recognises them as the work of Nematus gallicola, the •willow sawfly. During April or lay the parent insect lays her eggs by means of her wonderful twin-saw oviposi. tor, within the. leaf buds ; and cc the •leaves unroll the gall-structares develop. For several weeks each gall is a solid mass of vege table tissue with the egg lying in. a small cavity near the centre. Then the larva hatches and feeds upon the inner portion of the gall, from which, when full fed, it isstic-a and drops to the -ground. Here it forms a tiny cocoon of earth grains, becomes a chrysalis or pupa, and ultimately appears as a perfect sawfly. This happens in August or September, and each • newly-emerged female sawfly oviposits in developing leaf buds, with the. result that a second generation of galls shortly a pp,,.s. sawfly is said to be double brooded i.e., it achieves two complete life t:ieles in the course of each twelve months, . . . .

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Hill Chile Baptist Church.

There were large congregations at the above church on Sunday afternoon and evening when the autumnal sermons were preached by the Rev. A. Waller, of Bradford. Special anthems were rendered by the choir at each service and special hymns were also sung. The collections were iu aid of the Church Funds.

div.head: Baptist Church, Latchford.
div.p: Baptist Church, Latchford.

Harvest thanksgiving services were held at the Latchford Baptist Church on Sunday, when the preacher, morning and evening, was Councillor James Ball. There were good congregations, especially in the evening. Special music was renderstd by the choir, Mr. H. E. Butt presiding at the organ. The church had been tastefully decorated with flowers, plants, fruit, &c.

div.head: Methodist Free Church, Buckley-Street.
div.p: Methodist Free Church, Buckley-Street.

The harvest festival was celebrated on Sunday, when large congregations assembled. Mr. H. Clinch, of Birkenhead, preached morning and evening, nod the church was beautifully decorated with flowers, fruit, corn, &c., for which every credit must be given to those who had the work in band, In the afternoon a service of song was given by the choir, Mrs. Simpson taking the connective readings, !sir. J. Ryder being the con- ductor and Miss Plinston organist. On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held in the schoolroom, the room being packed, when Im excellent programme was got together by Mr. E. Taylor, Mr. E. Plinston being in the chair, and the following artistes taking part :—Misses Lomas, Adams, and Cotterill ; and Master M. Farring- ton, the latter causing roars of laughter with his humorous songs. Miss Plinston accompanied. At the close of a very enjoyable evening a bag of fruit was given to each person. The total proceeds realized a little over

div.head: Baptist Church, Golborne-strect.
div.p: Baptist Church, Golborne-strect.

On Sunday morning the Pastor took for his tex Judges viii. 4., " Faint, yet pursuing." After passing lin rapid review earlier scenes in the life of Gideon, Mr. Letheren pointed out the reason why this report of the captain on the condition of the troops had become one of the most familiar watchwords of his life, and 'after showing how common the temptation to faint was, suggested where the secret lay of triumph over it. The evening subject was taken from the conversation of Christ with the woman at the well of Sychar. Mr. Letheren referred to the opinions of Jewish teachers concerning women and to the wonder of His disciples at seeing him talking to a woman, by common repute the" worst woman in Sychar." It was a meeting of the Best and the Worst Christ sees the soul of good- ness in things evil and in this story we watch Him observingly distil it out. The conversation revealed Christ's knowledge of human nature in its heights and depths ; its hidden springs of purity and truth which He came to discover and re-inforce. How near men and women may come to what can make all time and eternity different to them and yet be ignorant of its presence and possibilities. How Christ lifts the store from men's lives and reveals what is under it and pierces the layers of thought and habit and makes men face the facts. How He opens the fonntains of affection and enthusiasm within the soul and sees it free from base affections. How He shows that the human soul is the shrine of God and that God is a Father who loves and forgives and there is a Divine Spirit that can inspire our human spirits to the love of purity and truth. How a life thus lifted must seek to lift other likes so that others may come to know that this is indeed the Saviour of the i World. Rev. J. Scott Lidgett at Penketh.

The Penketh Wesleyan Church anniversary and the opening of the new organ were celebrated on Sunday. The congregation were favoured by a visit of the Rev. J. Lidgett, M.A. (president of the Wesleyan Methodist Conference.) At the morning service the rev. gentleman preached from Isaiah xxxvii. 2. The choir effectively rendered an anthem entitled "Sweet is Thy Mercy"

(Hamby), Miss Johnson taking the solo. At the evening service the president preached to a crowded I congregation from St. Mark xii. 28-34. The choir sang the anthem " God that madest earth and heaven." (Naylor) with good taste, Miss C. Atherton and Mr. Herber a Plurnpton rendering the solos. Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ at each service. In the afternoon a musical service was held, Dr. Bennett, of Padgate, presiding. After the singing of the hymn "Lord of the worlds abeve," Mr. W. IL Payton delighted the congregation with the following selection of music on the organ : Sonata 111 (Mendelssohn), " Serenade" (Widor), Andante Pastorale (Lefebure- Wely), " Toccata " (Dubois), " March Triurnphale " (Lemrnens). A collection was taken at each service in aid of the organ ad school enlargement fund. Preaching in the evening, the Rev. J. Scott Lidgett's remarks were based upon the query addressed to our Lord by one of the scribes : " Which is the first com- mandment of all." He said that this man had a true and sincere perception of the things which really matter in religion. That was by no means a common quality. The history of religion, while in some respects the most glorious part of the history of man- kind was. ii some respects, the most disappointing. Again and again throughout the ages and in all parts of the world men have built up and maintained elabor- ate systems of doctrine, of observance and of super- stition, under which the reel true eternal meaning of religion has been buried. There was a tendency to get their minds wrong in regard to the meaning of religion. This 11,,”3, if he had not always taken a true view of religion was ready at once to respond to it, when it was presented to him by our Lord. There was another thing about him, which was almost of more importance—what his judgment discerned, his sympathy approved. Tnere was no reluctance on his past to accept what he clearly saw to be true and right. Here both sympathy and judgment were captured. The man's mind and heart were sound. There was but one thing lacking and that thing lacking was the one which is anstantly lacking in the Christian Church. This man had quite enough religion to make an elder, a deacon, churchwarden or a circuit steward, but he had not enough religion to make a Christlan. The reason why, was just because of this : The outworks of his nature were captured,but the stronghold still held out. Let judgment and sympathy be the means of approach to the Inmost heart, and then only would they become members of the Kingdom of Heaven. From another standpoint this incident of thc young man was remarkably striking. It was an instance of the generosity of Jesus. They had here one of the best side- lights upon His sinless perfection. He was in the atmos- phere of controversy. Party after party of those who were at warfare with one another agreed in this, that they tried to take Bins captive in his talk. It was a difficult thing to to, as those who read His series of questions and answers to them might easily see. Our Lord is immediately conscious directly a man of nobler trait comes near Him, who may have been drawn into the discussion. It might have been in a sort of hesitat- ing way that he asked his questions ; there might have I been an inner conflict between the world end the Lord's world : a deep spiritual desire—not the mere curiosity to have a question answered. Christ at once responded to his nobler spirit, and in responding to it, calls it out. They were conscious for the most part of the barrenness of this age. They looked upon its MediTvalisin,its Phari- sees and its Scribes, and they supposed that true religion was still, night and day, in the thoughts when Jesus I Christ was on the earth. And yet, here In the prayerful influence of his truth and spirit, they had this man brought up in the schools of Scribes. Christ linked the two great commandments together, but He was asked to single out one great one as high above all others. He I was perfectly sure that if Jesus Christ came back, there would be people who would ask Him to give a verdict as to the Sermon on the Mount If He did come among men there would be such an activity and they would go to Him and say, "Master,which is the first com- mandment of all ?" Might they come to the rescue of the first commandment and believe that the life and service of their neighbour is Pc nothing unless" Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy mind and soul and strength." Christ singled out the first command- ment, but let them take both to heart. The second was, "Thou shalt love tby neighbour as thyself." A great many people supposed that religion consisted of giving assent to a particular creed and going to a certain place of worship. What religion is he ? "they said. They called him a Methodist, a Presbyterian, an Anglican, a Roman Catholic, or whatever it might be. There had always been that tendency to suppose that the mere observance of religion was the real thlng. A good many had got the impression that religion was nothing less than a restraining power and that left to them- selves they might run riot ln this way or the other. What was religion ? Love. Simple;positive, all embracing :—not a tyranny, but a freedom ; not a restraint but an inspiration ; not a limit but an emancipation. "Thou shalt love." That explained the wonderful impression that was made upon them as they read the sermon on the mount. One scarcely know what to say as to the saving feature of a religion so deeply spirits-al, so frfir'.ly natural, so profoundly moral, a completely social in its teachings. Not a word about chin-ober., not a word about crc3ds. He did not say they were not important. They had a painful spectacle to-day and they would read of it in the papers next day, of a religion which had lost all touch with modern thought end modern progress, with all the appeals to the reeson,to char to the great progres- sive idcils of h len nature, and which makes up for it by magnificently ordered pageant. They had the one great vital principle which eel carry religion from age to age and which can build up religion. Religion was the same in all sanctuaries of the world ; end the same in all churches whenever tide spirituality prevails. The one great essential of spirit of tf ae religion was this : " Positive inspiratlon of a spirit feeling love." Christ said " Thou shalt love the Lord Thy God." Just pause for a moment in that phrase. The Lord thy God. The whole of the Old Testament was there. The Lord, Infinite Perfectior, and the All Holy ,reaching the human life, controlling the heavens, ordering history, unfolding all things in the puipose which He carries out from agate age How many people talk about how they believe in "a" God. God's revelation of himself has alstays been, the Lord thy God. The God who enters into communion and fellowship with them. There were people who talked about the love of

humanity and they placed the love humanity first in the palca of the love of Gad. If they simply took God and generalised Him into humanity they got God, a sort of personation, and a sort of sovereignty without absolute perfection. The scripture knew they would meet to-morrow their neighbour. What a contrast to the perfection of Gad and—the imperfection of their neighbour ; the Sovereignty of God and the hopeless- ness perhaps of their neighbour. " Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." lie should to exactly as much an object to them or a warning, as they were to them- selves. They should never du anything which would injure him, they should be actuated in all their conduct by such a self-responsibility for all his interests. That was true religion. The only way they could love their neighbour as themselves was to lov3 Gad with all their hearts.

div.head: TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL.
div.p: TRADES AND LABOUR COUNCIL.
The Problem of Unemployment.
The monthly meeting of this Council was held at Friars' Green [louse on Tuesday evening, Mr. Richardson presiding over a fair attendance.
MR3. STOTT'S THANKS.

A letter was re-td from Mrs. Stott thanking the Council for their kind resolution of appreciation of her services. She stated that the knowledge that her husband had gone away with the respect and love of his fellow men fully repaid for the past and strengthened the desire to continue to do what little she could in the future.

div.head: TIIS NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.
div.p: TIIS NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.

The SF.CRETARY (Hr. E. Plinston) read a letter from the Warrington branch of the Independent Labour Party stating that they had discussed the prospects of Labour candidatures for the Town Council in Novem- ber. It was understood that the Trades and Labour Council contemplated contesting one or more wards and it was therefore decided to formally intimate that the Warrington branch of the Independent Labour Party intended making a strong effort to retain the seats now held by its nominees in Orford and St John's Wards. _ _

• It was also stated that the secretary of the Trades Council had circularised the branches ask;ng them if they were in favour at least one seat being contested and if they would con- tribute to the expenses. Twelve of the twenty-six affiliated societies sent favourable replies and the importance of early action being taken by the others was urged.

div.head: S'ALYATION ARMY AND ALLEGED SWEAVNG.
div.p: S'ALYATION ARMY AND ALLEGED SWEAVNG.

A letter was read from the Workers United Prot Committee appealing for financial assistanc 3 in their agitation against" the inquitous sweating system " of the Salvation Army, and emphasising the serious economic issues involved.

It was pointed out that the demonstration arranged by the Committee had already been hold and the Council decided to take no action in the matter, one member remarking that the money would be better spnt on the unemployed.

div.head: PEA CE_ QUESTION.
div.p: THE PEA CE_ QUESTION.

The Federation of Trade Unions asked the support of the Council to a petition to the Governments repre- sented at the second and third Hague Conferences, which asked that a general international arbitration treaty should be agreed upon by virtue of which it would be a matter of honour with each nation to adjust by arbitration treaties all its international interests singly or in groups at a time, at the earliest dates possible, and further to refer all differences which might arise before the completion of bach adjustment from any interest not yet adjusted by an arbitration treaty to an international Court or Commission of Arbitration for examination and decision, admitting of a last recourse to arms only in case such decision endangered the safety of either of the litigant nations. Mr. MOORFIELD said the question of peace and arbitration was one in which every workingman should take au interest, and they ought to support the petition by every meals in their power. Mr. BERD said a great deal of the money spent on armaments might better be devoted to relieving the unemployed. It was decided to support the petition.

THE UNEMPLOYED PROBLEM. A letter was read from the Right to Work National Council stating that Board of Trade figures conclusively proved that considerable distress and destitution pre- vailed owing to the lack of work. The present Govern- ment, speaking through its mouthpiece, the President of the Local Government Board, had no remedy to offer, no proposals even for temporary relief, and was content to wait for the coming of winter, satisfied that all was well. The Right to Work Council was not con- tent to sit down quietly knowing, as all trade unionists knew, that industrially they had reached the high water mark in this worst of all evils which affected their class. They at least did not share the breezy optimism of the President of the Local Government Board. They knew that literally hundreds of thousands of men, women and children were suffering untold mise.y owing to the lack of employment,and under those circamstances they confidently appea'sd to the organized workers to join with them in a vigorous and deter- mined agitation for the purpose of compiling the Government to amend its policy, not only in regard to the administration of the present Act and grant but to secure the enactment of a Right to Work Meclure which would place upon ons public authority the obligation to provide useful employment under fair conditions for every able and willing worker, women as well as men. Co-operation was invited on the following Unes : ',a) to at once in conjuncl 'on w:th all other bodies of organized workers in the district set on foot an r 3itation to secure the re-opening of the Distress Committee registers and to urge all the unemployed worl ws, both organized and unorganized, ski"ed and uns! 'lied, to at once register themselves, not because in the past registration had resulted in securing emplo, cent but because it was absolutely necesr'J that the actual facts as regarded unemploy- ment should be known ; (b) to supply the rght to Work Comic— w a stat3ment shon:ng the total nemb3r of trade unlon members and others out of employment in the district in the third week of September, and the total number who were or had been on short time during the present year, specifying the trades ; (d) to co-operate with the Right tp Work Committee in organizing demonstrations in the district in order to bring the question of unemployment prominently before the public. Mr. FIALEY pointed out that the Warrington Labour Bureau had never been closed but a great number of unemployed did not register themselves. A great many of the trade unions kept their own registers of unemployed and therefore their members did not make use of the labour bureau. Mr. J. H. JONES said the high officials of the Govern- ment did not seem to believe the distress was so great as was represented. If the unemployed would sign the registers it would be a means of making the facts known. He moved that the Council recommend all workers to register their names at the labour bureau. Mr. OWEN : You will never get trade unionists to sign the registers, because they have to answer such. disgraceful questions, for one thing.

div.head: WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB. Rewiew of the Past Season.
div.p: WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB. Rewiew of the Past Season.

We have now said " good-bye" to cricket for a few months,and the time has once more come to review the season's doinga of the Warrington club. The most dis- appointing feature has been the inability of the eleven to make a bold bid for the championship of the West Lancashire League, but although their achievements in the League tourney have been of a somewhat mediocre description, they have proved themselves capable of holding their own with some of the best clubs outside League cricket. In all, 21 matches were played, and of these seven were won, eight lost, and six were interfered with or spoiled too completely to allow of any definite issue being arrived at.

Coming to the individual performazes, there have been several worthy of special notice. Upon the shoulders of Cresswell (the professional) has the bulk of the attack fallen and it is pleasing to rt. zord that for the third year in succession he his achieved the distinction of carrying off the prize offered by the West Lancashire League for the best bowling analysis in that competition. The old Warwickshire pro- fessional ha s bowled steadily throughout the season, and on no single occaaion can he be Enid to have been "collared." Perhaps his finest performance was at Earlestown, for on going on a sczond time he delivered 118 over; eleven of which were maidens, for seven wickets and had 18 rims knocked off him. Altegether lin the season he captured 75 wickets at a cost of 7.77 Iruns per wicket', the aggregate being four more wickets than last season, but his average then was the phenomenal one of 4.70 per wicket.

-- H. Ceylon has scarcely E: )n so successful as last season, when together with the professional he shared the bulk of the bowling. This season he has taken 30 wickets against 44 last year and his average now reaches 13.70 against 7.72 par Ccket I t season.

E. Sileock. who carried out the duties of clptain with every degree of efficiency, has at times proved himself a good change bowler,and mention hes only to be made of his work against Wigan, when he routed that side out after they had apparently held victory in the palm of their hens will not be readily forgottten. On that occasion the Warrington esptain secured six wickets for seven runs, and was mainly instlumental in seeming for lOs side a remsrkable victory by three my's.
NV. if. Podmore has also done good work wioi the kill, and considering that he is usually regarded as the last change his 25 wickets for 299 runs is ex. ,ptioually good

The Rev. H. Gray's b3st work was against Boughton Hall and in the League engagement at Stanley, and on the flrey wicket at the Liverpool ground the home side did not relish facing his dangerous deliveries.

T. Wright heads the batting averages, and the good work he accomplished against Preston, St. Helens Recreation and Newton gave him a substantial lead over his confreres. At Pieston and St. Helers Recrea- tion he showed masterly skill and the feature of the exhibitions was the power he infused into his strokes. J. W. Bainbridge, third in the averages, has done bis best work in the last three matches, and strange to say, the quality of his batting has improved when the pitch has bean at its worst, J. W. Bibby has only played in a few matches, but evidence was forth- coming in theee that he is yet to be regarded amongst the first flight of batsmen in this district. A sound innings by B. Si!cock against Stanley was amongst the best performances accomplished during the season, but Creswell claims the honour of making the highest aggregate of the season, his 73 against St. Helen- fittingly appropriate seeing that it was his benefit match, being made with- out a faulty stroke. IV. Richardson, after opening well against Boughton Hall, when he went through tl_,3 innings with 35 to his credit, has been a trifle erratic, and his record by no means comes up to that of 1903. W. H. Podmore has improved splendidly on his last two seasors, and what with his good work in the field at cover he is yet a wcicome commodity in the eleven. The Rev. H. Gray, after starting well with a dashing 40 against Boughton Hall, at Arpley, had a run of ill-luck which reduced his average in wholesale fashion. The ycangest member of the team, Stanley Partridge, has justified his place in the eleven, and to possess an aver- age of UK in this his first season in first-class cricket is a record upon which he is heartily to be congratu- lat

The fielding of the whole of the team has heel smart , and whilst Duckworth has at times kept wicket in first- class style, the achievements of Bainbridge, Partridge, and the younger members of the team serve to prove that the eleven is not short of promising talent.
