It is to be regretted that THE the election at Newcastle- NEWCASTLE on-Tyne is not to be per- ELECTION. 'Bitted to turn wholly on Tariff Reform, as the Con- servative candidate desires. Mr. GEORG RExwrox, who has previously sat for the constituency, is a decidedly interesting Tariff Reformer. He was a fiery Protectionist when Mr. CHAMBERLAIN was among the most energetic and convincing defenders of Free Trade. He held to the faith that was in him when Mr. HENRY CtukriaN abandoned Protection and took up with the milder heresy of bimetallism as a preliminary to entering the Cabinet of Lord SALISBURY. He may honestly enough declare that he has boon faithful among the faithless, holding the fort, as it were, till Mr. CHAMBERLAIN came over and Mr CHAPLIN came back again. The importance which the Conservatives of Newcastle attach to his Pro- tectionist views may be measured by the fact that Sir WALTER PLUMMER, another former Member for Newcastle, has been induced to stand aside in his behalf, and on the ground that he is not suffi- ciently sound on Tariff Reform. The Conservatives of Newcastle apparently like to have their favourite doctrine stated in its crudest form. They ask for a sort of rural simplicity in politics, and they get it. Mr. RENWICK tells the electors that Tariff Reform will lead to more shipbuilding on the Tyne; because big ships must be built to trade with the Colonies, and only small ones need be built to trade with France. As Mr.Rmiwrcx is himself a shipowner, he is not speaking in pure ignorance, as might be supposed. He is not unaware that our biggest steamers are employed

in trade with the United States, a branch of oar commerce which would either be cut off or injured beyond recovery if political philosophers like Mr. RENWICK had their way. He would exchange, it seems, our trade with forty millions of French people for a problematical increase in the trade of the six or seven million people of the Austra- lasian Colonies. He thinks—or shall we say, as being more probable, that he professes to think a change of this kind would lead to the building of larger ships. There should be a good deal of sport in Newcastle if Mr. RHNwrcx defends the Protectionist mania by arguments of this fragile and foolish description. But it is by no means to be assumed that Mr. RENWICK will fail to capture the seat, though, for our own part, we think his success improbable, even though the Socialist candidate should, as he threatens, fight to the finish. Taere is not the smallest justification for the appearance of a third candidate in this instance, unless, indeed, that section of the Socialist Party, of which Mr. HYNDMAN is the head, would much rather defeat a Liberal than a Conservative. The representation of Newcastle has been divided during the life of the present Parliament between the Liberals and the Labour Representation Committee. The conditions at the last election were almost as nearly ideal as they could have been. Mr. CAIRNS, the Liberal candidate, stated at all his meetings that he did not wish to be returned to the House of Commons unless Mr. HUDSON, the Labour candidate, was returned along with him. The Liberal electors responded nobly to this invitation to split their votes between Liberalism and Labour, and as the Independent Labour Party did not split with nearly the same unanimity, Mr. HUDSON was placed at the top of the poll. An analysis showed that there are in Manchester about five thousand electors who vote independently of both parties. The Newcastle Liberals gave a representative to these five thou- sand votes, Mr. HUDSON polling 18,659, against Mr. Camxs's 16,423. It seemed to the casual glance like a tremendous victory for Independent Labour; but the analysis of the votes left no doubt as to what had been meant and what had I been done. The Liberals had been as determined to return Mr. HUDSON as to return Mr. CAIRNS. The Labour Representation Committee was,there- I fore, taking the only possible course when it advised that there should be no third candidate on the present occasion It has too much common sense to wish to interfere with so excellent an understanding. The really difficult feature of the situation arises out of the conditions which have been produced by the recent labour troubles in the North. The engineers' strike is not at an end, and there pro- bably survives much bitter feeling among the I shipbuilders. Many thousands of labourers who had no quarrel with their employers have been thrown out of work. ft may be presumed, there- fore, that there is present in Newcastle a great deal of vague discontent which is ready to launch itself against the party system generally, and under any sort of leadership. In such cases Liberalism always loses most, and though the margin for loss is large in this instance, it is not so large that a feeling of absolute confidence can be based upon it. Newcastle returned a Tory Protectionist and Home Ruler in 1874 ; it did the same thing over again in 1895, giving him a majority over Mr. JOHN MORLEY. During many years past elections in Newcastle have been associated with sudden and remarkable changes in the tide. One thing is certain. The absurd character of Mr. GEORGE RENWICK'S views on the subject of Protection will do him no harm,though there may be some Conservatives who do not like them. The Newcastle Tories are grandly regard- less of the personal opinions of their representatives, when they happen to have any. They only want a man who will vote "straight."
The well known enthusiasm KicuTsrann Dtvistox of Mr. and Mrs. Ztha LIBERALS. Armitage in the Liberal

cease was once more essemplified on Saturday when they entertained a gathering of Knutsford Division Liberals at their charming residence, Newton Bank, Preston Brook. Fortunately the weather was on its best behaviour and everything conspired to make the function most enjoyable: The presence of the popular member for the division, Mr. A. J. King, and his good wife was welcomed by all. Mr. King spares no effort to keep in close touch with the I dwellers in the large and scattered constituency and his speeches on current political events are always well reasoned and full of interesting information. On Saturday he had to cover a wide field in a very short time but he fulfilled the task admirably and had no difficulty in showing that the Government is doing its beat to grapple with the pressing social questions of the day and to improve the conditions I of life for the masses of the people. Their Old Age Pensions Act is a boon which will be appreci- ated by thousands of our industrial veterans, as a 1 means of alleviating the hardships to which too many have unfortunately been subjected in their declining years. Overshadowing everything else at the present moment is what Mr,King described as the terrible and urgent problem of unemploy- ment. Lest the depressed state of affairs should be successfully used by - the Tories as an argument for tariff reform, Mr. King pointed out that in highly protected countries the problem is even more acute, so that to abandon our Free Trade system would be a piece of folly which could only result in disaster. Mr. King does not profess to forecast what the solution will be, but he is in hopes that the information Mr. Lloyd George has obtained whilst in Germany together •with the forthcoming report of the Royal Commis. sion on the Poor Law will be utilized to bring about an important change in our methods of dealing with poverty. As was only to be expected, Mr. King is whole-hearted in his support of the Licensing Bill, which he has no doubt will go through the House of Commons by a large majority. As to what is likely to happen in " another place" he could not speak with any certainty, but he does not believe the Lords will dare to reject a measure which has such a powerful backing from so many sections of the community.
Like that of the poor, this SCHOOL question seems to be always ACCOMMODATION, with us. The Education

Committee has been almost continuously trembling under threats of boiling oil—or some other punishment designed to fit the crime—from the Board of Education owing to the lack of accommodation for the elementary scholars of the town. Every now and then a crisis arises, the Board of Education's cauldron is heated, and the Committee fearfully and rapidly builds a now school. The Board has made made matters worse by re-assessing the accommodation on the basis of ten square feet of floor space for each child, and threatening a reduction of grants; As a result there is considerable trepidation among the members of the local authority, and for their guidance Mr. J. Moore Murray (the Director of Education) has prepared an exhaustive, but not cheering report on the accommodation on the revised basis. He has Ireported exhaustively on the accommodation in each Ward of the town, pod it seems that only in 'Latchford Ward will there be more places than scholars. In Orford Ward, notwithstanding the opening of the Beamont School last year with accommodation for 1080 children, there is to•day

an excess of 273 children in attendance at the various schools of the Ward. There is a deficiency of 390 places in S. Austin's Ward, while the rapidly growing population in Whitecross Ward has caused congestion there. In the aggregate„! the new assessment will cause a -loss of 2,30 a existing places, and a shortage of accommodation for the scholars already on the school rolls, of 1333; places. The various el2edieots for keeping the Education Bcard at bay cannot be extended' any further, and a recommendation Will come before the Education Committee on Monday' to proceed forthwith with a school for the West end of S. Austin's Ward, and to secure sites for, schools in Fairfield, Orford, S. John's, and White cross Wards. This is a big building progranahls) for the ratepayers to face, but they are " between* the devil and the deep sea." If the new schools I are not provided the present financial burden will be ad led to by the reduction of grants. The ne schools will partly pay for themselves in increased; grant-earning power, while the value of theq contribution to educational efficiency cannot be estimated in pounds, shillings and pence,

Not geographers alone Wilt SVEN TIEDIN be interested in the accountilli our OF THIBET. which are beginning to coraei to hand of Sven Hedin'a4 I journey this year through hitherto unexplored regions of Tnibet. Dr. Hedin was prohibited,' under political necessity, from entering Tnibet from British territory in 1908. Last year we beard that he had added to our knowledge of Central Asia, particularly in respect of the true sources of the Brahnaaputra, the autlej, and tha Indus, and he has been busy filling in detail on oal ct. maps of Central Asia since 1900, when he travailedi ' through Khorassan and Turkestan. Imme ately to the south of Turkestan lies Kashmir,:) and from Kashmir the enterprising travelleegi set out in December to link' up his nevil explorations with the scene of his first 1 From the Aksai China Lake one might draw e !line to Lhassa and say, speaking roughly that Hedin followed it over three-parts of the waY I Then he turned south-west, and made out th icourse of the Chartatsango, a big effluent, fed, ' it seems, from snow peaks, and issuing, after form 1• Img a lake, into the Brahrnaputra. Dr. Hedi. I crossed mountain tops and glaciers, painted ii skin night and morning to look like a nativ drovor, came on gold mines between latitudes and 34, got separated from his caravan in a saaal= storm, lost his sheep from cold, and had a narro escape from detection when a Lhassa merchant sen to tell the Governor that it was time the authori ties were looking after this strange sheep driver. His greatest discovery was that of a continuous mountain chain which, taken as a whole, is th ' most massive range on the crust of the earth, its average height above sea level beimg greater tha that of the Himalayas. Its peak; are 4,000 tci 5,000 feet lower than Mount Everest, but i passes average 3,000 feet higher than the Hirn , layan passes. These are surely the mountain told of by Rider Haggard in " Ayesha " th thrilling sequel to " She."

There is no blinking the THE FUTURE OF fact that the motor bee TELE MOTOR COMO to stay, or perhaps PROBLEM, would be better to say to rush onwards unceasinglY: Motor power is a great discovery, and one whis3 the world is not going to refrain from making use of. Further, the public roads are the places in which to make use of it. It ig true someone has talked about private row:l3 for motors, but where is the advantage of such thorongkfares ? Why not take a firsV. class railway ticket and have done with it Tne real problem is caused by the fact that the • streets and roads are the principal area for children to play in, for invalids and old people to walk in and also for motors to run in. The outcry is mainly against motor-cars, but why the motor omnibus and the lorry which is used for cartage should escape condemnation it is not easy to see; If the car were to be prohibited and the 'bus lorry remain, who would be benefited? The is that the very existsnce of. the problem caiss attention to the crying need for more parks and playgrounds, in order that the roads may be reserved for their legitimate purpose of transit. This may, at first sight, seem an extreme attitude to take up, but it is a strictly logical one. It isfq course, necessary at the present time to do all that can be done to modify the evil, but it must be recognised that the tendency towards speed is in accordance with the spirit of the times, and wherever the interests of speed are colvi cerned accommodation must somehow be 4 found for it. As regards the other aspects cf 0014 motor problem, that of dust will no doubt bs, overcome are long by the genius of some inventati while as to the tearing up of the roads, motorists themselves do no oppose the suggestion that tbsY should be specially taxed to provide grants t° local authorities for the repair of those roau! which can be shewn to have suffered througu motor traffic.

div.p: THE POLITICS OF THE WEEK.

* * * An interesting development is likely to take place under the Patents Act of last year. A large number of patents granted to foreign firms have lapsed, and 6 there is nothing to prevent English manufacturers 1, taking up these intents and working them. Most of 1 the patents which have been allowed to lapse are Probably worthless, but some of them may be useful and valuable. The matter is now being investigated - by competent authorities, and if it is found that any I. patents of real value have been left unworked a com- pany will be formed to take them up and endeavour tO utilise them. It is believed that this action is Perfectly legal, though some of the foreign firms whose Patents are to be worked may bring the question nsfore the courts.

* , * Pea Hill, a well-known landmark to all who pass through the neighbourhood of Crontorr; is latterly engaging a good deal of consideration in Widnes Town Council schemes, mainly owing to the possi- bility of its development as a town recreation and holiday ground being much easier of realisation now that a bus service is within calculable distance. At a Council meeting some two or three months ago, Councillor Clarke introduced a suggestion that the cultivation of the hill should receive attention, and at i last week's meeting he brought forward a definite pro- -4' Ppsal for its reservation as a Widnes resort. Coon- ' cidlor Clarke had in mind the, invasion of numbers of picnic parties from outside the borough, who, if the 1 Spa t were developed by the Council, would share the , benefit without the slightest contribution to the accorn- P9nying expense. Of course, those who pay the . Piper have the right to call the tune but the large .., . Parties from neighbouring towns, including Warring- ton, who occasionally visit Pea Hill, would hardly relish the suggested reservation. Everybody knows that the trade in patent medicines 4!las now reached great proportions, but few perhaps iiliagined that the figures were so remarkable as those • Riven by the President of the British Pharmaceutical CDnference on Tuesday. This is what he said : The amount expended in remedies of this description in the years mentioned was approxi- mately as follows : 1860, £350,000; 1870, £530,000; 1880, £1,080,000 ; 1890, £1,740,000; 1900, £2,310,000; 1907, £2,620,000. Reckoning the population of the British Isles at about twenty-three millions in 1860, and thirty-nine millions in 1905, it followed that the amount spent in patent medicines per head is now about five times as great as it was half a century ago. , All this consumption of patent medicine ought to "ve an appreciable effect on the death-rate, one way or the other.

* * * The first case under the Education (Provision of Ilea1s) Act of 1900 for the recovery from a parent of the cost of providing meals for his children was heard 00 Wednesday at Wiest London Police Court. The representatives of the Education Committee of the London County Council proved their case against the defendant, who, in spite of his earning good wages, had neglected to provide the children in question Nrith the necessary food, and an order was blade by the magistrate for the payment of the very zeasonable amounCcharged. It is important as being the first case, and it will be a warning that the exist- ence of arrangements for feeding children who attend Ihe public elementary schools does not absolve from Parental responsibility. In Warrington, the Act has not yet been put into operation, though most of the Preliminary details have now been arranged. Garven Cottage is to be the centre for the provision of meals.
[FIIOII OUlt LONDON CORRESPONDENT.]

At a moment when home politics are temporarily la a state almost of suspended animation, the incident of the Premier's intervention regarding the ceremonial Procession of th 3 Eucharistic Congress has received, perhaps, a disproportionate amount of attention. The bY-election at Newcastle seems likely to be one in 'which local conditions will play a more prominent than any single outstanding issue, though the ,ers will certainly spare no pains to procure the Teturn of a candidate whose opposition to the Licens- ing Bill is uncompromising. An interesting announce- n3,.ent is made of a scheme of arbitration in industrial sputes which Mr. Churchill has prepared ; and the ederation of Welsh Free Churches has issued a fl_aanifesto to its constituent bodies, urging them to ee P the question of Welsh Disestablishment to the 4roat.
THE GRIEVANCES OF A MAJORITY.

Of all the problems with wliich serious statesman- P has to grapple it is a trite observation that none 4111 more embarrassing or distasteful than those which ,arise out of religious differences. They generally 'elle the form, as in this storm in a tea-cup, of finding Z.mertua virentli in which the rights or the suscepti- ilities of a minority will be sympathetically treat•cl Without irritating the majority. But the religious question in Wales is peculiar. There it is the majority. thich is labouring under an acute sense of grievances 4/10 Esta bushed Church in Wales is in the anomalou. Position of being associated in the minds of the people nst only with the predominance of a privileged 1 rninority over the wishes of the majority, but with alien habits of thought and speech. What Burke said 5 the ingrained instincts of Dissent in the people of ‘ute United States can be applied with great exact- to the population of Wales. And the fervour of elsh Nonconformity is invigorated by the strong cinscionsness of nationality. The Established Church is isolated in Wales alike through being out of tune n:ith the prevailing note of Welsh religious life and Ihrouo•h failing to respond to the national spirit. lab very recently the highest preferments in the lanrch fell to men who could not speak the native t?,ngne. The question of Welsh Disestablishment, narrows itself down to a very simple issue. It 3 not the principle of an Established Church that is !=in trial, but the anomaly of an Establishment that is la no true sense a national institution. THE DEPUTATION TO MR. ASQUITH. 1, The Federation of the Welsh Free Churches, which 'Las just issued its manifesto, sent a deputation, it be remembered, to Mr. Asquith on this question Disestablishment during the earlier part of the e'ession. The Prime Minister reminded the deputation °I the words which he used, a year before, when he Zeceived with the late Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman similar deputation of Welsh Members. He had then 42clared that he would regard it not only as a matter c't disappointment but of reproach if this Parliament rellle to an end before a Disestablishment Bill had I, en carried through the House of Commons. The atilae Minister went on to announce, on the part of "ie Government, that " most clean + ld distinctly it

Itat " mom. _ —rly an ...itinctly i - Ivas their hope and it was their intention, to submit text session to Parliament proposals dealing with this ' Ipatter." No one, as Mr. Asquith pointed out, can ,°rsee the course which events may take in the next relve months or two years, and the Government can 2,at indicate their hopes and intentions. But unless ' .0 flat) unforeseen emergency should arise to change , entirely the political perspective, the Government ' t.:lPect to have put the House of Commons in posses- ofli their proposals before the end of the session of e4O. A Liberal Government, of course, can only - Peak with assurance about the future of a Bill as far ,:ii its last stage in the House of Commons. It is only teenservative Premier who can treat the House of ; (3tds as a negligible factor. However large a follow- ill'g a Liberal Prime Minister commands, he knows Nat all his work may be undone in the Upper anther if the Leader of the Opposition chooses. AN ARBITRATION SCHEME. thlf Mr. Churchill's wedding does not quite come into category of political events, it is at least not thaPPropnate to notice the genial recognition which tqett?Pposition journals have given, on this occasion, 'Tr e hold which the young president of the Board of has obtained on the minds of his countrymen. ''ule great qualities," to quote from one of the kindly
IL

!references characteristic of the amiable side of English political life, " of pluck and independence of thought which distinguish him will never fail of their meed of appreciation in this country." One of the last acts of If r. Winston Churchill, at the Board of Trade, it appears before leaving the office to make preparations for his wedding, was to give the finishing touches to an important scheme for creating a permanent tribunal of arbitration. A panel is to be formed, composed equally of business men and Labour representatives, from which arbitrators can be selected to settle trade disputes, with another panel comprising "persons of eminence and impartiality " from which the chairmen of such courts can be drawn, while expert assessors may be appointed by the Board of Trade, at the request of the Court or of the parties, to explain the peculiar con- ditions of the trade to the Court. The Trade Union Congress has pronounced emphatically against compulsory arbitration. Whether the creation of this tribunal will remove the trade union opposition to compulsion, since Labour will be represented in equal proportions upon it, remains to be seen. But it is certain to promote a greater frequency of resort to arbitration, even though it still remains necessary for both parties to a dispute to make their applications, before the Board of Trade can intervene. The suffer- ing and loss involved in the stoppage of industries by strikes and lock-outs is so great—a fact driven home to us by the protracted strike in the North-East Coast and the threatened strike in the Lancashire cotton trade —that any step towards amelioration of this evil is an enormous boon to the community. THREE SPECIAL FEATURES.

It is not intended to supersede by this new standing Court any of the powers and functions conferred upon , the Board of Trade by the Conciliation Act of 1890. But there are three features in the constitution of the Court which avoid the chief difficulties that stand in the way of settlement by arbitration under existing conditions. Workmen frequently object to the appoint- 'meat of individual conciliators and trbitrators under the Conciliation Act, that, however fair they mean to be, they do not intimately understand the position of the manual labourer. Therefore the class of workmen and trade unionists will be represented on the new tribunal. It is said, too; by those who have had large experience of trade disputes, that workmen are more ready to submit to the judgment of twd of their representatives than one. By the appointment of two arbitrators from the employers' panel and two from the workinens' panel, in difficult cases, the decisions of the Court will be rendered more authoritative. Finally, to avoid the danger that the Court itself might become unpopular with either class in conse- quence of any particular discision, the personnel of the Court will be constantly varied.

An admirable bird's-eye view of the Liberal record since the General Election was offered by Dr. Nfacnainara in a speech at the opening of the Liberal Club at Crediton. This record, Dr. Ilacnamara said, presents four remarkable features. There is reorganization of nationat finance. There is the settlement of South African affairs on a secure and peaceful basis. There is the initiation of a scheme of old age pensions. And there is the harvest of social legislation gathered in by the patience and firmness of the Government, in spite of ." the storms and winds revelled against it by the House of Lords.

div.head: -BLESSINGS OF SOUND FINANCE.
div.p: THE -BLESSINGS OF SOUND FINANCE.

The obligation under which the people of this country lie to Mr. Asquith for bringing order and economy into the system of national finance is often overlooked, because it is a subject less exciting than matters of a more controversial nature. The Liberal Government has reduced the National Debt by 32 millions, and will have reduced it by 47 millions at the end of the financial year. It has raised no money by new taxation except the super-tax on the death duties, which falls on the shoulders best able to bear it. It has abolished a duty of Is. per ton on coal exports; it has taken Id. per pound oft the tea duty ; it has more than halved the sugar tax at a cost of over three millions ; and it has adjusted the income tax so that its burden is reduced by 25 per cent. upon four out of every five income-tax payers, without making the Treasury poorer by a single farthing. It is perhaps not irrelevant to recall in this connection the words in which the historian Lecky,commenting on the financial administration of Pitt, reminds his readers that financial questions, " resolving them- selves for the most part into dry and intricate details, make little show in history and rarely excite an enthusiasm or an interest at all commensurate with their importance. Nations seldom realise till too late how prominent a place a sound system of finance holds among the vital elements of national stability and well-being . . . . how widely and seriously human happiness is affected by the downfall or perturbation of national credit, or by excessive, !injudicious and unjust taxation."

-- Swimming Gala. The annual gala promoted by the Warrington Swimming Club will be held at the Corporation Baths on Thursday evening next, when the annual local championships will be decided, and a polo match played between Warrington and Leigh. Professor and Miss M. Barlow will give an exhibition of ornamental swimming. BUTTER and Bicox are much DEiRER.—Advt. Victoria Park Allotments. Yesterday the members of the Small Holdings and Allotments Committee, including Alderman Forshaw (chairman), inspected the allotments in Victoria Park, Latchford, and found everything in a satisfactory condition. There are twenty-three allotments and the rent of each is 17s, per annum. PROVISIONS ARE DEARER.—Advt.

Old-Age Pensions. The first meeting of the Warrington Old-Age Pensions Committee, which consists of the whole of the Town Council, will be held at the Pown Hall on Monday afternoon. The business will include the appointment of Chairman, Clerk and sub-committees and the selection of the districts for which such com- mittees shall act. The question of the representation of organizations outside the Council will also be considered.

PROVISIONS ARE DEARER.—Advt. Workingmen's Mission, Bank Quay. A. service of song entitled "Little Abe " or "Bishop of Berry Brow" was rendered on Wednesday evening, in the above schoolroom, by a choir consisting of about 35 of the members of the Women's Bible Class, assisted by about a dozen male voices (husbands or sons of the members). The singing was hearty and effective, reflecting credit upon Mrs. Moore (the leader of the class) who had trained the choir. The connective reading was given by Mr. George Dale, the pathetic and humorous life story of the " Little Bishop" holding the interest of the audience to the end. During the evening songs were rendered by Mrs. Tonga, Mrs. Highley, Mrs. Williams, and Mrs. Moore, a duet by Mrs. Marsh and Mrs. A. Edwards, quartettes by Mrs. Tonge, Mrs. W. Taylor, Ur. J. Peel, Mr. Cannon, and Mrs. Williams, Mrs. Thomas, Mr. Hackney, and Mr. Lawson. At the close of the service Mr. T. Dale expressed the thanks of the meeting to all who had contributed to the success of service. Mr. Perey Moore efficiently acted as accompanist.

BACON and HAMS are much DEARBR.—Advt. " Brotherhood" Meeting. A meeting of the newly-formed Brotherhood was held in the Upper Room in Regent-street on Sunday afternoon. The Rev. R. E. Letheren was in the chair and the attendance was very satisfactory. The lesson was read by Mr. Clatworthy and Mr. B. Few offered prayer. The address was given by Mr. A. S. Elliott who announced his subject as "A Despised Prophet," and said he might have dropped the adjective as it was the lot of prophets to be despised. He gave an account of the conditions of the national life in the prophet's time and developed in a very delightful way the prophet's own description of his call—that the word of the Lord came to him. These words were used as a central thought from which the speaker led his hearers to several excursions in various realms of experience showing .that God's revelation is made to he mind and conscience and that reason and faith both have their share in it. The address was listened towith the deepest interest and a helpful conversation lollowed.
BACON and HAMS are much DEARER,—Advt.

The Medical Officer of Health. Dr. T. Coote Hibbert, the Medical Officer of Health for Warrington, was one of the five candidates selected to appear before the Health Committee of the Black- pool Corporation yesterday, for the position of medical officer of health for that town. After interviewing the candidates, the Committee decided to recommend the appointment of Dr. Jones, of Lincoln. Music in the Park. - -

- The Warrington Borough Prize Brass Band will play the following programme of music in the Park to-naorrow.—llymn," Gladsome Bounds," J. A. Green- wood ; march, "Honest Toil," W. Rimmer ; overture, "Golden Star," J. A. Greenwood ; selection, "Bohemian Girl," Balfe ; selection, "11l Barbiere," Rossini ; " Hallelujah Chorus," Handel; " God save the King," Conductor, Mr. T. Griffin.

Band of Hope Conference. The fortieth annul Conference of the United Kingdom Baud of Hope Union has been held at Leeds this week and the enthusiasm characterizing the pro- ceedings has afforded convincing evidence of the vitality of the movement. Four thousand delegates have attendsd from all parts of the kingdom representing Band of Hope Unions and Junior Temperance Societies The Warrington Band of Hope Union representatives are Mr. George Whitfield and Mr. James Hamblett, whilst Mr. William Wright and Mr. H. Blacker al e the delegates from the Warrington District of the Independent Order of Rechabites.—A resolution in support of the Licensing Bill was passed. Last of an Old Church. _ .

The Scottish Presbyterian Church of St. John, in Winwick-street, Warrington, which is upwards of 100 years old, having become dilapidated and unsuitable for service, has been sold by treaty to Messrs. Guest, Brothers, tanners, for business developments. Bodies interred in the aisles have been exhumed and reintered in Warrington Cemetery. There were only two coffins, one, dated 1827, containing tho remains of the Rev. Alexander Hay, a former minister, and the other, dated 1838, containing the remains of Mrs. Bird, widow of a former minister. The church is a Lady Huntingdon church, and became Presbyterian in 1851. It is hoped to erect a new church in another part of the town. Harvest Festival at Golborne-street.

There was a large congregation at Golborne-street Baptist Church on Thursday evening,when the harvest thanksgiving services commenced. The church was beautifully decorated by the ladies of the church under the supervision of Mrs. B. Few, Mrs H. Buckby, Mrs. T. Davies, Mrs. Hanky and Mrs. Muir. The choir, conducted by Mr. C. Dawson, rendered special music in a highly creditable manner. Mr. S. Rickers presided at the organ. The Rev. Robert Lewis,of Black- burn (late of Prince's Gate, Liverpool) preached a highly appropriate sermon for the times, dealing with the unemployed and the social problem. The pro- ceedings were brought to a close by an anthem beautifully rendered by th 3 choir. To-morrow (Sunday) Rev. R. E. Letheren will preach at 10.45 and 0.30, and will conduct a Bible object service at 2.30 when the chair will be taken by Mr. Tames Dodds. On Thursday evening a harvest supper will be held. Ancient Order of Foresters.

The monthly meeting of Court 210 A.0.F., was held at the Roe Buck Hotel on Saturday evening last, when the members were called upon to accept the resignation of Chief Ranger Bro. George Reeves, who is about to leave England for China, to take up an important appointment which he has secured there. —The resignation was accepted with very much regret, and the District Chief Ranger (Bro. W. Smith) was asked to present to Bro. Reeves a dressing case and illuminated address, together with a Past Chief Ranger's ribbon, presented by the Court as a mark of their esteem. —Bro. Smith, in making the presentation referred to the valusble services rendered to Forestry, by Bro. Reeves, and wished him every success in his new venture.—After a suitable reply from Bro. Reeves, the business of the evening was proceeded with, and Bro. Smith gave an account of his stewardship as the District Delegate to the High Court of the Order held at Northampton, which position he has filled with distinction. PROVISIONS ARE DEARER.—Advt. Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Church. Harvest thanksgiving services were held at this church on Sunday and were largely attended, the church being crowded in the evening. The Rev. E. Blanshard Keeling preached at the morning service and in the evening the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. F. Walwyn Kernick, the discourses of both these newly appointed ministers creating a favourable impression. The choir rendered special music, Mr. E. G. flickers presiding at the organ and Mr. Muir conducting. On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held and occasion was taken to extend a hearty welcome to the Rev. F. W. Kernick whose new sphere of labour will be largely in the Sankey Bridges district. Speeches were made by Messrs. Charles Jones, J. Wadsworth, C. Johnson and I. Johnson, and the Rev. F. W. Kernick warmly acknowledged the greeting.An excellent programme was submitted,items being contributed by Mrs.Cope,Miss Cartledge,Miss M. Moody, Miss Seddon, Mr. C. Jones. Mr. E. G. Rickers played the accompaniments. BACON and HAMS are much DEARER.—Advt.

1 Warrington Adult School. On Saturday evening Dr. C. R. Brown, of the Infirmary, was entertained at a supper and social at Atkinson's Cafe by the members of the Adult School and their wives. Dr. Brown,cvlio was the secretary one of the organizers of the school about eighteen months lage, is shortly leaving Warrington. The school which has now a membership of forty,owes much of its success to his work. The chair was taken by Mr. IL Gray, in the absence of the presid.vit, Mr. John Ransoms. The following programme l'as rendered : —Pianoforte solo by Mr. W.Pemberton ; song, Mr. E.Jonss song, Mr. G. Bennett; conjuring entertainment, Mr. Lloyd; humorist, Mr. Da.rbyshire ; song, Mr. Wilson. During the interval a presentation in the form of a framed photograph of the members of the class was made to Dr. C. IL Brown, who replied, thanking one and all for their kindness, and was greeted by the singing of "He's a jolly good fellow." After a few remarks by Messrs. Elwell, C. Cox, Clair, John Morton (vice- president) and J. A. Bradley (secretary), the rest of the programme followed, and a most enjoyable evening was br9ught to a close with the usual vote of thanks to the chairmen, artistes, &c. BUTTER and BACON are much DTIARER.—Advt. Crystal Palace Band Festival. This great festival, the ninth of its kind, will be held at the Crystal Palace on Saturday next. Local interest in the event is particularly keen, owing to the fact that the Perfection Soap Works Band will com- pete in the championship section for the one thousand guinea trophy. The contest will be exceptionally keen, the entrants including no fewer than five previ- ous winners of the trophy-1000 Denton Original, 1902 Black Dike Mills, 1905 Irwell Springs, 1000 Wingates Temperance, 1907 Wingates Temperance (second time). The test piece is a grand selection , from Wagner's " Rienzi " arranged by Mr. S. Cope, a !gentleman who has been prominent in the brass band world ever since he was fourteen years old, and is himself a judge of the first rank. The railway authorities are again running hundreds of excursions into London and it will be difficult to name a town or village from which intending visitors cannot obtain cheap facilities. The great evening concert will be given by twelve of the best brass bands in the Kingdom— in fact, the world ; and included amongst the new , works which will be performed is another interesting work from Mr. Cope's pen entitled " A Rural Wedding." TRAVELLING TRUNKS, ETC., compare Our quality and prices. Dress Baskets from 155.—J. S• GARLAND, 51, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Local Exhibitors at the Royal Photographic

Show. The fifty-third annual exhibition of the Royal Photographic Society of Great Britain was opened in the New Gallery, Regent-street, W., on Thursday. No aspect of the art appears to be neglected. There is a pictorial section, a department devoted to scienitic and technical work, a large collection of work by pro- fessionals, many beautiful examples of colour photo- graphy, and a comprehensive assortment of the latest apparatus and material. The three galleries, with the balcony and fountain court, are utilised to their utmost capacity, and the result is a display full of interest to all devotees of the camera. Our readers will be pleased to hear that works of two of our local photographers find a place in the exhibition. In the pictorial section which includes over 300 works, covering the whole field of photographic art, Mr. Henry Bond, of Warrington, has a picture entitled " The frozen Mere." The scientific and technical exhibits are a fascinating feature of the show, for they comprise many charming studies of animal, bird and fish and vegetable life, photo- micropaphs, radiographs, cloud and lightning effects and astronomical subjects. Mr. Arthur Frost, of Newton-le-Willows, has been highly successful in this department with sir lantern slide studies of bird' nests and eggs Mr. Frost is photographer to Messrs. Gartons, Ltd., Warrington.

div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
BOLD HIGHWAY ROBBER.-GIRL ASSAULTED
IN -R-te-ORK

A daring highway robbery with violence took place at Runcorn on Monday morning, the victim being Miss Gertrude Rowland, a school teacher, at Colne, near Skipton, Yorkshire, who had been spending a few days with her mother at Eversley, Higher Runcorn.—Miss Rowland intended to travel by the 4.50 Liverpool r express, and on approaching the station a man on a bicycle passed her. Under the station railway arch the man jumped from his macjaine, met her, and, seizing her by the shoulders, threw her violently to the ground and maltreated her. Ho then snatched the satchel, con- taining gold bangles,money, &0., and afterwards jumped on his bicycle and raced away. Miss Rowland's agonised screams were heard by a number of people on the station platform, and a porter and a postman ran to the spot and found her in a collapsed condition. Her assailant is described as a short, thick-set man of dark complexion. The police have been unable to trace him. Miss Rowland suffers severely from shock.

div.head: INCREASE or RATES.
div.p: INCREASE or RATES.

THE COST OF MAIN ROADS. The Clerk submitted his estimate of expenditure for the half-year ending 31st March, 1909. The probable expenditure on common fund expenses was £5,367, less probable receipts, £2,100 ; county rate £9,709, con- tingencies £3,721, total £16,397. Deducting the probable balance of £2,691 at September 30th, left a net expendi- ture to be provided for of £13,706. The assessable value of the Union is £237,811 and a rate of Is. 2d. in the £ would produce £13,872. It was recommended that a call for that amount be made on the overseers, being an increase of 3d. in the £ on the corresponding period of last year. The Clerk said he expected the members would con- sider it was a tremendous increase but it was accounted for entirely by the increase in the county rate. Last half-year tne advance in the County rate was made after the calls had been made upon the overseers and proved to be 11d. in the £ more than they had previously collected. It was estimated that they would require a further 11d. and as no provision was made last half-year the full 3d. had to be met this half-year. The parish of Runcorn would be still more heavily taxed on account of school erections and their c^ll would work out at about Is. 4d.
The Chairman : That is the Urban District of Runcorn?

The Clerk : Yes. He also added that the two parishes of 14 nitley would be rather heavily taxed because they had special calls upon them in connection with schools. The amounts required would be :—Whitley Inferior, £O4 ; Whitley Sul )rior, £lOO ; which worked out at about is. 51.
Mr. Roylance : What is the cause of this extra 31. ? The Clerk : A great deal of it is the expenditure on main roads.
The Chairn-ln : Then there have been many schools built all over the county. Mr. Hallow: Are we going to swallow this sugar- coated uill without a protest ? _ _ .

The uterk: You have already made a protest, I think. Mr. Hallows : It has not been strong enough. It is time there was a stop somewhere. We cannot go on paying like this for ever. It is an increase every time. It is all nonsense to say they are as careful as they can be. They spend as much as they can, and it is time something was stopped. It may be that in some parts of the county there is plenty of money, but in our neighbourhood people are feeling it very keenly. The Chairman: It is the same all over the county.

- - Alderman Norman said the whole of the increase or nearly the whole of it was owing to the increased cost of main roads. No one regretted more than he did the necessity for increasing the rates but it was there and what could they do ? The County Council this year had had to spend between £B,OOO and £lO,OOO more on main roads than they expected. Mr. Hallows : Let those who spoil our roads pay for them. I don't think we ou;ht to go on making roads for these chaps. If these motor cars belonged to workingmen they would have been stopped twelve months ago but because they belong to big folks and magistrates they will go on for ever. The Chairman : IL is not only motor cars. It is the heai y traffic. I Alderman Norman : The County Council has no I power to tax these motor cars and traction engines but they have appealed to the Government to help them in dealing with this extraordinary expense. That is all they can do. The estimates were approved. div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
ALLEGED CYCLE THEFT.

At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Tuesday. William Cowell, of no fixed abode, was charged with breaking and entering the Liverpool Farm School at Newton-le-Willows, between August 29th and 30th, and stealing a bicycle and a suit of clothes. The evidence showed that an entrance had been effected by unfastening the catch of a sitting-room window, and the articles were missed. Prisoner attempted to pawn the bicycle for £l, saying that it belonged to his brother, but the pawnbroker, being suspicious,informed the police, and he was arrested. The magistrates com- mitted him for triarto the Liverpool Quarer Sessions. The Prescot police have also a similar charge against prisoner.

, MR. SEDDON, M.P. AND THE LICENSING BILL. Speaking at a non-party meeting in support of the Licensing Bill at Wavertreo on Monday evening, Mr J. A. Seddon, M.P.,said he was there as a representative of Labour in the British House of Commons. That party was supporting the present Licensing Bill. Those who were responsible for leading the forces of labour that day recognised that sobriety, if labour was to have its share of the wealth, must be one of its leading factors and forces. Proceeding, Mr. Seddon referred to the chief points of the Licensing Bill,and added that it was not a teetotal bill. It was a citizens' bill in the direction of sobriety. (Applause.) It was a wise' statesmanlike measure. It was one of the boldest things that had been attempted in the lifetime of any of them thero dealing with the licensing question. So far as the time-limit in the bill was concerned it was more than just. The bill gave to the community the power, through local option, to say how many public. houses there should be. It laid down, so far as the children were concerned, that they should be kept away from the public-house. He opposed grooers' licencea. (Applause.) He was prepared at any time to vote for their abolition.

div.head: ST HELENS.
div.p: ST HELENS.
IN PRAISE OF ST. HELENS.
"Itis a very goad little town. 1 have tramped the towns up from Cardiff to here, and this is one of the best," said an itinerant vocalist to the St. Refers Bench on Monday. CRUELTY TO A BLIND WOXLIN.

John Hanley, of Victoria-street. Winn, who is partially blind, was sent to prison for six months by the St. Helens magistrates on Monday for throwing cayenne pepper into the face of a blind woman named Clara Peacock. She is separated from her husband, and has lived with the prisoner at Wigan for several years. A few days ago she left him in consequence of his brntality. He came to St. Helens, and whilst he was in Bridge-street be met her begging for alms, and asked her to go back to hire and threatened her several times. On Saturday night prisoner threw something in her face, which was found to be cayenne. When arrested at the railway station a packet of cayenne was found in his bag.

div.head: ANOTHER PLAYGROUND.
div.p: ANOTHER PLAYGROUND.

At the St. llelens -Parks Committee mee ' tia',, on Wednesday, Mr. Pugh asked if the ParliarneataryCom- mittee had done anything in the matter of securing laud on Hardshaw Fields for a playground.—Mr. Peet (chairman) said that nothing deGnite had been done.— Mr. Pugh said he did not intend to raise that question before the November elections lest his friend Mr. John Phythian should say he had done it because of the elections, but the matter had been discussed publicly, and he suggested that they should ask the Parliamen- tary Committee to deal with it. The railway company might let them have land near their line.—Mr. John Phythian said that if Mr. Pugh got beaten, and did not return to the Council, the matter would not be forgotten. —Mr. Pugh said he was glad to know that the work of the ward would b& carried on by Mr. Phythian. He moved that the Parliamentary Committee be asked to move in the matter in view of the d'stress in the town. —Mr. Woodward seconded, and this was agreed to.

ST. HELENS LICENCES TRANSFERRED. The Mayor (Alderman H. Martin) presided at the licensing transfer sessions for the borough of St. Helens on Monday. Richard Leadbetter asked for the licence of the Victoria Vaults, 32, Ellarnbridge-road, Sutton, and said he had kept the Rolling Mill beerhouse, Sutton, for twenty-four years. The previous tenant, Henry Wood, was reported by Caief-Inspector Goodall as having beea fined £5 and costs for allowing drunken- ness after hours on April 21th last. The transfer was granted, as well as of the following full licences :—Star Inn, Merton Bank-road, from John 11. Walker to Alfred A. Holland ; Elephant Inn, GO, Elephant-lane, from George Parr to Thomas Boardman •, Vine Tavern, 16, Elephant-lane, from Paul Owen to George Parr • Bridge Hotel, 15, Liverpool-road, from Thomas Hartley to Ellen Hartley. Beersellers : Rolling Mill Tavern, 31, Rolling Mill-lane, from Peter Leadbetter to John Cobb. —Mr. Haslam Fox made application for leave to make alterations at the Bull and Dog public-house, Marshall's Cross-road, by rearranging the interior and constructing a larger clubroom upstairs. He also mentioned that on the opposite side of the road Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. proposed to widen a rather dangerous place by putting down a weighing-machine and setting the fence 18ft. back.—The Mayor, after the plan had been dis- cussed, asked if it was proposed to use the clubroom for drinking purposes.—Mr. Fox said that at present they only used the room for parties, meetings, and festivities.—The bench granted the application on con- dition that an undertaking to this effect was given, and also that a plan of the alteration on the opposite side of the road be submitted. STRUM TROUBLES.
THREATS TO NON-UNIONISTS AT ST. HELENS.

The St. Helens magistrates completed on Tuesday the hearing of two sammonses for intimidation against William Curley, of Oxford-strect, the prosecutor being George Nicholson. The inciden's of the case have arisen in connection with tho moulders' strike at St. Helens, Curley being one of the society men on strike, and Nicholson a non-society man at present working in the town. Nicholssn and other non-society men had lodged in Charles-street, end every rOght had to be escorted from the Brookfield works to their lodgings by policemen. It was alleged that Curley met Nicholson in the street and said to him, " We 1-we got you marked, you had better be careful. You know the dark nights are coming on. "If the blue bottles' had not been with you at 5.30 to-night we would have pot you out." In consequence of these threats prosecutor and the other non-society men were afraid to go out after dark.—Nicholson was severely cross-examined by Mr. W. Hutchens, who appeared for defendant. He admitted he had had considerable trouble with the Moulders' society in Manchester, but a slander sction was pending by him against an official of the society. He denied that he had been fined as a book-maker in Manchester, or that he had been expelled from the society for obtaining contributions by false pretences, but he said that, in consequence of the trouble he had had with the soicety, he had twice attempted to commit suicide.— Defendant and a number of the strikers gave a com- plete denial to prosecutor's story.—The Bench considered the charge of intimidation proved, and bound defendant over for six months.

The European Baptist Conference. At a social hold in the Baptist Schoolroom, Latch- ford, on Mondays, evening, the Rev. J. F. Matthews gave an address on b;s recent visit to the European Baptist Conference recently held in Berlin. After describing some of the meetings he said the remark- able feature about the gathering was that all Europe was practically represented, Baptists coining from Belgium, Bulgaria, Denmark, Germany, the British Isles, France, Holland, Italy, Hungary, Roumania, North, South and West Russia, Livonia, Fin- land, Sweden, Switzerland, as well as Jamaica, America, South Africa and India. (Applause.) So eager were the promoters of the Congress that there should be this wide representation that the poorer delegates 4.70 M Russia and Bulgaria and other places not only had their travelling expenses paid but were proslded for while in the city.(Applause.)As to the probable effects of the Conference, Mrafatthews said it would cement the bonds of brotherhood between the Baptists of the various nationalities and promote the peace spirit tl—oughout the countries represented. Their() would be an increased spirit of toleration and a broadening of human sympathy towards all sorts and conditions of believers and 'unbelievers. The Baptist Churches of Germany \Niue particularly alive, at least two of them in Berlin having over 1,000 meml ;rs each. Certainly Baptists had no need to despair, for throughout Europe they were on the increase. A Labour leader was also a Socialist and a High Church- man, after askindmany vigorous questions about the Baptists, said to Dr. Clifford, "Your religion is just the religion that we men are looking for Why don' you let us know all about it." Ho (Mr. Matthews) had come back prepared to let the people "know all about it." (Applause).—The Ilev.C. Harvey Cook expressed the pleasure it afforded him to be present and said he was delighted the church at Latchford had been able to send llr.Mattliews to Berlin. He hoped they would save up and send him in 1910 to tne "Baptist World Alliance "to be held in America. (Laughter and applause.)—Songs were contributed during the evening by Miss Bacon, Miss Winnie 'Jones, Master Harold Jones, and Mr. Trovr, who also acted as accompanist and played several pianoforte solos. A duet was well rendered by Mr. Trow and Mr. Banner. Light refreshments were provided.

div.head: FIVE NEW SCHOOLS.
div.p: FIVE NEW SCHOOLS.
Serious Lack of Accommodation to be Met.

At the meeting of the Education Committee on Monday evening, the question of school accommodation will have to be faced. The School Attendance Corn mittee's minutes state : "A statement was subs itted showing the school accommodation and the number of children in all the elementary schools. As it appe.tred that in addition to a present financial loss t here was an immediate prospect of more serious loss owing to the reduction of grants by the Board of Education, it was resolved (a) that the Education Committee b 3 recom- mended to instruct tab Sites and Building Committee to proceed forthwith with the provision of a site and school to serve the requirements of the inhabitants of the West end of St. Austin's Ward ; (b) that the attention of the Education Committee and the Town Council be called to the necessity for further school accommodation in other parts of the town, and that instructions be given to the Sites and Buildings Corn- mittee to provide sites and schools in the following wards, viz. :—Fairfield, Orford, St. John's and \ V hi tecross."
THE ACCOMAIODATION REQUIRED.
DIRECTOR OF EDUCATION'S EXH.AUSTIVE REPORT.

In the course of a lengthy report, Mr. J. Moore Murray estimates the number of children of school-age in Warrington at 15,010 on the ratio of one to every 473 of the population. lie adds : It'would appear from the figures given that the supply of increased accommodation for the normal growth of the popula- tion has been met during the last few years by (1) the provision of the Beamont and the Bolton Council schools, (2) the exclusion from the schools of children under four years of age, and (3) the retention of older scholars in infants' schools and their instruction there as senior scholars. The last two methods of meeting the increase of children in the town cannot be further extended without educational loss to the children and financial loss to the Committee. The immediate difficulty of meeting the normal growth of the population is increased by the fact that, in February last, the Board intimated their intention of surveying the whole of the schools in the Borough for the purpose of re-assessing their accommodation so as to secure a minimum floor space of ten square feet for each child. The preliminary steps have already been taken by the Board's officers, and no doubt before long a revision of the accommodation on that basis will ba made. Bearing this in mind, it is perhaps necessary to explain some of the figures in table A. Towti HALL WARD.—The figures for this ward show an apparent excess of accommodation of 565 places, but it will be seen that 253 of these places are in Infants' schools, which have fewer children at this time of the year than at any other time. Thus, the normal excess of accommodation is to be found in the boys' department of the Heathside and the Mixed department of the Wycliffe schools, but both of these schools are at present quite full, and it would be impossible to arrange for another class in either. Assuming that the Board of Education reduces the accommodation to the ten feet basis, the accommodation in this ward would be reduced I to 2,085 which would mean that there would be 180 more children in the schools than they could accommo- date. Fortunately, the population in this district is not growing so rapidly as in other districts, but, in I considering the accommodation of the ward, it would be unwise to ignore the condition' of the Wycliffe school.

ST AusTnes Warw.—This ward is divided into two distinct parts by the L. and N.-W. Railway. On the East side there are two schools for senior children, the Arpley-street and the Trinity schools, accommodating 1,038 children, whilst on the West there is the Sacred Heart school, accommodating 172 senior children. A glance at the figures will show that, even upon the present basis, the schools are quite full, and, when it is remembered that the Board of Education have allowed the continued use of the Trinity Infants' school on the understanding that the Committee are supplying a new school in thedistrict, and that last year the Government gave the Committee a final warning with respect to the Sacred Heart school, it will be seen that a new school is an immediate necessity in this district. On the ten feet basis the accommodation would be 1,923, or a deficiency of 390 places. Sr. JOHN'S WARD.—The figures for this ward show that there is an available accommodation of 1,071 places for 914 children, leaving 128 vacant places, but, on the revised basis, the number of places would be 933, bringing the available accommodation to 41 places fewer than the number of children already in the schools. For several years the Board of Education have complained of the overcrowding of the Hamilton- street school, and einally children had to be excluded therefrom. It will be seen that, although the Beamont Council school has only been opened for eighteen months, the Hamilton-street school is again over- crowded. SEWSEY WArtD.—This ward contains the smallest number of inhabitants, and there is in it only one school, which provides accommodation for 93 more children than are on the registers. Included in this accommodation, however, are two rooms which have already been condemned by the Board of Education, so that the accommodation of this school on the revised basis would be only 530, leaving a deniency of 103 places for children already attending the school. WHITECROSS WARD is one of the most rapidly grow- ing parts of the town, having in 1901 a population of 7,480. There is only one school in the ward, and this has 35 more children in attendance than there is room for. For several years this school has been overcrowded and each year it has been necessary to take steps, resulting in the disorganisation of the school, in order to avoid the grant being withdrawn. The population in this district is still rapidly increasing, and, before I long, there will be no site for a school available. The revised accommodation of this school would provide for 108 fewer children than there are at present attend- ing the school. ORFORD WARD.—The number of children in attend- ance at the schools in this ward is at the present moment 273 more than there is available accommoda- tion for, notwithstanding the fact that the Beamont Council school, providing accommodation for 1,080 I children, was only opened last year. The schools in this II area are supplying the needs of the adjacent wards. On the revised basis the other two schools will lose 127 placer', making the number of available places 400 fewer I than there are children now attending the schools. HOWLEY WARD.—The accommodation in this ward falls short of the number of the children in the schools by 13, but, on the revised figures, it would be 214 less. FAIRFIELD WARD.—Thero is only One Wheel in this ward, accommodating 730 scholars, or 17 more than there are in attendance. There is no accommodation whatever for older boys in the ward. On the revised figures there would be accommodation for 19 fewer children, and two less than are now in attendance. LATCHFORD WARD.—The accommodation in this ward now provides places for 293 more children than are in attendance. The number of children in the schools has increased since the opening of the Bolton Council school without any reduction in the number in the other schools. The revised accommodation would I be 1,780 0r:62 more places than there are children in the lschools. - -

In 'order to show more clearly the effect of the re-assessment of the accommodation, table fl is appended. From this it will be seen that there will be a loss of 2,305 existing places, and a shortage of accom- modation for the scholars already on the rolls of the schools of 1.382 places. THE NEW SCHOOL AT STOCKTON HEATH.

The preliminary arrangements for the erection of the new Council school at Stockton Heath are in progress and the construction of a 401 t. street from the Red Lion Inn to Walton-road, to be called West Avenue, has commenced. The site of the school is on the northerly side of the proposed new street. Mr. C. W. Davenport has obtained the building contract, and Mr. Holt, of Manchester, is the architect. The new school will at first provide places for 500 children and ultimately it may be extended to accommodate an additional 300. The church school is also to be extended at a cost of £7OO or £BOO.

div.head: WARRINGTON PARLIAMENfARY DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON PARLIAMENfARY DEBATING SOCIETY.

This Society which had so successful a run last season opens its new session on Thursday next. From present appearances there is every indication of another successful season, for the membership which numbered upwards of 200, is expected to 1. ) largely increased, and further members are already being enrolled. The Liberal party were in office last season and as they were undefeated, owing evidently to the "wise legislation " which they placed before the House, and also to the co-operation of their own party, and members of the Socialist and Nationalist Party, they will again resume office. The first meeting will be a business meeting—to elect officials and to pass and revise rules. Afterwards the King's speech will be presented, in which the Bill to be laid before tho House during the coming session will be announced. The headquarters of the Society will be up to the end of November in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street.

SACRED CONCERT AT THE HIPPODROME. How deeply the sympathy of Warringtonians has been stirred on behalf of the sufferers by the Wigan colliery disaster was evident from the very large audience which assembled at the sacred concert promoted by Mr. Frank Macnaghten and held at the Palace and Hippodrome on Sunday evening in aid of the Mayor of Warrington's fund. The spacious building was filled in every part and so many sought admission to the circle that there was not seating accommodation for all. The Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Smethurst) were present. The public spirit which prompted Mr. Macnaghten to lend the theatre free of any charge was everywhere warmly commended and the audience also expressed vets, cordial appreciation of the efforts of the local artistes who so readily responded to the call of charity and gave their services. A high class programme was submitted and afforded much pleasure. Miss Marie Houghton maintained her high reputation by the tasteful and expressive manner in which she sang "I know that my Redeemer liveth " (llanael), and "Nearer my God to Thee" (Caret,), her sweet voice being used with beautiful effect. Mr. J. Rabbitt was suffering from a cold and hardly did himself justice in Gounod's exacting composition "Lend me your aid " but he interpreted "The Sailor's grave " (SaUiran) with a soulfulness which appealed to all: Mr. J. B. Poole submitted " Nazareth " (Goanol) and " Veen art passing hen ca " (Sullivan) with appropriate felling. Mr. W. Ryder's cornet solos " The Lost Chord " (Salli ran) and" The Better Land" (Cowca) were creditably performed and proved very acceptable. The attractiveness of the programme was con- siderably enhanced by the selections of the augmented Palace orchestra under the baton of Mr. Ernest A. Widdop. The items presented were the overture "Raymond " (Thomas) selection from " 12th Mass " (Mozart), overture Pique dame " (Suppe) and War March " from " Athalie " (Mendessoltn) and the varied beauties of these popular com- positions were well brought out, the effect being altogether pleasing. The orchestra consisted of the following I.—First violins, Messrs. R. H. Pearson (principal), Ainscough, Boothroyd, Mellor, Green and Barnshaw ; second violins, Messrs. Dainty, Wood, Leslie and Frain ; violas, Messrs. Balmford and Scott ; 'cellos, Messrs. Balinford, Phillips and Jackson ; basso. Messrs. Peck and Allen ; oboes, Messrs. Davies ffEd Stanley ; flutes, Messrs. Freeman and Podmore ; clarionettes, Messrs. Payne and Lamb, bassoon, Mr. Convery ; cornets, Messrs. Ryder and Mahoney ; trombones, Messrs. Rawes and Higgs ; euphonium, Mr. Bedforth : tympani, Ste., Mr. Dandas ; accompanist, Mr. W. Latham.

I Befoi:ii-tiie concert closed the NIAYOR took the oppor- tunity of thanking the townspeople for the generous way in which they had responded to his appeal.lt spoke volumes for their sympathy with the dependents of the miners who met their death in the pit disaster that he had been able to forward to the Mayor of Wigan no less than £lOO in the course of a fortnight. Another I £5O would be forwarded early in the week. It had been decided to keep the fund open until Tuesday, the 22nd inst.,as Messrs.Crosideld's Band intended to give another 'concert in that theatre on Sunday. Having expressed regret that the Mayor of Wigan was unable to attend, his Worship warmly acknowledged the generosity of Mr. Macringhten in granting the free use of the theatre. He also thanked Mr. Bradbury, the manager ; Mr. Mainwaring, jun., who originally intended to promote a concert on his own account, but at his (the Mayor's) suggestion decided to co-operate in that effort ; the soloists, orchestra and staff of the theatre, and all who had in any way assisted. Mr. BRADBURY briefly thanked the Mayor for his attendance, and said that whenever there was a good cause to be supported, his Worship was always to the fore. The singing of the hymn " Through the night of doubt and sorrow," in xvhichldie whole audience joined, brought the proceedings to a close. CLOSING OF THE FUND. Our readers are reminded that the Mayor's fund will be closed on Tuesday next. CONCERT BY PERFECTION SOAP WORKS BAND.

A sacred concert in aid of the relief fund will be given at the Palace and Hippodrome to-morrow (Sunday) evening, by the Perfection Soap Works Band assisted by Mr. J. W. Willett (tenor). A most attrac- tive programme has been arranged and there should be a crowded attendance. Plan of reserved seats may be seen at Wadsworth's, Sankey-street.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

There is a capital programme at the Palace this week, the comic element predominating, so that those feeling.;:- - the need to laugh and grow fat should not fail to see - the show at one of the two " houses " this evening. The Ten Loonies are apparently inmates of a private •,- •asylum, judging by the St-up of the stage, and their i 's peculiar form of insanity has obviously run wildly . into music. Each man appears " dotty: " in the • - musical sketch of the name, until the opening bars of - . some popular selection are struck up and then the troupe chimes in with some really clever instrumental music. Mimicry, music, and idiocy are cleverly intermingled and a bright and busy turn is the out- -- come. There is nothing like the Ten Loonies''- outside Winwick or some similar institution. A charming comedienne and dancer is Mabel/e : • May, whose high kicking and cart-wheel terpsi- chorean feats are worthy of admiration. Jack Lane, described as "the Yorkshire rustic at the VV V - piano," is responsible for many of the shrieks of merriment. His make-up is screamingly funny to begin with, and when he gets to work with his vocal chords combined with pianistic effects he brings down the house. One feat of Jack Lane's is to play different tunes on the piano with his right and left hands and sing a song (also different) simultaneously. Lawrence Barclay earns plenty of applause as a character comedian, and has a capital song for each role that he • assumes. As "the pet of the ballet, who ought to • be hit with a mallet "—to quote the song —he is to t • • - funny for mere newspaper description. Gibbon and - Bell give an acrobatic and dancing turn, quite out of the ordinary. The lady dances airily, while her male partner does some amazing contortions in the back- ground. He ought to be described as the human snake, for we should not have thought the frame of mere man could be twisted into such postures. Jimmie Laurie has a smart turn as patter comedian, and takes you on from one laugh to another without a stop. A charming soprano vocalist is Georgina Middleton, whose sweet yet powerful voice is heard to great advantage in a couple of songs, of which Annie Laurie "is the favourite. The orchestra gives several tasteful selections and Raymond's bio-tableaux wind up the programme with a series of striking pictures. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. A bright and interesting programme is announced for next week. The bill is headed by the Tally Ho! Trio who will appear in their latest comedy and harmonising vocal act. Kelly and Ashley will present their original comedy act "Fun in a billiard saloon" and other contributors to the entertainment will be:— Polly and Elsie, dainty duettists and dancers; Jock Walker, Scotch comedian and whistler; Cullen tmd. earthy and little Cluley, the premier comedians; Bertha Winders the dancing marvel; Three Slaters Silcott, vocalists and dancers.
