div.head: GARDEN PARTY.
div.p: GARDEN PARTY.
MR. AND MRS. ZIBA ARMITAGE ENTERTAIN CHESHIRE LIBERALS. -- Mr. A.. J. King, M.P. and Oa Unemployed Problem.

Mr. and Mrs. Ziba Armitage gave a garden party to local members of the Knutsford Division Liberal Asso- ciation at Newton Bank, Preston Brook, on Saturday afternoon. Delightful weather favoured the event and the visitors spent a most enjoyable time in strolling about the pretty and well kept grounds or indulging in games of bowls and croquet. Light refreshments were provided in the house, the catering being in the hands of the Winmarleigh Cafe Co. The garden party hai been arranged with the object of affording the visitors an opportunity of meeting Mr. Alfred J. King, the member for the division, Mrs. King and the racers of the Association. Mr. and Mrs. King motored to Preston Brook accompanied by their two sons, Masters J. F. 0. , and P. F. King, and received a hearty greet- ing. Amongst others present were :—Miss Lee (Broughton Park), Miss Leo (KersaH, M. J. Deakin, Mr. Harold Lee. Mr. Kenneth Leo, 11r. Cedric Lee, Mr. end Mrs. R. Billington, Mr. Thomas Miller. Mr. and Mrs. Josiah Longland, Miss Bcasie Dutton, Mrs. Darby- shire, Rev. J. S.and Mrs. Hughes. Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Billington, Mr. and Mrs. John Rose, Mr. and Mrs. Lightfoot, Mr. Henry Booth, Mr. and Mrs. B. Lloyd Jones, Mr. H. P. Greg, Mr. Alfred Atkins, Mr. Mark Mounfleld, Mr. Joseph Smith (divisional secretary) and _

Mrs. Smith. In the evening a short meeting was held, when Mr. King delivered an interesting speech on the work of the Government. Mr. Armitage presided and reed a letter of apology for non-attendance from Mr. W. H. Sherburn, who said that in Mr. Ring they had a representative of whom they had good cause to be proud. Whatever motives inspired many men to seek a seat in Parliament, they had already had proof that with their Member, dis- interested motives, working for the good of his fellows without fear or favour had characterised his tenure of &Ice so far. Might he live long to continue that good work for peace. retrenchment, and reform. (Applause.) Mr. A. J. King, M.P. said he must first express his thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Armitage for giving him that opportunity of meeting a few of his cons'ituents who lived in a rather remote part of the division. It was important that such meetings should take place. for he found that the atmosphere of the House of Commons had the effect in some ways of making one lose one's perspective and it was therefore a good thing now and then to come down into the country, meet one's constituents face to face and see how the work which was going on in Parlia nent pre- sented itself to them. That night he was going to London on his way to Berlin to take part in the inter- Parliamentary Conference which was to be held there and which he hoped would do something, if only little, to promote that good feeling between this country and other civilized nations which they were all so anxious to promote and maintain. (Applause). With reeard to the position of the present Government, he did not know what his hearers felt, but he for his owe part had never regretted for one moment any action he took or any part he played in bringing about a change of Government in MI. (Applause). Ile thought they all came to the conclusion that they had had quite enough of the Tory ways and it was time the Liberals came into &lice to see what they could do. Of course, the Government had not been without its critics,—no Government that was doing any good ever was—brit there was this satisfaction about the CRITICISMS OF THE PRESENT GOVERNMENT —that they came from two entirely opposite sides. On the one hand they were told that they were doing nothing for the working-men and that no one was any the better for their having bean in office. On the other hand, they had the more timid people who said they were rushing on revolutionary courses, that they were encouraging policies of depredation and that, in other words, the whole country was going to the dogs owing to their Radical and revolutionary policy. He did not think the truth was with either of those statements. It lay in between. The Government had been carrying tent the Libor 11 policy of steady, well considered progress, and had endeavoured to fulfil their election pledges to do whet they could gradually to improve the conditions of living for the great masses of the people of this country. That was the whole character of their work and the fact that it had been almost entirely devoted to home and social legislation showed what had been their aim. He admitted there was a great deal yet to do. We were faced this winter and even at the present time with that TERRIBLE AND URGENT PROBLEM of unemployment. He did not know what the solution was going to to and it was not much consolation to us—though we must not forget it—to know that in other countries which were highly protected, the con- ditions of unemployment were worse than they were here. Whereas the percentage of unemployment in England was 9 per cent. in Germany it was something like 25 per cent. while in the United States 30 per cent. of the trade unionists were out of work. That was not much comfort to us, but it was a warning that the remedy of the tariff reformers was not the remedy we should seek. He thought our Free Trade policy had been more than justified by the record of the past three years. Whilst our Government had teen paying off debt at an unprecedented rate—he believed they had paid off some- thing like 50 millions in three years—we found that Germany was constantly faced with deficits. They were now faced with a deficit of 20 millions on their year's expenditure. and they were hard put to as to where to get the money for the purposes they required. That was a highly protected country, and moreover those protected countries were feeling the slump in trade even more severely than we were. With regard to what the Government had done in the way of soe ter, REFORM, they had, at any rate, passed one great meesnre last session which had been mile talked about and much promised, not so much by the Liberal esrty perhaps as by the other side, and especially by Mr. Choral- 3rlain— the Old Age Pensions Act. (Applause). Mr. Chamber- lain bad a scheme which he said was so simple that anyone could understand it, tont it was never produced. (Laughter). Mr. Balfour went to the Manchester electors in 1913 with the request on his el( tion card : " Vote for Balfour and Old Age Pension- " but the Tories never produced their scheme. This Government through Mr. Asquith, had produced and carried a measure which would provide for some 600,000 peeple pensions for their old age. That at any rate, would do something to alleviate the 1 %reships of the poorer cltsses of this country. The Lit ;ral ministers even in vacation time, were not idle. NI -.Lloyd George, now • Chancellor of the Exchequer, had re nt his vacation in Germany, studying the Garman ssheme of contributolf perrsions. He (Mr. Ring) had reason to hope that with the information he had obtained from Germany and with the report of the Royal Commission on the Poor Law which was expected to be issued almost any day, the Government would be able if not in the autumn session early next session, to bring in Some really important change in our methods of dealing with poverty. 1 nere was no doubt that OUR POOR LAW SYSTEM needed thoroughly overhauling. Heelselieved we spent more in this country over our Poor Law arrangements than any other country in the vvorld, but he was afraid we bad got worse results than any other c ountry. He hoped the results of the inquiries now taking place might lead to some measure, perhaps after the German lines, by which a scheme of compulsory insurance might be introduced, which should provide not only fcir old age and sickness but even for temporary unemploy- ment. (Applause.) There was no doubt that the great problem which was facing the people of this country to-day was the contrast between the ever growing wealth of the country and the bad dis- tribution of that wealth We saw, on the one hand, the country growing enormously in wealth end on the other hand masses of people living in abject poverty and misery. That was the problem the Government had to deal eith and he believt 1 Mr. John Burns Sag spending his entire vacation in grappling with the problem and in dealing with applications for greets for the unemployed from various towrs. They had in Mr. John Burns a splendid lkynister, a hard worker, a man who had put real life into the office which he held—in fact when they looked th ,ugh the list of members of the Government, he did not think this country ever had a better set of men in office and they owed a debt of gratitude to their late Prime Minister, Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman for the discretion he showed in selecting his ministry, (Applause.)They ell regretted the loss of so great a leader. lie (Mr. King) thought the late Sir Henry was the very BEST FRIEND OF PE 10E this country ever had in so high a position. The idea of maintaining friendly relations was never out of his mind during the whole of the time he was in office, and they felt they had lost in him a very good friend. They were, however, fortunate in his successor. Mr. Asquith, at a meeing of the party which was held soon after Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman's death, cheered the Liberal party very much by saying what they all expected him to say—that he had no programme to put before them ; the old programme of his late leader was good enough for him and he was quite content and determined to carry it out if the party would back him up. At the last election a great deal was said about CHINESE LABOUR in South Africa. The Tories were now going up and down the country stating that the Liberals had not carried out their promises in that respect and that I actually after this Government came into ()Mee more Chinamen came into South Africa. The Warrington Arts and Crafts Society is as yet in its infancy, but the organization is full of promise sad bids fair to take a worthy place amongst the many useful institutions of the town. Evidence of the encouraging progross already made is forthcoming from a visit to the society's second exhibition which was opened in the School of Art, Niuseurn-street, on Wednes- day afternoon and will continue until this (Saturday) evening. Both in regard to numbers and variety there is a gratifying improvement and we would advise oar readers not to miss the opportunity of inspecting the interesting collection which has been got together. This time the works shown are not restricted to local artists, but include those of artists of repute in other parts of the country. Another variation from lost year's exhibition is that the display consists less of specimens of pictorial art and more of craftsmanship. Work in jewellery forms an interesting section, and bookbinding, leather, lace, gesso, enamels, metal repousse, carved wood and pottery also find a place, with etching and oil and wator colour painting. Among the artists represented is Mr. Oswald G arside who shows some characteristic studies,' ncludi ng "A breezy day," "Plough- ing in Disc^ ay," The creeping tide,"" Autumn morn," and Autumn winds," which have Come in for a great deal of admiration. Mr. C. Mawsore headmaster of the School of Art and presideat of the Arts and Crafts Society, has some beautiful pictures of scenery in the neighbourhood of Llangollen. Widnes would not appear to offer much in the way of artistic possibilities but Mr. Herbert Royle has succeeded in producing quite an attractive painting entitled " On the Mersey, near Widnes," while Mr. G. Williams has a capital view of " Runceia Bridge, Evening." Local artists are well to the fore and the exhibition well repays inspection. There may be SC3II arranged upon the walls a loan collection of museum specimens from South ICensing- tor. of Italian 16th century work in leatheeembroidery, wood, gesso, metal-work; some photographs of English cast-iron fire-backs ; Indian cotton printing and French boule-werk. The exhibition was opened by Canon Morley Steven- son in the presence of a fairly large gathering. Coun- cillor J. Fulton Smith (chairman of the Education Committee) presided, and amongst ()theta present were :—The Mayor and Mayoress (Aldermse and Mrs. Smethurst), Alderman Bennett, Revs. Colon Penrhyr Canon Stevenson, and C. Harvey Cook, Messrs. C. White, C. afawsor, J. Moore Murray, C. Madeloy, 11. Roberts, and J. A. McGregor. The Crterameer said it was a credit to the town to have a society which had for its object the realization of ideals of beauty and usefulness. The society was no doubt helping on the good work of education which was exercising the mincis of so wens, throughout the covetry at this time. " Arts arid crafts " was a high title to give it, and it seemed to comprehend all that was best in our human life. It was not °Ply by the use of tools, as in sculpture or carving, that models were copied in all their exactitade and nicety. That corld be done by mr ahhery• Put when the work was done by hand it only reelized its tree purpose when the artist put his heart and soul into it so that it should be the expres- sion of his 05.2 thought that he was trying to ammuei- cate. The more that feeling imbued the mind of the artist, the more was he 'lading to create right thoughts ie the onlooker, and to raise them to the level of hia own. That Wtl the true object of education—to improve the thoughts of those around us, and to give them that high tone which would relic tt itself in the life and conduct of the r3ople. (Applause.) Canon STEVENSOI veld thet two or thr days ago there stood upon the steps of the Walker ArS Gallen/ at Liverpool two young and fashionably d-ersel hdiee and one was over-heard to say to the other, r I ought to have been playing tennis te day but (loot" eg at he. dripping umbrella) you see 1 hive had to come here." (Laughter). Canon Stevenson remarked that although there were dripping umbrellas tt•it day, he hoped it ould not t s said of that essembly that they had had to come there, but that they were vete glad to be present. He nag sure that in all their hearts there was a very 3rd'll welcome towards that new off spring of the tuna. They were very glad to see a second repetition of the little exhibition of arts and crafts which they welcomed aye r age He dare ry that a great many •oplle who were not so intimately e sivainted with Warrington might not arsociat 3 the tone with arts, though be had no doubt they would associate it with crafts. They in Warringtor however, t sew that many e.eat names in art which it would be superfluous to mention in that assembly—names, great both ; t paint- jog, aulpture and other aii,s—bad been connected with tt's ancient Borough, and although in perhaps just the last few years we had not produced the great artist, sculptor, or craftsman of the day, still as we had done it in the past there was no reason why we should not do it ira the future. (Applause.) He ventured to think that suce an exhibition as that if it were continued— and they all hoped it would be—was the vele thing to foster rising talent and to give the boy or girl of tie future something to look for and to work for in the hope of being able to place work upon those walls and in those rooms. It Wi'cl just that fostering of native and youthful talent which enabled the town to produce the vest artists end craLsmen which they hoped to see Warrington produce once more. in contrasting this year's exhibition with the previous one, they would notice a very desided increese in the exhibits of crafts, some very beautiful things being shoe a. Another feature was that exhibits tad come from all parts of the kingdom 'beat was a vele welcome thing, though on the other hand he hop 3d they would look more for the , exhibits from their own immediate neighbourhoce' thee from distant parts. Still. whether the exhibits were fro,n far or near,they might congratul ite the committee wko had worked so hard to promote an exhibition which was well worthy of a lengthened and cerefei obeervation. Canon Stevenson them extended a hearty welcome to Mr. Mawson who, he said, had entered upon those realms as their sovereign and presided over the School of Art. They looked to hirn—and he did not thirk they would look in vain—t promote the study of art within this town and to raise the school to that position which they all felt it ought to hold in the future as it he I held it in the past.lt would be ungracious not to mention the efforts of Miss Fairclough who had worked so hard in the cause of promoting that exhibi- tion. In declaring the exhibition open, Canon Stevenson expressed the hope that it might be the precursor of many even better than the preeent one. (Applause.) Mr. C. MAwsox moved a vote of thanks to Canen Stevenson and Councillor Fulton-Smith for their presence. The assistance of gentlemen who occupied positions such as they held in directing the education of the town afforded great encouragement to the members of the society which was an entirely voluntary affair, consisting not only of past students of the school but of once of the present ones and also of Some who were entirely disconnected with the school but .who were all more or less bound together in artts4c sympathy and who sought the occasion of letting their tewaspeople know what work they did. The exhibitors looked for some little encouragement in the way of purchases of the specimens shovsn, for the craftsman and the artist liked to get together a cc.inm :- titan and the exhibition would afford an opportunity of work being acquired by those who appreciated it. Alderman 13aNNE'rr in seconding, said the Arts and Crafts Society was the natural corollaii of the work of the Beautiful Warrington Society. They wanted not only make the outside Of the town attractive, with streets beautiful and gardens pleasant to the eye, but they wanted to make the homes of the people them- selves attractive. They wanted to sea them surrounded by useful and genuine furaiture and by pictures which really were pictures and the work of artists, instead of the daubs which disgraced and disfigured so treny homes in the town. No one could love Warrington without feeling the lamentable deficiency in the artistic side of life and every effort that was calculated to redeem it from its sonalid ugliness and to make it more worthy of a civilized and enlightened people dc-erved the heartiest encouragement and support. (Applause.) The vote was heartily accorded, and Councillor Fulton Smith responded. The arrangements for the exhibition were ably carried out by a committee consisting of Mr. C. Mawson, A.R.C.A. (Gond.), president ; Miss Laverock, Miss Broadbent, Miss Waring, Miss Fleming, Miss H. Fair- dough (hon. secretary), end Mr. A. Hayward (exhibi- tion secretary.)

Church Army's Work. At the invitation of Mr. and Mrs. T. H. Lyon, a drawing-room meeting to further the cause of the Church Army was held at Appleton Hall on Tuesday afternoon. The Hon. and Hv. C. F. Cross presided, and arnmg the company present were—Mrs. Lyon, Miss Juliet Macdonald, Mrs. Ussher, the Hon. Mrs. Rankin, Miss Egerton-Warburton, Miss St. George, Mrs. Broadbent, Miss Sylvia Broadbent, Rev. H. V. and Mrs. Pigot, Rev F. and Mrs. Evans, Mr. Charles White, Miss White, Mrs. Monks, Miss Monks, Miss Fairhurst, the Misses Burgess, Mrs. Fletcher, Mrs. Charles Whitley, and Dr. and Mrs. Bower.— Captain J. Tatham, of Manchester, gave a brief and interesting sketch of the Church Army's Work, with one or two practical illustrations. The Church Army tried to stretch out a helping hand—a very practical. hand—to the unemployed 1. )fore they became unemployable. Their keynote was " Come and help yourselves" ; they did not help to pauperise people. Paupers were being batched week by week and day by day by indiscriminate charity.—The Rev. H. V. Pigot thanked Captain Tatham for his address ; and the Captain expressed the Church Army's gratitude to Mr. and Mrs. Lyon for allowing them to meet at Appleton Hall, and the Chairman for presiding and for the interest he took in their work.—The lion. Marie Dalberg Acton, the pretty little grand-daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Lyon, then made a collection on behalf of the Church Army, and the satisfactory sum 'of 5:12 2s. hi. (including Hs. 4d. collected in a box by Mr. Hewitt) was realized.

DOCTOR WITNESSES GREAT • ZAril-BUK CURE.
Three Children " D3WI " for 18 Months. -- Ringworm and Catching Sores Cured.

Mothers who recognise what a fertile hr. 14:ling ground the Day School is for such " catching " dissases as ringworm, will do well to read how Mrs. Rogers' three children got awfully sore heads, and how after 18 months' suffering were they co' d,thanks alone to Zam-Buk.

" Dolly, aged 7, came home one day and complained of some itching pimples on her head ; and soon the sores burst out into nasty ringworms," Mrs. Rogers told a" Kettering Evening Telegraph " reporter who visited her home-63, King-street, Kettering. "Soon George, aged 9, and Freddy, aged 5, caught the com- plaint. It started in each case with little red pimples which sprang up all over the scalp until the children's heads were covered with them. Then these pimples massed togethcr and formed ugly ringworms. One of the sores was 4 inches across. "The children were always rubbing and scratching to ease the irritation, but this only aggravated the trouble. Then their hair began to fall out, and all three became quite bald. The doctor said the cases were very obstinate and would take months to care. After trying in vain his special treatment, I took the children to tbe hospital. Here they were put under another kind of treatment to burn out the ringworm. But the disease continued to spread, and little lumps like boils came on Freddy's head. After 15 months' trying I got quite disheartened. "At last I read of Zara-Bak, and thinking there was something unusual about the balm I got a boa. After I had t• en using this rich balm a day or two I noticed a decided improvement in all three cases. The ringworm and sores did not look so angry. The children themselves were brighter. Zain-Bick soon began to kill the disease and dry the sores up. A new healthy skin p,:evv, the desire to scratch passed away, and as the scalp was made sweetened a nice crop of hair once more appeared on each of the children's beads.

" The Medical Officer pronounced all three children quite cured,and they have been back at school for some time now, after an absence of nearly 18 months, I can't sly how thankful lam to Zara-Bak, which did what all ordinary medicine was quite unable to do."

I expect by this time most of you have got back to school again, and are spending all your spare moments telling your little friends what a lovely time you have had in the country or by the seashore. I expect lots of you are really sorry to have to trudge back again to lesson books and hard sums, and all the diffi- culties of geography and grammar; but never mind, peg away with a brave heart, and re- member that, all being well, the Christmas holidays will be here before long. Do you know I have already begun to think about what I shall offer for Christmas prizes this year. I was thinking—but there, I must not let on just yet, for you know a good uncle always has some nice surprise "up his sleeve." I have received some essays en 'Kindness to Animals." If yours has not been sent yet, just hurry up. With lots of love from UNCLE NIED.

Long, long ago a robin and a butterfly talked over their troubles one day. "How much nicer it would be to live in a house, as men do!" said the robin. "There's a black cloud in the sky, and I'm sure it's going to rain, I'll have to cuddle up under the leaves, and my feathers will be damp. I fear I'll take cold and lose my voice." "I have to hide away, too, when it rains." said the butterfly. " 'Twould be a great pity if the water washed off my lovely powder, and a big shower might drown me." Miss Butterfly was quick-witted. "Why not go to live in that house now? The window's open." And she flew in at once. The robin was more cautious. He lighted on the window-sill, and peeped around. "I don't see any place for a nest." .

"Pshaw You don't need a nest in a house," said his gay little friend. So Master Robin flew in, and perched on the first thilfg he found, which was a book; but he looked home- sick. Miss Butterfly fluttered to a quill-pen, and made believe it was a flower.
_ Pretty soon there were sounds, and the robin listened as hard as he could.

0 papa!" a child's voice said. "Look there! Sh-sh I Keep still! You'll scare them! What a beautiful butterfly for your collection! And. papa, mayn't I have the bird in a cage? I'd like a robin with my canary." A man's voice .answered low, "Run around outside then. deary, and close the window softly, so they can't get out." Master Robin's brains were wide awake now. He spoke qu:ckly "That man's an en--ento— well, I can't say it; but he's crazy on insects, and he'll stick a pin through you, my lady. And that girl thinks she'll put me in a cage! I guess not! Let's fly!" Out they flew, just as the little maid's hand touched the sash. They heard her cry of dis- appointment as they dashed past her. "0 rap! they just went out like a flash; and they're both gone!" But Master Robin and Miss Butterfly laughed happily to be out again in the free air. The black cloud was gone, and the warm spring sun was shining on the garden beds of crocus and hyacinth. How beautiful it was to be out of doors! Living in a house was not to be com- pared to it. "Better be content where our Maker meant us to live," said Mite Butterfly. A wise after- thought of the highty-tighty little creature!
-+-- A TRAVELLER'S FAD.

You have heard of the man who had em- ployed a• new servant, fresh from a country town. The man had come highly recommended as honest, industrious, and intelligent, and in appearance he evidently justified his sponsors. His employer returned after a couple of days' absence to find that the new servant had been cleaning up generally, and particularly in the wine cellar, where he had scoured all the dust and rust off the wine bottles. Well, there is a man who had a similar ex- periente, though perhaps not quite so readily comprehended by the general reader. This man had travelled a great deal, and had a fad. They sometimes go together. His fads was travel. He had trunks, travelling bags, and hat-box covered with labels. These labels showed just what an awfully wide-awake fellow he was, and where he had been and how often. They were the record of his travels over the world. And, as he had been about a good bit, they were curiosities. It used to give him im- mense satisfaction to see the look of awe with which these relics were regarded by porters and waiters • wherever he went. They were so plastered with steamship cabin marks, and hotel pesters; and Custom-house and railway labels, that you couldn't tell what they were except by the shape. But one day he came tearing out of his hotel bedroom and burst into the manager's office, half crazy with anger. As soon as' he could be got to converse intelligently, he told the manager that the chambermaid, in anticipation of an extra tip, had washed off every one of his pet labels, and that it was—. But we dare

not be more explicit. "And to think I have to begin all over again I" said he, the seven wasted years staring him in the face. And it was hard, you will admit. But that chambermaid didn't get her tip.

DEATII OF TIE REV. ADAM SCOTT, SOUTHPORT.

The death occurred at Vale of Arran, Scotland, on Monday morning, of the Rev. Adam Scott, rostor of the Chapel-street Congregational Church, Southport. Mr. Scott, who A rts well known in this district, was a man of considerable literary attainments, and had published many short stories, sketches and articles. He acted ss secretary to the Conference of the National Free Church Councils, held at Southport in March, and that proved such e tremendous strain on his health that he under- took a trip to Palestine. Since his appol atment at Southport he had received many oilers from other important centres, but refused them, preferring to con- tinue in his Southport sphere of labour.

A gratifying success in well-dire3te4 railway enter- prise has been achieved by the Great Western Company. To meet a growing need this company has linked up the North and :Midlands with Cornwall and Devon by well- appointed express through services which bring the climate of the Riviera and the glorious scenery of the unique holiday-land of Devon and Cu-nwall within easy access. The surpassing charms of th;s part of England in the autumn months must be seen to be fully realised. Those who wish for a prolongation of summer can by a few hours travel in luxurious fast trains obtain a climate as genial as and still more equable than the Mediterranean Riviera or far distant Me lairs at a small fare, of which the fullest information can be obtained from the suparintenlent of the Line, Paddington Station, London.

div.head: "A GERMAN SPY CLUB.'
div.p: "A GERMAN SPY CLUB.'

[TO TIE EDITOR Os' THE " WESTMINSTER GAZETTE•"] Sir,—l have just read Mr. Holthusen's letter in your issue of September 9th, in which he refers to an article in a recent number of " John Bull," entitled " A German Spy Club in London." This article I have not had the advantage of seeing, but from Mr. ifolthusen's letter it is clear that the " Deutsche o:fizier Club in London" is the object of "John Bull's" atf -.ck. I and several other officers of the British Army are hono- rary members of this, in " John Bull's” eyes, dangerous association. I have attended their gatherings for years, and all I can say is that the appellation accorded to it by the writer in " John Bull " is as insulting as it is groundless. We have already been gravely informed of the existence of a branch of the Garman Heade tarter Staff in the suburbs of Landon which is making pre- parations for the capture of the Metropolis ; also of the training of 200,000 German soldiers in embarking for a descent on these shore- ; we have read that German officers in hundreds are employed as waiters and hairdressers in order to spy in our midst ; and now John Bull has apparently joined the ranks of those who are in deadly dread of the great Teutonic monster, who, in their fevered imagination, is lying in wait and whetting its claws for the sole purpose of devouring the British Empire. As Solomon said, " The sound of a fallen leaf shall chase hire" and if the British scare- monger of to-day would only realise the estimation in which he is held on the Continent owing to his fears, which conjure up German spies "behind every bush," he might possibly pause and take the trouble to investi- gate, before making assertions which not only make him supremely ridiculous but which lower the dignity of his country in the eyes' of Europe.—Y our obedient servant, ALFRED E. TURNER. Innsbruck September 12th.

div.head: ETABLE C.
div.p: ETABLE C.

About two hundred years ego the governor of the island of Jamaica Sir Thomas Lynch, sent to King Charles 11. of England a vegetable neck- tie, and a very good necktie it was, although it had grown on a tree and had not been altered

since it was taken from the tree. It was as soft and white and delicate as lace, and it is not surprising that the King should have expressed his doubts when he was told that the beautiful fabric had grown on a tree in almost the exact condition in which he saw it... It had been stretched a little, and that was all.

But if King Charles wee astonished to learn that neckties grew on trees in Jamaica, what must have been the feelings of a stranger travel- ling in Central America, on being told that mos- quito-nets grew on trees in that ccuntry? He had complained to his host that the mosquitoes had nearly eaten him up the night before, and had been told in response that he should have a new netting put over his bed. Satisfied with this ctatement, the traveller was turning away, but his attention was arrested by his host's calmly continuing, "In fact, we are going to strip a tree anyhow, because there is to be a wedding on the estate, and we wista to have a dress ready for the bride." "You don't mean," said the traveller, in- credulously, "that mosquito-netting and bridal dresses grow on trees, do you?" " That is just what I mean," replied his host. "All right," said the stranger, who fancied a joke was being attempted at his expense, "let me see you gather the fruit, and I will believe you."
-- "Certainly," was the answer; "follow the men, and you will see that I speak the exact truth."

Still looking for some jest, the stranger fol- lowed the two men who were to pluck the singular fruit, and stood by when they stopped at a rather small tree, bearing thick, glossy- green leaves, but nothing else which the utmost ' effort„of the imagination could convert into the netting or the wedding garments. The tree was about twenty feet. high and six inches in diameter, and its bark looked much like that of a birch-tree. Is this the tree?" asked the stranger. "Yes, sefior," answered one of the men, with - a smile. "I don't see the mosquito-netting nor the wedding-dress," said the stranger; "and I can't see any joke either." "If the senor will wait a few minutes he will see all that was promised, and more too," was the reply. "He will see that this tree can bear 4 not only mosquito-netting and wedding-dresses, but fish-nets and neck-scarfs, mourning crape or bridal veils." The tree was without more ado cut down. Three strips of hark, each about six inches wide and eight feet long, were taken from the trunk and thrown into a stream of water. Then each man took a strip while it was still in the water, and with a point of his knife separated a thin ' layer of the inner bark from one end of the .? strip. This layer was then taken in the fingers and gently pulled, whereupon it came away in an even sheet of the entire width and length of thp strip of bark. Twelye sheets were thus - taken from each strip of bark, and thrown into ; the water. A light broke in upon the stranger's mind. Without a doubt these strips were to be sewn together into one sheet. The plan seemed a .; good one, and the fabric thus formed might •:i do, he thought, if no better cloth could be had. The men were not through yet, however, for when each strip of bark had yielded its twelves sheets, each sheet was taken from the water 4 and gradually stretched sideways. The spec- tator could hardly believe his eyes. The sheet broadened and broadened until from a close piece of material six inches wide, it became a filmy cloud of delicate lace, over three feet in width. The astonished gentleman was forced to confess that no human-made loom ever turned out lace which could surpass in snowy white- ness and gossamer-like delicacy that product of nature. The natural lace is not so regular in formation as the material called illusion, so much worn by ladies in summer; but it, is as soft and white, and will bear washing. which is not true of illusion. In Jamaica and Central America this wonderful lace is put to all the uses mentioned by the native to our traveller, ,'„,3 and to more uses besides. In fact, among the poorer people it supplies the place of manufac- tured cloth, which they cannot afford to buy; and the wealthier classes do not by any means scorn it for ornamental use. Long before the white man found his way to ".. this part of the world, the Indians had known and used this vegetable cloth; so that what was so new and wonderful to King Charles and Governor Sir Thomas Lynch was an old story to the natives. Some time after King Charles received his vegetable necktie Sir Hans Sloane whose t.rt-collection and library were the foundation of the British Museum, visited Jamaica. He described the tree fully, and was the first person who told the civilised world about it. The tree is commonly called the lace-bark tree. Its botanical name is Lagetto lint aria.

div.head: INLAND CORRESPONDENCE.
div.p: INLAND CORRESPONDENCE.

The term Inland Correspondence " means cor- respondence posted within the United Kingdom, including the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands. " Inland Correspondence" is divided into the following classes : (a) Letters (d) Newspaper. (b) Postcards (e) Parcels (c) Halfpenny packets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- mitted by post at all, may be sent by letter post, the only limitation being that of size.

LETTER POST. The prepaid rate of postage is as follows Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight ... ... Id. For every additional 2 0z5.... A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insufficiently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or one foot in depth.

POST-C 4.RDS. The prepaid rate of postago on evory post-card is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable oa delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official poet-card. They may not exceed 51 inches in length by 31 inckes in width, or be less than 3+ inches in length by 21 inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and :1-inch wide) bearing the address may now be affixed to the address side of card. If any of the rules relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter. HALTPENNY PACKET POST. The Halfpenny Packet Post can be used only for packets not exceeding 2ez. in weight. Printod matter, Asc., not in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method. NEWSPAPER POST. The prepaid rate of postage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is Id. Newspapers not registered at the General Post Office are treated in the pcst like any other punted matter.

PARCEL POST. The rates of postage on parcels areas follows: For a parcel ... ... not exceeding 1 lb. 0 3 exceeding 1 lb. II 2 lb. 0 4 91 „ 2 lb. II 3 lb. 0 5 f 1 71 „ 3 lb. fl 5 lb. 0 6 „ 5 lb. 91 7 lb. 0 7 ft I/ „ 7 lb. 2, 8 lb. 0 8 , I „ 8 lb. i, 9 lb. 0 9 9 lb. i, 10 lb. 0 10 „ 10 lb. 11 lb. 011 No parcel may exceed 11 lb. in weight. The size allowed for an inland parcel is : Greatestlenath 3 ft. 0 in. Greatest length and girth combined G ft. 0 in. For example—A parcel measuring 3ft. 6in, in its longest dimensions as much as 2ft. 6in, round its thickest part ; a short parcel may be thicker ; thus, if it measure no more than 3ft. in length, it may measure as much as 31t. round Its thickest part. The postage on a parcel must be pee paid. Mark each parcel ' Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post office, and the sender should seo that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving. PARCELS (FOREIGN ,kNI) COLONIAL). Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries nnd must be prepaid.

MONEY ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional part of a id. can be contained in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding £l, 2d. ; £3, 3d.; £lO, 4d.; £2O, Gd. ; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, 10d. By paying an additional 2d. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order may be issued for places abroad varies in each particular place. The poundage rates are exceeding £l,3d. ; £2, Gd. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of 6d. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. These are obtainable at any money order office in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by 6d., from 6d. to £1 Is. The poundage fees are :—ld. up to 2s. 6d.; id. up to 155.; lid. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- ma3ter-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd sums.

TELEGRAMS (INLAND). The Postmaster-General possesses,almost entirely, the privilege of transmitting,collecting and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. The charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of Cd. which covers 12 words, and an additional id. ?or each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office than within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not be. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handed to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nes rest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is is. TP.LEORAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are accepted in the language of futy of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here. POST OFFICE SAVINGS BAttIC.

_ These are established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed •C.:50, and the total amount £2OO. No person can have more than one account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaches that age, and then only under his or her own signs - tore. The smallest amount received at a time is Is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps a :lixed to a special fOrrn. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the amount of each deposit should be entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is £1 or over, a special acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 24 per cent. Any amount up to and including £1 may be withdrawn without previous notice, on presenting a bank book. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the date when the account was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for purposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal of money can he expedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telekrrarns. P.O. TELEPHONE AND TRUNK LINE CHARGES, The fees for the use of the Trunk lines are as follows : For 25 miles or under ... 3d. • 50 „ l; 75 IP „ 100 PI PP „ every additional 40 miles or fraction thereof... ... L.• 6d..
Between the hours of 7 p.m. and 7 a.m., six minutes conversation is allowed for the same price as three minutes between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., and a reduced charge is made for Vireo minute calls.

MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REGULATIONS. Each one must be registered with the council of a county or county borough, the fee being .£1 fored motor car, and ss. for a motor cycle. .A register a number is assigned to each, which it is an offence not to keep affixed when driving. Each driver must possess a license, coating 5 s., to be renewed every 12 months, and obtainable from the county authorities, which may be endorsed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other offences. The highest speed at which a car may be driven on the public highways is 20 miles an hour, which is reduced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions. It is an offence under the fklotor Car Act (1903), to drive a car in such a way on a pnblic highway as to be daegerons to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case. In the event of an accident to any person due to be presence of the motor car on the road, the river must supply his name and address, and the twner and number of the car, under heavy penal- odie The driver must produce his licence at the sequest of a police constable.

div.head: Surprise at Warrington.
div.p: A Surprise at Warrington.

Widnes were the first team to visit Wilderspool this season is the Northern Lancashire and South-West Lancashire Leagues, and they upset all calculations by gaining a meritorious victory. The home men could not have shown worse form or condition, and the younger players from Widnes practically ran them off their feet, It was a great shock to the home supporters, especially as the team was even stronger than the one which only lost by a point at Leigh. Fine weather prevailed, and a crowd of over 5,000 assembled to see the season opened. None of Warrington's crack Welsh players were available, but that is the only excuse they could find. Teams :

Warrington : Tilley, back ; Fish, Dickinson, Taylor, and Harries, three-quarter backs ; Brooks and Lloyd, half backs ; A. E. Boardman, P. Boardman, Jolley, Swift, Belton, and Kettle, forwards. Widnes : It. Jones, back ; Barlow, H. Taylor, Lambert, and Ditchtleld, three-quarter backs ; Lally and Hicks, half backs ; G. Aspey, Carr, Lloyd, Lynch, McCarthy, and Rigby, forwards. I Referee, Mr. E. Tonge, Swinton. Touch judges, I Messrs. Lee (St. Helene) and Jackson (Leigh.) Warrington, had the advantage of a stiff breeze during the first half, bat fine work by the Widnes forwards gave Taylor and Ditchtield opportunities, dashing runs caus- ing Tilley trouble. Fish eased the pressure momentarily but the siege being once more raised Ditchfleld took advantage of some faulty passing by the home backs, and racing clean away scored in fine style. The pressure was maintained, and after Taylor (Warrington) had got damaged, Widnes forced matters, and a fine forward movement resulted in McCarthy scoring a try,Warring- ton rallied, and Brooks led the way to a permanent position in the Widnes quarters, and Dickinson following up a cross kick, scored in a favourable , position for Fish to place a goal. ' In the second half Widnes, with the aid of the wind, had much the better of matters. Capital footwork harrassed the home defence, and after Lambert had been held up on the line Lalley was pulled up near the posts. Warrington attacked, but their efforts lacked finish, and it was not until near the close that any further score resulted, for from a mark H. Taylor placed a goal. Result :—Widnes 1 goal 2 tries (3 points), Warrington 1 goal 1 try (6 points).

div.head: RUNCORN a. ST. HELENS.
div.p: RUNCORN a. ST. HELENS.

Played at Runcorn before 2,G00 spectators. Early on the home forwards gained ground with dribbling, fol- lowing which St. Helens were penalised, Jolley placing a goal. Resuming, Toole and Presscott got well in the Runcorn half, where Maverty had two unsuccessful attempts at goal. Hughes intercepted a pass, and dashed over between the posts, Jolley adding a goal. St. Helens were hard pressed, but Bold relieved the danger. Jolley put in a short kick, and following up got possession and scored a try near the post, which be failed to augment. Immediately on the resumption Jolley wriggled his way through and again scored, but was unable to add a goal. Half-time—ltnncorn 2 goals and S tries (13 points), St. Helens nil. After the interval Toole and Trenwith got away, but only gained slight ground. Deakin got possession, and after running almost the length of the field handed to Kennedy, who scored, Richardson failing with the goal kick. On the resumption Kennedy intercepted a pass and added a further try, which Jolley improved. Play slackened somewhat, and St. Helens got to the home line, where Toole scrambled over and scored. The same player added a goal. Result :—Runcorn, 3 goals and 5 tries (21 points), St. Helens, 1 goal and 1 try (5 points). Teams : Runcorn—Harrison, back; Deakin, Unsw orth, Hughes, end Flanagan, three-quarter backs ; Jolley and Watton, half-backs ; Walker, Padbury, Richardson, Woods, Kennedy and Hodgetts, forwards. St. Helens—Bold, back, Manchester, Helsby, Prescott, and Flanagan, three-quarter backs; 'Foote and Trenwith, half-backs ; Briers, Smith, Wharton, Riley, Godfrey and Mavity, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Priestley, Salford. Touch judges, Messrs. E. Bennett, Liverpool, and A. Jones,Warrington.

div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.
FRIENDLY MATCEL WELLFIELD JUNIORS V. GREAT SANKET.

Played on the Lovely-lane ground on Saturday, N. Ray started for the visitors against the wind and sun, and T. Cook tested the homo defence. F. Millington chaared. J. Monks got possession and raced away in tine style, only to be stopped by T. Cash when he was about to shoot. J. Monks opened the scoring for the lords with a cross shot, twenty-lye minutes from the start. J. Nunnerley added a second. Just on half-time J. Bradburn, receiving a pass from the right, scored a third. Half-time Wellfield Juniors, three goals ; Great Sankey, nil. On restarting, the visitors had the best of the opening exchanges and F. Rituberloy and T. Cash went near with good shots. J. Bradburn scored a fourth goal for the locals. T. Cook scored with a fast ground shot, giving J. Bond no chance. F. Millington scored with a fifth goal from a penalty. Final : Wellfleld Juniors, five goals ; Great Sankey, one goal.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY PARISH COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held in the Council Schools, Great Sankey, on Monday evening. There were present :—Messrs. W. Taylor (in the chair), W. Furness, 11. Fairclough, J. T. Walters and Jos. Smith (clerk). A PPLIC ATION _FOR SMALL HOLDING.

Mr. Jose-ph Massey, Liverpool-road, Sankey, wrote applying for the conditions under which he could obtain a smallholding of about two acres in Sankey or Penketh. The Clerk said tbat was the only application they had received for a small holding or allotment up to the present. Mr. Furness said he was glad an application of that character had been made. It would give them an opportunity of showing how it could be done and would also put them on their merits as to whether they could offer facilittes for acquiring two acres of land. The Clerk said it would be his duty to ascertain from the applicant what experience he had had in agriculture and whether he had the needful working capital. It was decided that the Clerk should obtain the necessary information and lay it before the Council.

div.head: CHARGES FOR LIGHTING.
div.p: THE CHARGES FOR LIGHTING.

Mr. Furness said the Council might bo 'called upon shortly to provide more gas lamps and they ought to approach the Corporation with a view to getting some reduction of the charge made for lamps. During the period they had been taking gas from the Corporation there had been two or thrce reductions in price but they as large consumers had not got the slightest benefit from those concessions. _ .

The Clerk said the Corporation at present charged them £2 18s. per lamp per annum and if they obtained the same reductions as had been granted to ordinary consumers in the borough it would mean 7s. Gd. per lamp. Mr. Furness said that as a matter of common justice they were entitled. to some redaction, but he did not expect they would get is. 6d. The Clerk was instructed to communicate with the Gas Committee on the matter.

div.head: SANITARY ARRANGEIIENTS.
div.p: THE SANITARY ARRANGEIIENTS.

The Rural District Council forwarded a letter from Mr. Thomas Whitfield, Brook House Farm, Penketh, stating that unless srrangements could be made for him to be paid through the Council for emptying the soil and ash tubs in Sankey, he must give a month's notice. They had no idea what trouble he had to get his money in under the present arrangements. He was perfectly satisfied with.the job otherwise. Mr. Furness said the Rural District Council had pot% er to take the matter into their own hands and levy a rate, but they had decided to consult the Parish Council. It was not fair to the rest of the Parish that they should have to levy a special sanitary rate because a few of the residents were lax in their payments. They were indebted to the Clerk for a statement showing how a 6d. rate, which it-"was estimated would be required, would affect the ratepayers. As a matter of fact, the parishioners would save money as far as the sanitary arrangements were concerned, but the rate would probably press unrelsonably on the farmers—in fast it would mean that they would have to pay more than double the amount they were charged at pr:.sent. For instance a farmer whose rent was £lOO a year was at present charged Bs. 2d. for lighting purposes but if a 6d. rate were levied he would have to pay 19s. Id. A farmer who was paying rent to the tune of £l5O bad to pay 12s. now but under a 6d. rate the charge would be £1 7s. 3d. It would be a hardship on the farmers to have to pay for something for which they got no return whatever. Mr. Furness advocated the holding of a publia—meeting to decide whether a rate should be levied or not. They might start with a 6d. rate and in a year or so have to raise it to 9d. or Is. As the rates were at present 4s. in the £ it would be an important step to take. As Mr. Whitfield was unable to attend the meeting, no decision was arrived at.

LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.I NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication mat in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. WiLLLt H. Buda—The matter is hardly one for ventilation in our columns.—ED. "Ex." R. Ocaara—Space forbids, this week.—ED." Ex." Governments and Trade Depression. Sir,—We are face to face this winter with an industrial depression—a period of poverty and starvation amongst the toiling masses that has not been witnessed since the black year of 1379 and strong ptessure must be brought to bear on the men who are guiding the helm of the State to meet the difficulty with sympathy and courage. Of course the "Unionists" will take advent- tage of the depression to advocate their particular nostrums as the only reliable remedy for all the ills humanity is subject to. Indeed they are actively engaged in circulating their tales for the unwary at the present moment and the most preposterous Tory story dinned into my ears is that a Liberal Government means bad trade and that goad trade follows in the wake of Con- servative administration. This is absurd, but still it appeals just. now to some of the electorate who care little for abstract politics and can never be induced to take more than the faintest interest in political questions as such. But there are very few who are not interested in a prospect of increased earnings or better trade. Conse- quently the belief that one political party is able and ready to bring about an era of good trade will gain the support of thousands who care little for the most eloquent and forcible arguments to the contrary. Governments do not influence trade. Fluctuations of trade are not local or domestic phenomena but are world wide and occur about the same extent. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach (now Viscount St. Aldwyn) speaking on April 17th, Ism, in the House of Commons on periodical ca,pressions of trade said "In my belief these variations have nothing to do with Governments and politicians." And the late Duke of Devonshire at a meeting of the British Iron Trade Association in 1399 said " Most of all, the Prime Minister must watch with increasing anxiety the prospects of this and other great industries of the country. I doubt very much whether it is in the power of any Government to do much more than watch them, and I think that it would be an unfor- tunate delusion if it were to come to be supposed that any Government, could do much more. The navigator and agriculturist watch with increasing anxiety the rise or the fall of the barometer, and endeavour to obtain from it some indications as to the weather, on which the safety and success of their operatives depemd,and guide their operatives either in the direction of action or precaution accordingly. And tha statesman may also —ought also—to watch the signs of the prosperity or the depression of trade and pursue a bold or prudent polcy in accordance with those signs. But as neither thesailor nor the farmer can exercise any influence upon the causes which produce the rise or the fall of the barometer, so I do not think that it is in the power of any Government to exercise much influence on the causes which produce good or bad trade. Govern- ments will do well to discard the idea that it is in their power to do very much to promote the interests of trade, and to remove from their friends and supporters the expectation that they can do so." These statements are sufficiently clear and emphatic to dispose of the canard that Tory Govern- ment and prosperity are synonymous. In fact it must be admitted that under Liberal rule we have attained a higher industrial state of prosperity than under Tory management. 1573 was what is known as the "big money" time and indicated the highwater work of prosperity. Mr. Gladstone was in power. 1379, depression, poverty and insolvency abounded. Lord Beaconsfield was in power. Of course, examples can be quoted on both sides where trade has gone up and down under either party and shall continue as long as the present system of competition and individualism exists. Yours etc.,
