div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS,
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS,

A fashionable wedding of con—siderable local interest took place at St. Bartholemew's Church, Roby, on Tuesday afternoon,when Mr. Thomas Houghton Owen, son of Mrs.o wen, The Pollards,Penketh,was married to Miss Ethel Haynes, daughter of Mr. Harry Haynes, of Bradfield, Roby. A crowded congregation witnessed the ceremony. Owing to indisposition the Rev. Canon Sylvester, Rector of Ifohy, was unable to be present, and the R.ev. J. R. Jones, Vicar of Great Sankey, officiated. The service was fully choral, Mr. Taylor being at the organ. The hymns " The Voice that breathed o'er Eden" and " 0 Father All-creating" were sung. The bride, who was given away by her father, was charmingly attired in white chiffon taffeta, with tulle veil tient by mother of bridegroom) and wreath of orange blossom, and carried a handsome bouquet of lilies. The bridesmaids were the Misses Mary and Annie Owen who wore white muslin dresses, with pale blue and pink sashes, and pale blue only hats with a touch of pink velvet. Mr. B. Stanley Darby discharged the duties of best ruan. After the ceremony the guests, numbering over eighty, proceeded to Roby Parish Room, which was beautifully decorated, for the reception. The first letter to Mrs. Owen, wishing the newly-married pair every happiness, was sent by th 3 Rev. Canon Sylvester. Later the happy couple left for Scotland, being accompanied to the station by a large number of friends who gave them an enthusiastic send-off. The bride's travelling dress was a navy blue costume faced with green cloth, and hat to match. Numerous hand- some presents were received. Evans—Gandy. A large congregation assembled at Holy Trinity Church on Thursday to witness the marriage of Mr. Herbert Evans, son of the late Mr. Robert Evans,

A.R.C.0., of Warrington, and Miss Amy Gandy, daughter of Mr. William Gandy, of 231, Manchester- road, Warrington. . The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton officiated. The bride, who was given away by her father, was charmingly attired in a cream merve silk dress with lace and silver trimmings and hat to match, and carried a shower bouquet of white roses, lilies of the valley and orange blossom, the gift of the bridegroom. She was attended by two brides- maids—Miss Gertrude Gandy (sister of the bride), and Miss Elsie B3wcock (cousin of the bride) who wore pale blue cloth dresses, and biscuit coloured felt hats trimmed with pale blue. Their shower bouquets were composed of pink roses and they wore gold bangles, the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr. Robert Walsh discharged the duties of best man. Mr. B. Podmore was at the organ and the bridal party left the church to the strains of Mendelssohn's Wedding March. The recep- tion was held at the Winmarleifdi Cafe, and was large'y attended. Later the happy couple left for Bridlington, where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress was a mole cloth costume with hat to match. The bride's present to the bridegroom was a leather dressing case, and the bridegro-m's gift to the bride a silver brush, comb, mirror, &c. A large number of handsome presents were received, including one from the staff of the St. Helens Cable Co., Ltd. Wallington —Kershaw. There was a pretty wedding at Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church on Thursday when Mr. Harold Wallington, son of Ur. Edward Wallington, of Walton Rink, Lower Walton, was married to Miss Mabel C. Kershaw, daughter of Mr.' James Kershaw, Latchford. The Rev. J. Yonge officiated. Mr. W. H. Payton, Mus. Bac. presided at the organ and plard choice selections, including Mendelssohn's Weading march. The hymn "How welcome was the call " was sung. The bride, wh3 was given away by her father, wore a beautiful dress ' of crepe de chine and carried a bouquet of roses, lilies and white heather. The bridesmaids I were the Misses Agnes Wallington (sister of the bridegroom), Cissie Owen and Edna Knowles, who were attired in pink eolienne dresses. Their bouquets were composed of yellow marguerites, Mr. Herbert Wallington (brother of the bridegroom) acted as best man, and Mr. W. J. Ford as groomsman. The reception was held at Atkinson's Cafe, a large number of guests altendrng. Later the happy couple left for Llandudno, the bride's travelling dress being a mole costume with hat to match. They were the recipients of many useful and valuable presents. Sanders—Fairhurst. The marriage was solemnized at Latchford Baptist Church on Thursday, of Mr. Ernest A. Sanders, son of the late Mr. Sanders, Arthur-street, Warrington, and Miss Lily Fairhurst, daughter of Mr. Fairhurst, 63, Tanners-lane. The Rev. J. F. Matthews officiated. The bride, who was given away by her father, wore a pretty Saxe blue dress and white hat with blue feathers. She was attended by Miss Whittaker who was attired is a Saxe blue dress with black hat. Mr. Arthur Sanders discharged the duties of best man. After the ceremony a reception was held.st the house of the bride's parents and afterwards there was a social gathering at the Co-operative Hall, Winwick- street, between sixty and seventy guests being present. The honeymoon is being spent at Blackpool. Many handsome presents were received including the following —Mr. T. J. Ridgway, silver tea pot ;Mr. Ridgway, jun., silver water jug; Mr. Denham, silver sugar basin and cream jug; Mrs. Simpson, mahogany flower pot stand; Mr. Peacock, marble time piece; Mr. S. Beaman, antique cabinet.

WARRINGTON MUSICAL FESTIVAL PRESENTATION OF THE CHALLENGE SHIELD. There was a pleasing little ceremony at the Winmarleigh Cafa. on Thursday evening when the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) as President of the Warrington Musical Festival formally presented the challenge shield, kindly given by Mrs. A.H.Crosfield,to Mr. Harry Berrey, condactor of the St. Helens choir which carried off the first prize in the chief choral competition at the festival held in May last. The shield is a most handsome and artistic trophy and has been generally admired. It is of sterling silver and bronze, mounted on a green oak frame, and the dimensions are about 21 by 10 inches ' high. Mrs. Crosfield is, we understand, responsible for the design which is pleasing and appropriate, and calls to mind the ancient musical traditions of the chorus in the Greek tragedies. The shield will be competed for annually and it bears eleven medallions on which the names of the winning choirs will be inscribed. The first medallion already sets forth the fact : " Winners for 1903, St. Helens Choir, Conductor Mr. Harry Berrey." On the shield are the further inscriptions : " Warrington Musical Festival Challenge Shield," "Presented by Mrs. A. H. Crosfield " and, in Greek letters, the word " Chores." The trophy has been specially manufac- tured by Messrs. Elkington and Co., Ltd., of London and Birmingham, and supplied through their branch at 22, Regent-street, London, S.W. At the presentation there was a large attendance of members of the Festival Committee, Mr. E. Lloyd Jones, chairman of the committee, presiding. Amongst others present were Mr. Nathan Cook (vice-chairman) and Mr. R. W. Cook (secretary). The Ca 1111\IAN said he believed everybody who had seen the shield ha 1 admired its beauty and uniqueness. He had seen many shields—in fact he had seen the Blackpool shield this week—but he had not seen one that vveuld compare with the trophy presented to the Warrington Festival by Mrs. Crostleld. He was certain that so long as the efforts of the Musical Festival Com- mittee were attended with success, the choirs in and around Warrington would be proud to compete for the honour of holding that shield year by year. (Applause) They were very glad indeed that their friend Mr. Berrey had become the first possessor of the shield and they hoped he would not have to give it up. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He did not suppose there was any- one who had done more for the promotion of good music in this and neighbouring towns than Mr. Berrey and they hoped he would cont inne his work. If it were possible for Mr. Berrey to let other choirs know what a splendid shield the Warrington Musical Festival had, he was sure there would be keen competition for it. In calling upon the Mayor to make the presentation, Mr. Jones said he desired to emphasise the fact that his Worship was the president of the festival, and that in no formal sense. They hoped that the aldermen and councillors tif the borough would have the good sense to re-elect him for the coming year—(applause)—and that they would have the honour at their next festival of again welcoming Alderman Smethurst as president. The 'Mayox said he hardly thought he was deserving of the kind things the Chairman had said about him. He always believed it was an Englishman's privilege to try and do his duty and that was all he had tried to do. The office of Mayor of a town like Warrington was no sinecure if one wished to fulfil it with judicious care and with a true and clear conscience. It was indeed a pleasurable duty to have to present that beautiful shield to the choir which had proved itself the best in tho district in the chief competition at the last festival. It was a greater pleasure because his wife had the honour of being present at the festival and but for another engagement she would have been with them that night. To the man who had no music in his soul, life was hardly worth living. There was nothing so beautiful and elevating in churches and chapels as good music rendered with true harmony and feeling. Singing touched his heart even more than sermons. He hoped Mr. Berrey would continue in his good work of training choirs and, on behalf of Mrs. Crosfield, he had great pleasure in presenting him with that. beautiful and unique shield. (Applause.) Mr. HARRY BERRY said his choir was very anxious to see the shield and he was sure there would be a full attendance at the rehearsal on Friday when be had promised to exhibit it. The choir was delighted with the contest at Warrington and so far as he knew, the members would be anxious to contest again next year, and perhaps one or two of his other choirs as well, if the Committee would allow them to compete. It made no difference to him which of his choirs won. He had Ito fight hard with all of them and he knew there would be no favouritism shown, if there were twenty of his choirs there. That was not the first shield he had won but it was really the prettiest and he would like that sentiment to be conveyed to Mrs. Crosfield. He had held many first class prizes—in fact his choirs and pupils had won over 100 first prizes, 47 second prizes, and 32 third prizes, amounting to £1,700 in value. (Applause.) He appreciated the trophies because they enabled one to look back upon one's work with the feeling that it had not been in vain. Musicians were often decried and did not get their proper place but on occasions like that they were glad to realize that their efforts were appreciated. (Applause.) Mr. W. KsowLss in moving a vote of thanks to the Mayor pointed out that the shield belonged to the Warrington Musical Festival and could not, under present conditions, be won outright. Its beauty and uniqueness, however, made it well worth holding if only for a year. (Applause). Mr. W. HIPKISS seconded and the vote was accorded. The Ma.vort briefly responded, expressing the hope that Mr. Berrey would live long to use his energy in cultivating good music and that the next Warrington festival would be a great success. (Applause). The CHAIRMAN alluded to next. year's festival and pointed out that the dates decided upon were February sth and 6th. The committee had wisely decided to set apart February sth as a day for Warrington only, and he would like to appeal to the church and chapel choirs of the town to muster well for that occasion, because the future arrangement of a Warrington day at the festival would depend upon the success of the innovation. Two excellent adjudicators had been engaged—Mr. S. Coleridge Taylor, of world- wide musical fame, and Mr. Harry Evans, of Liverpool, who at the Welsh National Eisteddfod was described as the-Lloyd George of the Welsh musical world. He would like it to be known that the challenge shield belonged to the town of Warrington, and that Warrington ought to be proud of it. He believed Mrs. Crostleld had designed the trophy, and they were very grateful to her for giving them such a beautiful shield. He hoped a Warrington choir would be successful next year. Mr. Berrey, he understood, was going to train a Warrington choir, and they hoped it would prove better than the St. Helens choir, and keep the shield in Warrington.

div.head: GOLDEN WEDDING-CELEBRATIGN AT
div.p: GOLDEN WEDDING-CELEBRATIGN AT
PADGATE.

On Wednesday, at Grange Mount, Padgate, near War- rington, Mr. and Mrs. John Bennett celebrated the fiftieth anniversary of their wedding day. Unfortun- ately the weather was unpropitious, nevertheless a happy day was spent by all the members of their numerous family. Originally it was intended to hold a reception of some hundred guests in a large marquee, but owing to the weak state of Mrs. Bennett's health this part of the programme had to be abandoned. At six o'clock in the evening " high tea " was served by the Winmarleigh Cafe Co. in their usual excellent minner, also the golden wedding cake was provided by them, after which a very pleasant evening was spent. It was a source of great satisfaction to the revered couple that all their living children and grandchildren were able to be present. These comprise: Mrs. W. G. Bennett, IJrmston(widow of the eldest son)and her three children; Winifred, Hilda and Clifford ; Rev. and Mrs. J. Grange Bennett (London) and their son Ronald ; Mr. and Mrs, Joseph Bennett (Paddington) and their two daughters, I Irene and Dorothy ; Dr. and Mrs. James Bennett (Padgate) and their two children, Gwendoline and James Gordon; Mr. and Mrs. F. Stanley Bennett (London) and daughter Mona ; Mr. and Mrs. F. W. Flanagan and baby, Isle of Man ; Miss Emily Bennett and Mr. Leonard Bennett, auctioneer, Warring- ton. Mr. Bennett, who was the second son of Mr. William Bennett was born at Padgate December 14th, MO. For nearly forty years he resided at Bewsey Old Hall, the birthplace of his wife, the only daughter of Mr. William Grange. He was a i partner n the well-known firm of Bennett Brosaarmers and cattle dealers, Bruche, Warrington. His interests outside his business and family centred chiefly in Wesleyan Methodism,the church of his birth and choice of which he has been an active member for over sixty years, holding almost every office that is open to a lay- man. Mr. Bennett, who was brought up in the Church of England, became a member of the Methodist Church after her marriage, and has been deeply interested in all good works. Until their removal to Padgate, eleven years ago, they worshipped in the Bewsey-road Church, Warrington, of which Mrs. Bennett laid one of the foundation stones. As a thankoffering for their long and happy married life they have commemorated the auspicious occasion by presenting to the trustees of the Padgate Wesleyan Church(in which they now worshlp)a Communlon Service {individual cups). In the same spirit of thanksgiving their children are also providing a new altar cloth. A handsome gold pendant, containing their miniatures, I was given to Mrs. Bennett,and a pair of gold spectacles to Mr. Bennett by their family. It was a happy coincidence that the "best man," Mr. William Bennett (Lyndhurst), and one of the brides- maids (Mrs. Shanks, Urmston), at the wedding fifty years ago, were also able to be present once more. A unique event in the day's proceedings MS the christening of the baby (Frederick Livingstone) of Mr. and Mrs. Flanagan, by his uncle (Rev. J. Grange Bennett) in the house of the child's grandfather and great grandfather. Many letters and telegrams of congratulation and. good wishes were received.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, September 19,1908.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, September 19,1908.

Bowling. NEW WESLEYAN MINISTERS The Works Association handicap came to a close last Saturday, the final stages providing some interesting games. In the semi-final there was a close contest between W. Tomkinson and G. Shaw. They peeled at CIRCUIT RECOGNITION MEETING AT 6, 10, 11, 12 and 11, and then Tomkineon bowled the winning wood and triumphed by a margin of one. J. BOLD STREET CHURCH. Gleave had an easier task in accounting for W. Bibby. The latter made a plucky fight, and was on equal terms The newly appointed ministers to the Warrington with his opponent at 9, and actually lad 10-9. From I Wesleyan Methodist Circuit—the Revs. E. Blanshard that stage Gleave had matters all his own way, and won Keeling (superintendent), Thomas Gladding and F. by 15-10 Welwyn Kernick—were formally welcomed to their new sphere of labour on Thursday. In the afternoon a service was held in the Bold-street Church when the Rev. E. Blanshard Keeling preached a powerful sermon. Afterwards tea was served in the schoolroom to a gathering of about 200, the tables being presided over by ladies of the Bold-street congregation. The circuit recognition meeting in the church followed. There was a large attendance. Mr. R. H. Meldrum (circuit steward) presided and amongst others present in addi- tion to the new ministers were :—Rev. T. Miller, Dr. Bennett(oircuit steward), Messrs.J. Upson,F. A. Harris, J. G. Withinshaw and representatives of the various churches in the circuit. The CHIIRS(AN said that he had the pleasure of introducing Mr. Keeling at Bawsey-road last week, and the interest that pervaded the meeting he should like to be maintained there that evening. It was the spirit of unanimity, devotion and and co-operation. They wanted to get out of their ministers as much as they could—exactly the same as an employer got out of his employee. They gave them a hearty welcome and trusted that they might have a successful ministry. But it depended upon the people to a very great extent as to what the limit would be. They wanted to be as full of zeal and earnestness as they could, and God's blessing would rest upon all of them. Dr. BENNETT gave the new comers a cordial welcome on behalf of Padget° and said that the coming in of their minister was always a sudden change. Just as quickly as the daylight followed dark so the duty of receiving their new ministers followed quickly upon the darkness of the departing ones. They had got three ministers who were coming into their midst,to a town which had held a worthy place in Literature, Science, Art and Philan- thropy and many other fields. (Applause). Mr. HARRIS extended a greeting on behalf of Bold- street Church, and remarked that he had a very con- siderable amount of pride and pleasure in speaking for that Church. They had heard a great deal about the new ministers, and they believed they would carry on the work which would be laid in their hands with success, with profit, and with credit to the Church generally. The town itself might not be altogether, attractive, but to him it was the most attractive spot on the earth. Mr. Jolter Uesoer, speaking for Bewsey-road, said the Chairman had referred to what they had been doing at Bewsey-road, and they rather prided themselves on the fact that they had set a good example to the Circuit generally. They had had a meeting of domestic welcome to their own respected pastor, and they believed that the influence of that meeting would be a lasting one, and that the seeds of good work had been sown, and a larger number of people had become interested in the Church than ever before. While they had many faults no one could charge them with a " drawingroom " attitude of mind. He did not want them to make a mistake and think they had no culture and no intelligence. They thought they had quite as much of those things as other People had. They did not, however, put them in the first place. They set their minds on higher things. They realised that the ministers must of necessity be their leaders but a weight of responsibility rested upon themselves. That was a doctrine he had been trying to preach for some time. The success of the work of God in that district did not depend largely upon the work of the ministers ; it rested with the members. They had been concerned with the fact that there were among them multitudes who were out of touch with Jesus Christ, and as far as they were able, they were determined that under God's guidance and with God's help they would tozieh many lives in the immediate neighbourhood of their church. They did not sufficiently realise the shortness of the time they had to serve Him and the immediate amount of work that had to be done. They had the evidence of sin so stamped upon the personages of the men and women around them that tho persons themselves filled them saith disgust. To see some of the creatures in that town of theirs was enough to cause them to shudder. They had to realise that the Lord Jesus Christ did not turn from them in disgust. If they were to follow in the footsteps of their Blessed Master they must be prepared to do a great deal more than they had done. (Applause.) Mr. MOSTYN spoke on behalf of Lymm. Mr. J. G. WrriiresiLaw (Penketh) said a church's influence depended far more upon the amount of enthusiasm which existed in the paws than upon the power of the pulpit. The pews made the pulpit far more or quite as mush as the pulpit made the pews and unless those who attended church put their hearts into the work, no matter how a man might preach—not even if they hid the Archangel Gabriel himself in the pulpit—the church could not command success. He did not think the Warrington circuit was ever better manned than it was to-day. (Applause). • Mr. J. WADSWORTH (Sankey Bridges) urged the need for more vigorous work. Lie pointed out that eighteen years ago the Warrington circuit had practically the same membership as St. Helens but to-day Warrington had not a thousand members, whereas he believed St. Helens had over 1,500. Mr. 11IarrE (Latchford) said there was a glorious feeling of discontent at his church. They felt the time had come when they must do something to reach those who were outside the churches. (Applause.) Messrs. LLEWELLYN (Ellesmere-street), Laarrox (Moore) and Miusest (Stockton Heath) also spoke. The Rev. F. WALWYN KERNIOK in returning thanks quoted the remark recently made in an ordination charge that a minister was a shepherd and not a sheep dog. The more they realized the difference between a minister hunting and hounding up his supporters and a minister leading them instead of driving, the more would they tend to organized spiritual advance. After all it was the spiritual things that must come first and he thought the itinerancy system, of which he still felt himself to a certain degree a victim—(laughter)--had certain advantages of its own. It drew out on the part of minister and congregation just that faith and trust which was behind all spiritual work and advance. Although he sup- posed they had passed through the refining fire of various criticisms—(laughter)—at the same time the congrega- tion knew comparatively little of any one of the new ministers, and the ministers knew comparatively little of them, but they expected the best of each other. (Applause.) It was with that feeling that they could go forward to a three years' work, which should be as honest and complete as they could make it. Methodism did not depend upon any set of men. As they changed ministers they should try and remember what Methodism meant—that it was not only a great system but a great spiritual force, apart from any men that might be set to administer it, and perhaps the real test of the next three years' work would be not a test that could be measured by statistics, but by their adherence to the principles of Methodism. There never was a grealer challenge to Methodism than there was to-day. Even that great Eucharistic;Congress could never be met by obsolete laws, or by the bigotry of people who would place every obstacle in the way of their fellow Chris- tians, but rather it should be met by the Real Presence of Jesus Christ in Ells Church. He (the preacher) did not know of any organization that represented in itself as Methodism did, the society of which the Living Christ was the Head. (Applause.) The Rev. THOMAS GLADDLNG harked back to the days when he was at Didsbury College and Bold-street, Warrington was looked upon as an appointment to be regarded with a certain amount of jealousy, while Padgate was considered to be in a special sense a select church to be treated with a distant reverence and respect. (Laughter). The now ministers had come to Warrington for real business and they meant to put their whole strength into it. A passing allusion to Socialism led the preacher to observe that he had no particular objection to it but he liked to have mixed with it a certain amount of common sense and religions feeling. As a Wesleyan minister he had his place in a great co-operative agency whose object was to pro- duce the two most valuabfe things in this life—happi- ness and character—apart from what related to the things of the spirit or the eternal world. They were workers together with God and it was on His power that they relied. They hoped the coming three years would be a time when, to use the old-fashioned Methodist phrase, men and women would be born again, drawn from their sins and led to trust Christ as their Saviour and so begin a new life which should be eternal and which would only find its perfection in the world to come. So far as this world was concerned, entrance upon the Christian life would mean a complete change in their outlook, an increase of happiness and a growing up into a high, beautiful and Christ-like character. (Applause). The Rev. E.BLANSHARD KEELING said the itinerancy system served to emphasise the lovely spirit of brother- I hood which existed between the Methodist preachers and the Methodist people, and he hoped the day was very far distant when the warmth and affection of that brotherhood would be in any way lessened. He would tell them what would lessen it—neglect of the class meeting. As that fellowship diminished, the spirit of brotherhood, comradeship and mutual trust which had always characterised the Methodist Church would ssed. They had I certainly go down. The class mee,tingeargnaevset them class meeting and ' ey irsnt et mhceahit rui cru,cshe or feygtouhs lesaer that was one reason for its declension. They had cbt hathee n a n talked about their own feelings and happiness and had teo no narrowoo t hs forgotten the splendid opportunity that the class meet- ing gave systematic and aggressive Christian work on the lives of the people around them. In the congrega- tions of their churches he hoped there would always be plenty of people coming to see what they were like. He would like to say to the outsider that except in church discipline where sundry legal difficulties came in—perils of libel and so forth—they had no secrets and they were not ashamed of things. He wanted every business meeting to be a means of grace. What he had seen in the circuit already seemed to tell him that bright days were in store. He seemed to realise some- how in the very atmosphere itself the presence of Jesus Christ. During the evening Mrs. Arthur Booth gave a beauti- ful interpretation of "I will extol Thee" and the choir sang an anthem. Mr. Frank Hickman was at the organ.

In tha final Tomicinson was quite outplayed. At 5 the players were equal, and then Gleave had a ran of success and led 10-5. Tomkinson advanced to 9 but could make no farther headway and was beaten by 15—a.

The presentation of prizes will take place on Monday evening at the Bowling Green Inn, Bank Qaay, at 7.30. The proceedings will take the form of a smoking concert and Captain Crosfleld will hand the prizes to the successsul bowlers.

ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "The Hypocrites." It is not often that Warrington has the pleasure of witnessing the production of a play by the famou3 dramatist, Mallenry Arthur Jones,ancl quite naturally, therefore, large audiences have taken the opportunity this week of seeing his latest London success "The Hypocrites." The play is one of those daring studies in morals for which Mr. Henry Arthur Jones is famous, and while it may shock the fastidious there is no question of its inherent truthfulness to life and its healthy moral intent. The scene is laid in the little country town of Weybury. Mr. Wilmore, the lord of the manor, is in financial difficulties, and his estates are heavily mortgaged, but he and his wife see a happy issue out of their troubles in the marriage of their son Leonard to Helen Plugenet, the daughter and heiress of a wealthy baronet. When one of his tenants gets into trouble with a girl of bad character in the village Mr. Wilmore insists that the two must marry. The local curate warns him that such a union is most undesir- able, and must end badly,but Mr. Wilmore stubbornly observes that he has "only one rule in these cases." A little later, by the irony of fate, he learns that his son Leonard has been guilty of a similar offence in the betrayal of a young Canadian girl (Rachel Neve) only a few months earlier. What will Mr. Wilmore do now? Will he act on his " one rule in these cases" against his own sea ? The splendid situation that arises is so worked out that every line and every section palpitates with excitement. Filled with rage against Leonard for placing him in such an awkward position, he yet helps his wife and all their friends in an attempt to hush up the scandal. When Rachel appears on the scene they try to hurry: her out of the way, but on her way to the station Rachel sprains her foot and is carried into the house of the curate, who lives in the Station-road. While Rachel is in his house the curate accidentally learns of her relationship to Leonard, and he indignantly condemns his sci-called superiors for their callous treatment of Rachel and their attempts to keep Helen in the dark. He demands that Helen be told how matters stand and then left to judge whether she loves Leonard well enough to marry him notwith- standing. Mrs. Wilmore takes another view, and does all in her power to hush things up. In his fight for truth and justice the curate finds ranged against him all the influential people of the town,—the Wilmores, who are the patrons of the living, his vicar, and the local doctor, and lawyer, all combine to try "to avoid a scandal." First they try to buy his silence by offering him the living then they threaten him, and finally they prevail on living, herself to save her lover's reputation and career by saying that Leonard is not the man who wronged her. A meeting of all concerned is arranged, and Rachel lies bravely to them saying the curate is mistaken, as Leonard is a mere acquaintance. Leonard also denies his guilt and the curate is crushed. H 3 is charged with maliciously slandering Leonard, and ordered to leave the house. Flushed by her victory, Mrs. Wilmore taunts him as he goes out in despair. Stung by this, ha turns on them in righteous indignation, calling them liars, hypocrites and time-servers, and saying their lie is like a dead rat festering under the floor, and cannot long be hid. His vehemence overcomes Rachel, who staggers and faints. Leonard catches her in his arms and, stung by remorse, cries out that he is the man, and that he levee Rachel and her only. The situation is suddenly changed, and the curtain falls on as powerful and dramatic a scene as has been witnessed for many a day. In the last act, affairs are wound up as happily as possible. Leonard marries the girl, and his disappointed mother is prevailed upon to see that only the truth is tight and to a dmit the deeply-wronged Rachel to her affections. Mr. Charles Frohman's company gives an exceed- ingly clever presentment of the difficult situations which arise. The moral issues are delicately handled and no fault can be found with the way somewhat unsavoury matters are brought before the public purview. The Rev. Edgar Linnell is the dominating factor in the play, and his devotion to truth and righteousness added to a Christ-like sympathy and tenderness, make him a character which can only be described as unique. Curates do not usually fly in the faces of their vicars and patrons to the extent of risking absolute rain in order to see justice done to an erring girl. Mr. 'Tones presents the opposite view in the person of the vicar, Rey. E I ward Danbeney, who " deplores " most earnestly but keeps his delicate fingers clear of the mud-puddle. The attitude of the latter gentleman is obviously meant to be typical, and as such cannot cause the bosoms of the clergy to swell with pride. The curate is, possibly, too heroic to be easily conceived,but there is no manner of doubt that he takes the only course open to the true servant of Christ. Similar opportunities of risking martyrdom for right occur not infrequeatly in the experience of the Clerk in Holy Orders, but the play leads one to the conclusion that the average curate is not made in the mould of a martyr. Mr. A B. Imeson plays the exacting role of the curate with rare force, but it struck U 3 that his mien did not always accord with hie boldness of spirit. There was a whispering humble- ness about the outer man —especially in the presence of the local magnates—which hardly sug- gested the indomitable purpose within. The man had to be trodden on before one discovered the metal of which he was made. As Rachael Neve, an equally trying part fell to the lot of Miss Gladys Harvey, who played with an almost perfect assumption of sweetness and innocence. She was unmistakably the sinned against and not the sinner, and as such won all hearts except the stony ones of the society people who dreaded the breath of scandal. A brilliant piece of acting was that of Miss kmy Ravense,roft, as Mrs. Wilmore, the ambitious mother who would save her son at any cost. Her moral tussles with the curate were splendid, and her final surrender to cir- cumstances and an inner consciousness of right was I artistically pourtrayed. Mr. Cecil Brooking's study of the part of the sanctimonious, comfort-loving vicar was equally good in its way, while Mr. Alfred S. Barber cleverly illustrated the mental struggles caused the elastic conscience and_ the loudly-expressed principles of the over-bearing Mr. Wilmore. Mr. Charles Harley as Mr. Viveash, the family lawyer, was wonderfully realistic iii all he did and said. The bulk of the humour was provided by Mrs. Blaney (Miss Florence Steventon) who made an admirable parish busy-body, and 11r. Hanworth Browning as Dr. Blaney also did excellently. Leonard Wilmore, the erring son, was well-played by Mr. King Fordhana, who specially distinguished himself in the striking denouement of Act 3. Miss Gladys Purnel made an attractive Helen Plugenet, and minor parts were taken with a level degree of all round merit by Miss Madge Severne (Mrs. Linnell), Mr. Sydney Hamilton (Sir John Plugenet), Mr. Douglas Jefferies (Goodyer) and Miss Violet Harley (ratty). NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. Next week we are to have a welcome return visit from Mr. John Leopold's company, including the world-famed original Leopoldo, in the farcical musical absurdity entitled " New Frivolity." There will be new and elaborate scenery, up-to-date songs and pretty dresses, a troupe of lady dancers, and grand Roman statuary pictures, making one of the greatest attractions on the road. " New Frivolity will be preceded each evening by the Leopold's latest produc- tion " The Houseboat."

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football.

By " Ovalist." Saturday was a gloriously fine day ; brilliast sun- shine filled the air, the blue canopy of heaven glittered cloudlessly above, and yet in the course of the after- noon there was experienced all the effects of a crushing thunderbolt at Wildersoool. Ths storm-centre seemed to be at Widnes, only 'half-a-dozen miles away, but the full force of the cataclysm was felt at Warrington. Thirteen hither to-believed hardy and experienced footballers were completely annihilated. In fact so serious was the disaster that the local football club was unable to select a team at its meeting on Monday night, and had to postpone matters until some of the scattered remnants could be got together again. I need hardly say that the local supporters of the Club left the neighbourhood of the tragedy about 5 o'clock on Saturday with the aspect and mien of men bereft of all that they held most dear. 'Twas indeed a heartrending visitation. It may perhaps have dawned upon my readers by now that I am referring as sympathetically as possible to the unexpected defeat sustained by Warrington on their own ground at the hands of Widnes—the despised and rejected of men who follow football with a keenness unknown in the other and lesser pursuits of life. That Widnes should win at Warrington seemed I much less likely than that Count Zeppelin or one of the 1 Wright Brothers should aeroplane overhead and throw 1 bombs unkindly among the crowd. It is safe to say that the most dolorous of Warringtonians never expected anything of the kind—though 'tis true we have met certain prescient individuals who profess to have " backed" Widnes with a confidence born of second-sight or that special kind of folly which seems to be rewarded more substantially than the pro- foundest wisdom. Anyhow, Widnes brought an inexperienced but youthful and enthusiastic team, which refused to be made sport of by the Warrington " cracks" (?) and actually had the effrontery to earn and carry off the precious points which count in three Leagues. Woe is me, for being a Warriugtonian.

Really, I am not sorry—now. It takes an earth- quake to open men's eyes occasionally, and the shock 1 of Saturday has left them staring, but with a con- viction which probably nothing else would have brought about. The fact about which there is no doubt is that old-age has suddenly laid its heavy mantle on the shoulders of the balk of the Warrington players, and they are unable to carry it with any show of sprightliness. LTp to Saturday we looked upon them as experienced players ; now we know that most of them are merely time-worn veterans whose hour has come to quit the arena. It was nothing but the youth and energy of the Widnes men which brought about Warrington's downfall. I dare say the old cleverness was there, but the men were not given time to display it. The speedier movements of the Widnesians disarranged the favourite schemes, and 11 after eighty minutes play Warrington were reduced to the level of an impotent horde of punters and tacklers. No one would have recognised in them the team which, alone among Lancashire clubs, has twice won the Northern Union cup.

--- Of course, allowance must be made for the fact that men like Thomas, Shugars, F. Jenkins and J. Jenkins have not yet been available. Their presence on Saturday would, I have no doubt, have brought about a different result. They are not a team in themselves but their absence proved, as nothing else would have done, that the stalwarts of former seasons are only fit for the shelf. There were not more than half-a-dozen of the Warrington players on Saturday who gave any evidence of being fit and capable of going through the arduous campaign with which the club is faced. The farwards were completely outclassed by a lighter but younger pack, with the result that the whole team was practically helpless. Ouly once in the second half did Warrington pass the Widnes quarter line —an eloquent testimony to the weakness of the thirteen as a com- bination. It is a question whether, on the run of the play, they were ever so badly beaten at Warrington. The fact that the score was only 8 points to sis nothing to go by.

New blood is more urgently required now than it has been for a long time. The result of the Widnes match proves that some of the men who were thought good for another season or two are already a long way past their best. Dickenson, Taylor, Brooks, Lloyd and P. Boardman are about the only ones of Saturday's thirteen who can be expected to give much service in first-class football. With these five and the Welsh quartette available there is the nucleus of a sound thirteen, but others are wanted to fill the gaps. The new threequarter, Harries, did not give the impression on Saturday that he is likely to be of much use yet awhile, if at all. "A " team practice may develop him, but he is a long way from first-class yet. Even Fish must be numbered with the old stock on Saturday's form, brit I am convinced he can yet hold his own with the best, if he tries. On Saturday he was not a trier—in fact Brooks and Taylor were the only two who played up to form. The others had to play second fiddle to the Widnes lads, who could boast of little cleverness, but plenty of keenness. I know the Committee are alive to the demands of the situation. Let us hope they will prove capable of coping with it.

The selection of the team to go to Swinton to-day shows that considerable trouble has been taken to make the best of the resources at hand. A member of the Committee has been to South Wales this wkek and returned with the two Jenkins, of whom the half- back seems in capital trim and is down to partner Brooks to-day. The forward has to be tested by a i knee specialist before he can play. Shugars s expected in a week or so, while -Thomas can come when he moderates his demands, otherwise be is likely to be left in Wales. Several changes are made from last week, and a number of the young "A " teamers are getting the chance of their lives to earn promotion land prize-money.
The team is Tilley, full back ; Fish, Dicken son, Cartwright and Jordan, threequarters ; Jenkins and Brooks, half-backs ; A. Boardman, P. Boardman, Naylor, Belton, Hewitt and Chester, forwards.

Last season Warrington made mincemeat of S winton both at home and away, the Blues not registering a solitary pint in either game, against 51 compiled by Warrington. It will be no walk-over to-day, for Swinton have a young side which seems to be settling down into a workable organisation —to witness the defeat of Broughton last Saturday. The Swinton Lion will doubtless be licking his lips in anticipation of a meal off Warrington,but he may be disappointed. A battle royal should be seen, with little margin either way. I have more confidence in Warrington's thirteen for to-day than those of last week.

The " A " team will be at home to Wigaa Highfield with the following side: Mclntyre, full-back, Landor, Oakes, Daintith, and Harries, three-quarters; Lloyd and Smithson, half-backs; Harmer, Foster, Fairhurst, Bradshaw, Purslow and Harrison, forwards. The new men include Harrison and Oakes (local), and Smithson (a half-back from the land of the Leek).

Every effort is being put forth to secure players with acknowledged reputations, and tho team will probably be strengthened before long. A couple of men of international class are willing to sign when jobs can be found for them. Local employers who take an interest in the Club are invited to assist as far as lies in their p3wer.

The Northern League matches for to-day are : Swinton v Warrington Hunslet v Batley Barrow v Leeds Dewsbury v Hull Kingston Rover 3 Keighley v Bramlev Bradford v Wakefield Halifax v Broughton Rochdale v Huddersfield Hull v York Salford v Wigan _ Widnes v Oldham Merthyr v Barrow Leigh v Runcorn St. Helens v Aberdare Mid Rhondda v Treherbert Vet-040.7'. The first county trial match of the season will take place at Broughton on Monday. The teams will be found under Football" on another page. Warring- j ton can boast of only one selection for either of the ; picked teams, Brooks partnering J. Thomas at half- ; back for the Possibles. The Probables pair are i Jolley and White. One item of interest is the appear- , ance of G. W. Smith and L. B. Todd (the New Zealanders) at centre for the Possibles.

div.head: MR. A. H. GROSFIELD, M.P. As President of the Swiss Golf Association.
div.p: MR. A. H. GROSFIELD, M.P. As President of the Swiss Golf Association.
Tne following i 3 from the current issue of the " World" :

" It is generally acknowledged, by those who have the right to an opinion on the subject, that Montana is one of the best golfing places in the world. The pest week has seen the autumn meeting, and the players have included the President of the Swiss Golf Associa- tion, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, and his charming wife, who came down from the Kuhn, St. Moritz, via the Maloje Pass, and stayed at the Grand Bretagne, Bellagio. Visiting the Lake of Como Dervio links, Mr. Crosfield found them an attractive nine-hole course is excellent condition. Crossing over the lake to the Caclenabbia and Menaggio course at Croce, Mr. Crosfielcl was delighted with the situation of the links, which are capable of development into a very fine course. The hon. secretary of the Swiss Golf Association Mr. S. LT. March, was also there. Mr. M. S. de Montmorency and Captain H. M. Janes represented the Lucerne Golf Club. On Wednesday Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield gave a dinner party at the Palace, their guests being Baron and Baroness Heine-Geldern, Mr. and Mrs. Astburv, Mr. Morris Post, and Mr. S. H. March. On Thursday Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield left by the /axe, which stops at Sierre to pick up Montana passengers, for Paris and London. At Sierre is the charming Hotel Chateau Bellevue, where have been staying for a few days on their way down from Montana Mr. T. P. O'Connor (who later went on via the Simplon to Italy), Colonel and Mrs. Kinnaird, and Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Davey, as well as the English chaplain and Mrs. Messiah. Sierre is situated in the most sheltered spot of the Rhone Valley, and is a favourite winter resort as well as the starting-point for Zinal and Montana, being in the heart of the wine country. Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield reached London last week- end, and have since been staying at Gullane, North Britain.

div.head: LOCAL THEATRES SOLD. AUGTIONECRI-EULOGY OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: LOCAL THEATRES SOLD. AUGTIONECRI-EULOGY OF WARRINGTON.

A sale by auction of great interest to Warrington people was conducted at the Albion Hotel, Manchester, on Tuesday afternoon, by Mr. W. H. Robinson, the properties offered being the Royal Court Theatre, Rylands-street, and the Royal Theatre of Varieties, Scotland-road, Warrington. The sale was occasioned by dissolution of partnership. There was a fair attend. ance, which included Mr. William Johnson (one of the proprietors of the theatres), Mr. Frank Macnaughten (managing director of the Warrington Palace and Hippodrome), Mr. Bradbury (resident manager), Mr. J. R. Williams, accoantant, Sankey-street, Warrington, and Mr. McLeod Loader, of St. Helens, resident manager of the St. Helens Theatre. The Royal Court Theatre was first offered for sale. The site contains 965 square yards, and has a frontage of 33 yards to Rylands-street. The property is lease- hold and is up-to-date, having been built last year from plans prepared by Mr. F. Bennett Smith, F.R.1.8.A. Mr. Robinson, in his printed particulars said : "The theatre is thoroughly equipped for the most elaborate dramatic and stage representations ; is fully licensed, and contains, besides the usual auditorium with circle and gallery, two bars, ten splendid dressing rooms (heated), three property rooms, engine room containing gas engine (National, 1907), and complete electrical plant, and four extra rooms under the stage. The theatre is beautifully decorated, is brilliantly lighted by electricity generated on the premises (duplicated by a complete system of gas lighting throughout) and is heated by hot water, well ventilated, and capable of accommodating 1,300 persons." The conditions of sale having been read, Mr. Williams asked for a few figures as to the profits which had been made by the theatre. He had never seen any figures. What were the takings for the last five years? The Auctioneer : I am not here to answer conun- drums. (Laughter.) I am prepared to sell the two properties. Mr. Williams: Oh ! is it a conundrum ? (More laughter.) The Auctioneer: One man can make a profit out of a theatre while another would make a loss. It is really immaterial what has gone past. You are here to buy and you want to damage the sale by asking questions. Mr. Williams : Pardon me, but I wish to do nothing of the kind. You must know that people won't buy a pig in a poke'? The Auctioner : These (the theatres) are very sub- stantial pigs if I may use your simile. Mr. Williams : If you won't give figures we are all at sea. The Auctioneer : I don't think you are so much at sea as you would lead me to suppose. So far as valua- tions are concerned, you can get valuations and valua- tions, but we are not here to listen to a lecture. lam the only professional talker—(laughter)—on the present occasion. I cannot permit you to make a speech. I am so accustomed to moves of this character that they don't vex me. Mr. Williams : If your decision is final get on with the sale. (Laughter). The Auctioneer said it might be asked "Why sell a good thing or part with a gold mine ? " The reason for selling these good things (the theatres) was owing to the serions illness of one of the partners (Mr. Joseph Potter) and with a view to enable him to arrange his financial matters which was only natural having regard to his present condition. He was bed-ridden, and, like a wise man, wanted to realize the properties. The auctioneer added that both the theatres were within a few yards of the main streets of the town. The ques- tion of population entered very largely into the value of the property of the class they were about to sell. The inhabitants numbered over 0,000, but there was also a large population within easy tramway rides. Warrington was one of the towns that was exceptionally well favoured by nature for commercial and manufac- turing purposes ; in fact be knew no town equal to it in many respects. It was connected by waterways which went direct to the sea, it was near to the great Lancashire coalfields and the Cheshire salt mines, and these circumstances gave the town a value for manu- facturing purposes that not equalled by any other town in the kingdom. It also lay half-way between Man- chester and Liverpool, and there were dense populations to feed the two theatres. The bidding started at £lO,OOO, and the subseqctent offers were £ll,OOO, £11,500, £12,000, £13,000 and £13,250. The Auctioneer, after a short interval to enable bidders "to think the matter over," said the property was well worth £20,000. When the sale was resumed it was found that no further offer was forthcoming, and the theatre was knocked down for £13,250 to Mr. Joseph Beecham, of St. Helens who, it was stated, is interested in the St. Helens Opera House. The purchaser has to take over all the bookings from the date of the completion of the purchase. ' The Royal Theatro of varieties was then offered. The auctioneer's particulars read:—" This lot is freehold of ! inheritance and free from chief rent. The theatre has a dramatic licence. It was built in 1883, re-seated and , decorated in 1907 by Messrs. Dean, of Birmingham, and , contains pit and pit stalls, centre circle and side circles. During the past four-and-a-half years it has been run with great success on the two-houses-a-night system. The existing bookings do not extend beyond the date to be fixed for the completion of the purchase." The first bid was £1,500 and the last £2,000 and the Auctioneer announced that the lot would be withdrawn. if anyone wanted to buy it he could see Mr. Hart, the solicitor. Mr. Williams: May I ask another question? The Auctioneer: Certainly not. We understand that this theatre was subsequently sold by private treaty to Mr. Harry Carver, of Eccles.

div.head: Fiddlers Ferry Sailing Club.
div.p: Fiddlers Ferry Sailing Club.

The last race of the season was sailed over a 21 mile course to New Ferry last Saturday in a fine north-westerly breeze. The following six boats started :—lone (Thompson and Knowles) scratch, Maggie (S. Meacock) scratch, Nellie (H. Burthem) scratch, Nina (J. Whittaker) Bmins., Seagull (Rustage and Chadwick) Gimins. and Thelma (H. Warburton) 19mins. There was a capital start, only one minute separating first and last boats over the line. This I was one of the most interesting races the Ferry Club ' have had this season, and resulted in a victory for lone, who finished 4} minutes in front of Maggie. On ! the handicap times, the result of the race lone; 2nd, Nina; 3rd, Thelma.

div.head: WATER POLO.
div.p: WATER POLO.
WARRINGTON y. CHEST,

These teams met before a large attendance at the Corporation Baths, Legh-street, on Thursday evening. The teams were :—Warrington : Woods ; W.Sntton, S. Walker; W. Ashton; T. Pemberton, R. Allen and C. Turner. Chester : Cain ' • E. Edwards, E. Heylin, Williams' Edwards, Dutton and Reed. In the first half Chester were called upon to defend the deep end, and after a few minutes of exciting play Turner opened the score for the home team. After Ashton had made a futile attempt at goal, Turner again added to the score. Pemberton after a bit of good play notched a third goal, and W. Ashton a fourth. Half-time score : —Warrington, 4 goals ; Chester, nil. In the second half Warrington again pressed, and aided by Ashton, Turner , again scored. Pemberton incr2ased the score too, and immediately after the eighth goal was aided by Allen. The final result was :—Warrington, 8 goals ; Chester, nil. Squadron races also took place in connection with the semi-final for the Greenall Challenge Shield. The first on the list was Whitecross v. Co-operative Stores; the latter winning by a length. The second was Cor- poration v. Crosfield's ; the Soapery team being , successful by half a length. The Post Office defeated 1 T. Allen and Son by half a length.

Highway Assault. A young man named Richard Leather, of Booths llill,Lymm, was journeying to his work early yesterday morning, and when approaching the canal bridge on Warrington-road he was set upon by two men who appeared to be tramps. After severely assaulting him they snatched his watch and decamped. Leather was badly kicked about the body, and on arrival at home he was obliged to go to bed. PROVISIONS ARE DEARRR.—Advt,

div.head: WINDOW CLEANER'S DEATH.
div.p: WINDOW CLEANER'S DEATH.

A Fatal Fall. On Monday Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, opened an inquest at the Police Court on the body of William Durban Gibbons, a single man, 30 years of age, who lived at 1, Wakeneld-street, Warrington. Mr. Steel appeared for the relatives and Mr. Longland for the Warrington Window Cleaning Company. John Ernest Gibbons stated that ho and the deceased were window cleaners in the service of the Warrington Window Cleaning Company. Witness was working at Stockton Heath at the house of Messrs. Hayes Brothers, bakers, Stockton Heath on Tuesday morning .and his brother was with him. Witness was engaged in cleaning the front part of the house and the deceased went to the back part, and two minutes afterwards Mrs. Hayes told him that a man had fallen through the skylight at the back of the premises. Witness at once ran to the spot and found that two young men from the Spade Works were carrying deceased into the washhouse. He asked his brother how he had hurt himself when he fell, and he said "I have not fell."—One of the nurses from the Infirmary stated that death took place at 2.50 a.m. that morning. She did not know what the cause of death was.—The Coroner said he had no evidence of the- cause of death, and the nurse could not tell him. The man had only died that morning. It was ultimately decided to adjourn the inquest, the doctor in the meantime to make a post-mortem examination of the body of the deceased. 'The adjourned inquest was held at the Police Station on Thursday when Dr. Smith gave the result of the post modern examination. He stated that death was due to a fractured skull and laceration of the brain caused by the accident. A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned.

div.head: County Revision Courts
div.p: County Revision Courts

Mr. Clement Elphi-nstone Lloyd, revising barrister, attended at Grappenhall and Stockton Heath on Thurs- day and at Daresbury yesterday for the purpose of revising the voters' lists. There were no cases of public interest. Mr. Joseph Smith represented the Liberals and Mr. G. Duckworth and Mr. J. H. Dean the Conservatives. At Grappenhall reference was , made to an important alteration which has 1-' just been sanctioned, by which Latchford ownership .' voters will record their votes at Stockton Heath instead of at G-rappenhall. The Liberal and Con- servative agents intend petitioning the County Council ' during the coming year to allow the occupation voters in the Wilderspool portion of the borough of Warrington to vote at Stockton Heath.

Local Choirs at New Brighton. To-day, the eighth annual challenge Musical Eisteddfod will be held at New Brighton Tower, and as usual with this yearly tournament of song the num- ber of contestants is very large and promises a day of music to all who journey to the tower, as is seldom enjoyed by music lovers. The management offers numerous prizes both in cash, and of gold and silver medals, and in addition for choral competitions the massive New Brighton Silver Challenge Shield,which is valued at sixty guineas. Last year this shield was won , by the Colne Valley Choral Union,which same organiza- tion was the first to enter for the present contest, and i. confidently expects to succeed in once more - attaching this emblem of excellence in choral singing. ' The individual competitors number about 250, while . - the following choirs and choral societies have entered ' for the many contests : —Colne Valley, Talke,, Southport, St. Helens, Habergham, Hindley, Warring- .. r ton, Goodshaw, Wigan, Nelson, Sutton (St. Helene Junction), Present, Rhos (Ruabon) and Liverpool. ; The adjudicators will be Messrs. Roland lingers, Mus. Doc. (Oxon) ; Dan. Price ; Harry Evans and J. James - Hewson. Madame Maggie Evans and Miss Millicent Richards will act as accompanists.

Mr. lILLEv said exception was taken to certain questions and in ccnseinence a sub-committee of the Distress Committee drew up a scheme by which it was no longer necessary to answer objectionable questions Only a few necessary ones ware asked. The resolution was carried. It was further decided that the Secretary take steps to ascertain the information mentioned in the Right to Work Committee's letter and forward it to that Committee. The question of promoting a dommstration was referred to the L'xecutive Cammitee, TILE OFFICALS. The following were nominated for the various offices of the Council :—President, Messrs. Moorfleld, Delaney, Owen and Richardson ; vice-presidents, Messrs. Moor- field, Delaney, Owen, Seed, Elaley ; trer.surar, Mr. Howliston ; secretary, Mr. E. Plinston ; Executive Committee Messrs. Darbyshire, Haley, Moorfield, Plumb, Delaney, Owen, Podruore, Ellison and J. H. Jones. The election will take place at the annual naeeting in October. Messrs. Leach and Bullock were elected auditors. OLD-ACE PENSIONS. Mr. PLINSTON stated that the Town Council had constituted itself the Old Age Pensions Committee fur Warrington, and he thought that a re.olution should be passed asking for representation upon that body. After SOMA discussion, it was decided that the Council ask for representation. On the proposition of Mr. PODNIORE, it was decided that six members of the I.L.P.and Trades Council should form a Committee to meet in the I.L.P. Rooms one night a week to give information on the subject to intending applicants for pensions. Messrs. Plinston Plumb and Leach were elected to represent the Trades Council.
